content: laughed aloud at his silliness, at the barrier, at the sky and the trees and the brush. When his mirth settled, he lay on the loamy forest floor, staring up at the blue and brown and green overhead until a mouse scuttled up beside him, sniffed at his ear. He turned his head. “Hello, little one.” The creature’s whiskers vibrated; it squeaked twice, then scurried away into the thicket. He didn’t understand the rodent—he found the ones with the smallest heads most difficult to decipher—but it seemed important, so he climbed to his feet and followed. The tiny fellow headed straight for the green wall, then went scampering along the base, its passing denoted by the shiver of leaves and the pad of miniscule paws. It paused occasionally, waiting to make sure he kept up. As he chased after it, he let his fingertips glide over the expanse of the shimmering barrier, his touch sending streaks crackling over its surface. To him, it felt both pliable and resistant, as though he dragged his fingers across the surface of a shallow puddle, like the tips sank in ever so slightly, but didn’t go through. Nothing can get through. Or over. So says Sky. The mouse kept going, its tiny legs working furiously as it ran over flat patches, leapt errant pinecones and fallen twigs. The pursuer stifled a giggle at how adorable the small fellow looked with his dark bubble eyes and furry tail. As he followed, he took his hand away from the wall and let his gaze stray to the area on the other side. The translucent green boundary warped things, twisting everything out of focus and painting the world in emerald and chartreuse, but what had happened to the land after they raised the barrier stood out stark and obvious. Blackened ground stretched from the base of the wall to the top of the distant hill where trees began again, the nearest ones charred and bare of needles or leaves. Other than a few burnt tree trunks, the fireballs had cleared the area of the metal men who’d chased them and everything else, too. Losing the trees saddened him and he slowed his pace without realizing, looking at their scorched remains and entertaining the grief in his heart. What beauty they brought to the world, what loveliness they contributed to life. A manic series of squeaks returned him to the here and now, and he halted, half a step from where the mouse had stopped. Any farther and he might have crushed the poor thing under his foot. “I sorry, little one,” he said, crouching. He held his hand out in apology and the tiny rodent sniffed his fingertip, nose wiggling against his skin. It looked up at him and squeaked once more before scurrying off into the forest. “Are we done?”

He stood, watching the minuscule shake of leaves at the mouse’s passing. The mouse darted behind a tree, gone from his sight, and he lost its path after that. He drew a deep sigh in through his lips, sad for losing the company. Maybe he’d try to find his friend, Raven; the sun’s height above the horizon suggested enough time, but where to look? He faced the wall again and the figure standing adjacent his position startled him, making him jump back, feet scuffling in the undergrowth. The silhouette on the other side of the barrier stood rigid, staring at him. Eyes narrowed to slits, he moved closer, staying an arm’s length away from the shimmering green veil. He couldn’t tell if the person was male or female, despite its lack of clothing. Fire had burned everything off the body—hair, nose and lips, skin. Peering through the jade sheen, the flesh appeared brown, though he suspected it might appear red if he saw it through a clear lens, perhaps black in places. Only the eyes remained unscathed. They appraised him with a softness he thought suggested this was woman. “What happened to you?” he whispered and inched closer. A sheet of skin, charred at the edge, had peeled away from her chest; blisters—some whole and others burst—covered her arms and legs. A hole burned through her right cheek flexed and stretched as she pulled apart her lips with a crackle of burnt flesh. The sound she made would have been more expected from a forest animal, though he’d have had a better chance of understanding one of them if it had a head as big as hers. A croak, a gurgle, a hard breath, a squeak. If what came from her mouth followed any pattern or possessed meaning, he didn’t understand. He edged closer, leaned toward her. Her eyes followed, but she remained unmoving. “Need help?” He paused, swallowed. “I do anything for you?” The woman lifted her arm, skin crackling again with the action, and he jumped away despite the safety afforded by the green veil. They’d made it to keep them safe, to hold others out. He’d touched the surface himself and experienced its solidity, but the movement startled him, nonetheless. He shook his head at his nervous reaction and his fast-beating heart. “You scare I.” He settled and watched as the woman reached up and took the edge of the flap of skin hanging from her chest between her thumb and finger. Her eyes remained locked on his as she pulled, peeling it away from her body in one long sheet; he gritted his teeth and sucked air between them, imagining the pain doing such a thing must cause her. If it gave her any, she made no sign. When it reached her waist, she jerked her arm to the side, tearing

the piece of flesh free, the freshly exposed muscles of her torso glistening. She took the top in both hands then, working her wrists, twisted it into a tube. He shook his head, not believing what he saw. His forehead creased, and tears for her threatened at the corners of his eyes. “What you do?” She didn’t respond with words; they both realized he wouldn’t understand. Instead, she moved her arm forward. The rolled-up sheet touched the green partition, then passed through. He jumped again, legs tensed and ready to run, compassion for her all but forgotten. Her hand penetrated the barrier to the middle of her forearm. He readied himself to bolt, but she stopped, hand, wrist, and tube of skin on his side of the curtain. As he’d suspected, the flesh on her fingers and the rest of her protruding through was red and scaled from extreme heat, as though she’d plunged her fist into a bonfire, held it in the flames too long. But the same wasn’t true of the roll she gripped—tan, yellowing at the edges, not skin-like at all. He looked from her offering to her face; she stared, her gaze not having moved the width of one of the mouse’s whiskers the entire time. He sensed pain in them, but not a physical suffering, despite her appearance. Something deeper, worse, a wound beyond healing. Not knowing what else to do, he hopped forward, snatched the roll from her hand, and scuffled away. He stared at it, rolled it between his fingertips. As he’d thought, it wasn’t made of skin. It was smooth but rough, its edge uneven with fibers, warm to the touch. He’d heard of parchment before, but had never touched or seen any. He believed this might be the genuine thing. With great care, he held the top end in one hand while using the fingers of the other to unroll it. Strange, curved shapes wound their way across its surface. He’d experienced nothing like them before, didn’t understand what to do about them, so he lowered the scroll and peered over top of it toward the veil. “What do…?” The burnt woman no longer stood on the other side of the barrier. Gone. Alone. He released the bottom of the parchment; it rolled itself up with no prompting. Two steps forward and his nose brushed the green curtain, a stick of lightning flashing across the surface where he touched it. “Where you go?” He stepped away, looked at the roll gripped in his hand, then up at the sky, darkening around its edges while he’d engaged with the woman for a much longer time than he’d thought. His heart jumped— he needed to get home before dark. Without a consideration to where it came from, he put the scroll to his lips and cushioned it between his

teeth, then got down on hands and knees and bound off through the brush. He didn’t know his new home yet as well as he would but he always sensed where to locate the others. He leapt over logs and dashed around dense thickets, his animal-like strides eating up distance faster than he could have run on two feet. Each time his hands touched the ground, he took care not to let the impact jar him into clamping his mouth on his precious cargo. Might not harm it to wear an impression of his teeth, but better to not have to find out. He didn’t recognize the shapes it bore, but he knew someone could decipher them. A direct path, much straighter than he’d taken to get to where he met the woman, got him home to the rest as the sun’s bottom edge disappeared below the rim of the distant sea. Upon arriving at the clearing, he stood, took the scroll from his mouth, and glided past the others who tried to talk to him as he passed. He wanted to stop and tell them of his adventure, but it would have to wait until he delivered his cargo where it needed to go. He found Sky right where he expected, sitting on the stump near where the firemakers were building the night’s bonfire. She raised her head from her conversation with Twig who sat on the ground at her feet, and her expression brightened at seeing him. “Back again, young one. Sky is happy to see you.” Twig moved aside as he marched up to her and held the scroll out in front of him. She stared at the offering, then peered past at his face, a puzzled look crossing her brow. “What have you brought Sky?” He shrugged and pushed his hand nearer to her, urging her to take the suspected parchment from him. She hesitated for the space of two heartbeats, then reached out and clasped it with a nod. He lowered his arm and waited, expectant. Sky pursed her lips, turned the roll over in her fingers, regarding it from all sides. Satisfied, she grasped the top between the index finger and thumb of her right hand and unrolled the full length with her other. By her feet, Twig stretched his neck, trying to get a peek at what the paper held. When he couldn’t, he settled in, resting his chin on his knee and watching. Sky looked at the document, tilted her head first one way, then the other, the crease made by puzzlement remaining on her brow. After a moment, realization dawned, and she flipped the parchment around; she cleared her throat. “It rained fire the day the Small Gods fled.” Twig stretched closer, but she read no more. Instead, she lowered the page, releasing it from one hand and letting it roll up. Sky looked at the youth standing in front of her and nodded.

“You have done well today,” she said, a warm smile spreading across her lips. “Thorn has done well.” He couldn’t stop his own grin from turning up the corners of his mouth, but didn’t want to anyway. Energy and delight filled him, making him dance from foot to foot. Sky laughed. “Thorn can go,” Sky said. He spun on one foot and set out away from the stump and the almost-ready bonfire. I have a name, he thought, then corrected himself. Thorn has a name. He hurried across the clearing and made for the edge of the forest, hoping to find his friend Raven before the darkness came to end the day.

I Teryk - Ikkundana The trees to the sides of the dirt track fell away, widening the road enough for eight riders to advance abreast, though the column’s formation did not change. The soldiers of the king’s army rode side by side, their perimeter outlined by warriors of the Goddess. Teryk traveled beside Trenan as brush and forest turned to flatland, an expanse of yellowed grass stretching toward the walled city in the distance. But the field did not lie empty. Near the walls, plain canvas tents stood in straight rows, their washed-out colors in danger of disappearing against the gray fortress wall. Though they weren’t yet close enough to make out any more than the tents themselves, he suspected soldiers moved amongst those structures. But to whose army did they belong? He considered asking Trenan, but the master swordsman’s attention flickered from side to side. Sometimes, he jerked in his saddle, as though startled by things he alone saw. He grunted once in a while, guttural sounds emanating from deep in his throat. Despite his gaze jumping around between so many things, he rarely appeared to focus on things near him. “It’s good you’ve recovered, my prince.” His stomach knotted at the undeserved title as the rider ahead of them had slowed to ride beside him. Teryk looked across at the man— a sergeant-at-arms Trenan called Osis. He bit back his response, nodded instead of speaking. “Thank you,” he said, though he wasn’t sure recovered was the word he’d use. Only the night before, the healer and his companion had visited him. Were they even real? And every thought of his sister pained his heart as if the sharp tip of a hot poker prodded it. He sighed. Osis stretched in his saddle, looked past the young man at the soldier riding beside him. Trenan’s gaze may have danced over his subordinate’s, but if he recognized him, he made no indication. His attention darted to the roadside. The sergeant-at-arms leaned closer. “What’s happened to him? I’ve known Trenan a very long time and never experienced him like this.” Teryk shrugged. He’d overheard the master swordsman mumbling about ghosts and dead men sent to haunt him. He’d even seen them himself once, but he found it difficult to believe the souls of the deceased returned to besiege the living. And he certainly wouldn’t suggest such a thing to Osis. Doing so would make him appear as crazy as he likely now considered Trenan. “The black priests have made him sick,” Teryk replied, though he knew of no sickness capable of bringing ghosts to haunt a man. “This

place might be the best place for him.” The sergeant grunted. “This isn’t a place for any of us. Naught here but death.” The former prince suppressed a shudder. He knew nothing of Ikkundana except for its other name: the City of the Sick. But if the Goddess worshipers brought their ill and dying here, wouldn’t they have physicians, surgeons, and doctors? Could her followers bring the dead to life, as the black-robed healer claimed? Is this where he is from? His eyes widened, and he stared straight ahead at the distant walls. He’d never heard of a man serving the Goddess, but his lack of knowledge didn’t mean such a person didn’t exist. But what he’d seen the healer do went against what he perceived of the women. He understood them to stand for life and peace; perhaps that was a front to distract the outside world from their true intentions—they were a secretive order. Osis spoke but, distracted by his thoughts and a rising angst, Teryk didn’t catch what he said. “What?” “I asked what you think turned Trenan traitor to the king. You know him better than I do.” The question surprised him and Teryk faced the man riding beside him. The sergeant wore an expression suggesting more lurked behind his words than what appeared. You know him better than I do. Did he suspect the truth of their relationship? Did Trenan tell him? He didn’t imagine he’d risk the queen’s reputation, but strange things happened in these times. Perhaps he and Osis were closer than Teryk realized. “He is no traitor.” “And yet he rides with the enemy.” “He may not be himself, but he’d never turn on the…my father.” He swallowed hard, wondered if the sergeant-at-arms noticed the pause. “He’s sworn his life to the kingdom.” Osis leaned over in his saddle, lowered his voice. “Then why does he appear so at ease with these—” his gaze flitted to the riders around them, “—women?” “He told me nothing of them. We had no opportunity for conversation.” Teryk’s mind flashed through the time since Trenan showed up at the Green. First, he hadn’t known himself, then rage had consumed him, and finally he’d been paralyzed by something done to him by the healer. “More is happening here than either of us understand. Perhaps you should ask him.” “He is in no state to respond.”

“Then maybe her.” He tilted his head toward the front of the column where the leader of the women soldiers rode. He didn’t remember her name, but he’d seen her speak with Trenan several times. She must be the reason for his willingness to ride with them. She sat her mount with the straight back and confidence of someone who’d spent much of their life in the saddle, which made Teryk wonder. The kingdom perceived the followers of the Goddess as farmers, gardeners, craftswomen. In his memory, he’d never seen one of their order sitting a horse, and now dozens of them rode nearby. And is this another? Against the backdrop of the yellowed grass, the rider might have been invisible but for the thin cloud of dust kicked up by her horse’s hooves. The steed beat a straight line from the cluster of tents toward their group. The sight of the dirt hanging in the air reminded Teryk of a thirst burning in his throat that he’d forgotten. “What’s this, now?” Osis said. The leader of the women raised her hand, reined her mount to a stop. All those behind her did the same, the action passed down the column like a line of dominoes falling one after another. When it came time for Teryk to halt, he reached across and grabbed the bridle of Trenan’s horse in case demons distracted the master swordsman’s notice. A murmur followed along through the troop, the words spoken by the voices of men. The women sat their horses, holding their ground and their tongues as they waited for what news the rider carried, what orders their leader gave. Teryk squirmed in his saddle, aware of the hard leather pressing against his behind. He stood in his stirrups, both taking the pressure off and to peer past those stopped ahead of him to watch as the messenger approached. The horse was close enough now he recognized the rider as another woman. She closed on the leader of the column, reined her steed in. The two women leaned toward each other, too distant for him to hear what they spoke to each other; the murmuring of the men wondering what transpired drowned out their words, anyway. They didn’t speak for long before the leader coaxed her mare about and urged it down the column. Both male and female riders alike moved aside before her, clearing a passage. Her gaze appeared to rest on Teryk as she approached. He swallowed around a lump rising in his throat and sat down on his saddle with a thump. When she arrived, he realized he needn’t have worried—it wasn’t him she’d been eying. She pulled up in front of Trenan and surveyed him up and down. “The war is here,” she said, speaking loud enough for everyone to take notice. “It is time to fight.”

Teryk looked to the master swordsman, awaiting his response, as did the woman. Trenan’s gaze flickered from the side of the column to her, held for a few heartbeats, then withdrew again. “They’re everywhere.” His voice sounded little more than a whisper. “Don’t let them take me. It isn’t my fault.” The woman’s expression hardened. She pressed her mount nearer to his, reached out with her left hand to grab the edge of his chest piece. She pulled him toward her, then slapped him across the face with her other palm. The crack of flesh on flesh rang amongst the riders, and Teryk glimpsed from the corner of his eye as Osis clutched for a sword absent from its accustomed spot. Trenan blinked and redirected his gaze to her, but showed little other reaction. “Do you understand me? The time has come. We need you.” His eyelids fluttered open and closed a few more times, then he nodded once. His eyes flickered away and back, away and back. The woman huffed an exasperated breath and released her hold on him, turned to face Osis. “I have no time to explain. The kingdom is at risk and we need your sword arms. Your men will have their weapons returned now and we expect you to fight by our sides.” The sergeant shook his head, but it appeared to be more out of disbelief than disagreement. “What? What are you talking about? Fight who?” The woman’s lips pressed into a colorless white line across her face but her burning gaze didn’t change. It felt to Teryk like the air grew thick around them as they awaited her response. Everyone within earshot leaned toward her. When she replied, he suspected he wasn’t the only one amongst them who wished she hadn’t. “The black priests and their followers,” she said, then she raised her arm, extended a finger. Teryk tilted his head to find out what she pointed at. Two white streaks marred the blue expanse, a yellow ball at the front of each. “And the Small Gods who will fall from the sky.”

II Ishla – Road to Ikkundana For so many turns of the seasons, Ishla’s travels happened in the comforts of a carriage—although instances of travel had been few. She couldn’t recall the last time she’d sat a horse for more than show or pleasure, and not for traveling any distance. It surprised her to find how naturally the mechanics of it returned to her; it didn’t surprise her in the least how much the repetitive bouncing in the saddle hurt her backside. Not long after leaving the city, they’d stopped for her to change into clothes given her by the servants of the Mother of Death. Ishla had slipped into the woods, discarding her expensive frock for a layer of simple cotton and an unadorned gray robe big enough to hide the sword belt and weapon also provided. As she changed, she thought she glimpsed the queen’s guard peeping between the trees. “Strylor?” She froze, awaiting a response, arm crossed over her bare breasts. When none came, she finished dressing and made her way through the tangle of brush and foliage to the road. When she arrived, she found him busying himself with adjusting his saddlebags. She said nothing to him of her suspicions, but she thought how he looked at her after confirmed her misgivings. This memory came to her as they rode in silence, the soldier a horse-length behind her, probably ogling her ass pressed against the saddle. She put the incident aside. What did it matter if he’d seen her bare breasts? Far more important matters required her mind space— Teryk, Trenan, finding out if her daughter yet lived. The lustful stare of an oaf of a queen’s guard meant nothing. She sat straighter, gritted her teeth against the pain in her backside, and concentrated on her riding form. No point for concern over him, or getting herself emotional about the others. They’d arrive at Ikkundana soon. The sun had dipped far enough to fall behind the trees and throw shade across the road. The encroaching darkness reminded her they’d ridden through the previous night without stopping, except for her to change clothes or when meals or bodily function required it. As much as she wanted to reach their destination, she understood both humans and horses needed to rest. She tugged on the reins, slowing her steed, and let Strylor catch up. “Time for a meal, and to find a place to sleep.” The soldier nodded. “We ain’t far from the town of Woodsel. Krin’s tavern makes a delicious bowl of stew.” She didn’t relish being amongst people who might recognize her, but neither did the prospect of bedding down on the ground excite

her, especially with fresh bruises from riding. After so many nights sleeping on the best mattress in the kingdom, any love she’d had for hard surfaces was long gone. “All right,” she said, gesturing with her arm. “Lead the way.” Strylor nodded and urged his horse forward, his eyes remaining on her until he passed. She forced a wan smile, then put heels to her own steed and followed along behind the man. *** He sat on the edge of the thin mattress, stomach full of Krin’s stew, head swimming with thoughts. He’d disliked how the barkeep kept eying the queen while they ate at the table by the fireplace and Strylor drank his pint or two or three of ale. His suspicion provided a favorable happening, though; it caused her majesty to sit closer, even lay her hand on his forearm twice. Not because of him; because of me. He would’ve admitted to anyone to not having the greatest of memories, but certain things stick with a man. For him, he remembered every time Ishla offered him a kind word, a knowing glance, the barest of touches. Perched on the edge of the bed wearing nothing but his underclothes, his ale-prompted brain cataloged each instance. Sometimes she’d acted angry toward him, too, but not so many as he’d seen her have with the king, her husband. He closed his eyes, thought of her fingers on his arm, and excitement stirred in his gut—and lower. It’s why she wanted to stop at the inn. To sleep in comfort… together. But she asked for two rooms, and Krin himself had led them up the stairs to show them where they’d slumber, side-glancing at both of them the entire time. The way he’d looked at them didn’t sit well with the queen’s guard. Did he not think him good enough for a woman of her ilk? What did he know, anyway? A barkeep in a broken-down town. Likely wouldn’t survive if he wasn’t so lucky as to have his tavern sitting right smack on the main road through the kingdom. Jealous, is all. He saw the way she looked at me. How she touched me. He wants her for himself. The thought angered him, but he understood at the same time. Ishla was a comely woman—the most beautiful in Windward. Every man lusted for her, but few got as close as Strylor, and she invited only one to stay overnight at an inn far from Draekfarren and the king’s probing gaze. Probing. A grin tilted his lips and more stirring occurred. He grabbed his crotch, intending to arrest it, but the action prompted the opposite effect. Breath whistled between his teeth, then he released it in a

lengthy sigh and thought of the times he’d entered her chambers to find her in her nightclothes. He recalled every instance of her bumping into him when she came through a door or turned around, pretending to forget his presence right behind her. On more than one occasion, her breasts had touched him. He released his hold on his now half-swollen man thing and stood. His mouth flooded with excited saliva and he licked his lips, eyes darting place to place in the unlit room. He didn’t know how much time had passed since he extinguished the lantern and sat on the bed, but he saw no light shining through the space under his door. Holding his breath, Strylor impersonated a statue, listening, hearing nothing. He took the three steps toward the exit, a board creaking beneath his foot, and grasped the handle, waiting. When no sound came in reaction to his movement, he opened it a crack, put his eye to it and peered into the hallway. When he saw it empty, he pulled it wider, careful to limit the groan of the hinges, and stepped out of the sleeping chamber. Enough moonlight shone thorough the window at the end of the hall to cast shadows, but not sufficient to reveal more than black shapes of doors to other rooms. The stairs to the tavern lay the other direction, and he took one step toward them, eyes straining for any sign of lamp or lantern spilling up the stairway. He saw none. Strylor let out his breath and grabbed his crotch again, like doing so might act as a good luck charm to ward off suspicious looks. No sounds, no movement, no light. He moved another careful pace, gently placing his foot to limit the noise emitted by the ancient wood held together by rusted nails. Two steps along the darkened hall, he stopped. Four doors lined each side of the corridor. He knew Krin had shown the queen a room before his, but which one? The queen’s guard took his hand from his underclothes, scratched his cheek, his odor wafting from his fingers to his nose. Was it on the same wall as his? How far along? Should’ve paid more attention. He hesitated, thought of retreating to his own chamber, but how many more opportunities might exist for him to fulfill his destiny with the queen? They both knew they were meant to be together, if only for a little while. The attraction between them was often palpable, and the way she’d acted tonight confirmed to him she felt the same. Hadn’t she looked at him with an expectant expression when they’d parted? Didn’t she wish him goodnight in the loving, sing-song voice of hers so even the barkeep realized what percolated between them? She had, and he did. Strylor swallowed and nodded to himself, squinted in the dark as

his gaze darted from door to door. Which one? He thought about Krin escorting them up the stairs, recalling which handle he laid his hand on to show the queen her sleeping quarters. The innkeeper had grabbed it with his left, so it must be on the opposite side from Strylor’s own room. Four to choose from instead of eight. He concentrated harder. They’d passed at least one door before stopping, and walked by at least one more before reaching Strylor’s chamber. Down to two. The queen’s guard crept down the hall until he stood between the possibilities, eyes flicking between them. Behind him, someone snored, the sound muffled but not muted by the thin wooden portal. He snickered to himself—definitely not where the queen slept. He doubted the possibility of her delicate mouth’s ability to make a noise like a miller sawing a log. The two doors before him appeared identical. With enough light, he might have identified differences in the wood’s grain or color, but the lack of illumination stole the opportunity. Wouldn’t have helped him at any rate—he’d paid no attention to such things. The queen’s overpowering desire for him had distracted him from everything else. He stared at the door to the right, willing the barrier standing between them to disappear to find out who rested within. It refused to budge, so he tried the same on the one to his left and encountered the same result. Nothing to do but decide for himself, then. Closer to the stairs than to my room. He pursed his lips, nodded to himself, moved his hand from where it had fallen to his crotch again and reached out for the handle. The metal was cool to the touch, perhaps because of the excitement and expectation warming his skin. He lifted the latch, opened it the width of his finger, taking care to limit the squeak of the hinges. They proved quieter than the ones on his door, and he pushed it the rest of the way, then stepped across the threshold and swung it closed behind him. As in his room, a thick curtain shut out any light attempting to creep in through the window and, without the dim moonlight, blackness crowded the space. Strylor stood in place by the door, breath held as he waited for his eyes to grow accustomed to the darkness. He presumed the rooms were laid out the same, but couldn’t be sure, so he delayed until he saw the shape of the bed, the queen’s shapely figure upon it. He paused and listened to her breathing, the gentle in-and-out flow adding to the passion building in his gut, spilling up into his chest to speed his heart, down into his groin to harden his man parts. The warmth in his face made it difficult to hold his own air. He let it out

through his nose little puffs at a time, inhaled again taking in her scent as he did. The outline of the bed formed, the hills and valleys of her figure laid out atop it. She appeared to lie on her side, the peak of her shoulder trailing down to her waist, then rising again in the hips he desired to grasp and pull against himself. He considered finding the lantern, lighting it to gaze upon her, and so they might stare into each other’s eyes while making love for the first time, but he didn’t. If he went searching for it, he’d doubtless knock it over, waking her and spoiling the surprise of his presence. Besides, he carried no flint hidden away in his underclothes, only a different implement ready to light a fire in the queen. He stifled a giggle at the thought and took a tentative step toward the bed. His toe encountered something soft and pliable—her clothes left strewn on the floor in her hurry to disrobe and climb onto the mattress to await his inevitable visit. He smiled and pushed them aside with his foot, moved another pace closer. One more would bring him to her bedside. He paused, relishing the moment. How long he’d waited for this, and now his desire lay an arm’s length away. As he stood, he considered how to proceed. Should he wake her, fall into her arms? Grab her and throw himself on top of her, immediately giving her what she desired? No, he decided on taking it slow, to draw the surprise and enjoyment out as long as possible. Strylor reached out and grasped the edge of the covers, peeled them down slowly and steadily as he took the last step to the bedside. With a portion of the mattress exposed, he put one leg on, then the other, bed frame groaning under his weight, but she didn’t stir. Luckily, Ishla lay pressed to the far side, having left space for him to join her; she must have guessed his plan. He set his head on the corner of the pillow and yanked the blanket up, sidled closer so his chest touched her. He rested his fingers on her torso and snuggled his face into her hair. “Mmm.” He smiled to himself, ran his hand along the curve leading from waist to hip. Not exactly how he expected her to feel, but still good. “Sshhh.” She wiggled her buttocks, and he sighed, pushed himself against her. “Get back to your own room,” she said, the grogginess of sleep slurring her words so she sounded like a different person. “We have to be up so early.” “We have to take the opportunity when we can, your highness.” He pressed his increasing hardness against her, rocked his hips. “Your highness?” She giggled, the laugh gruffer than he’d heard

from her before. “You are a playful one, aren’t you, Krin?” Strylor’s body went stiff as sudden anger flooded him. Krin? The barkeep? This was who the queen expected to join her in her private chamber when she’d broken out from under the thumb of the king? His hand on her hip curled into a fist, gathering her nightshirt and a pinch of flesh beneath it. “Ouch, you’re hurting me.” “Krin, is it? That’s who you want to have in your bed?” Despite the small mattress offering limited space, the queen jerked away, simultaneously turning toward him and pushing against his chest. He maintained his grip on her hip, keeping her from getting too far from him. “Who is that?” she screeched, the sudden and piercing tone hurting his ears. “Krin!” Strylor didn’t realize his mistake until her shrill voice broke the night’s calm. He scrambled away from the barkeep’s wife, feet tangling in the sheets. He spilled out onto the floor, jamming his wrist as he attempted pulling himself away from the now-hysterical woman and extricating himself from the bedclothes tangled up with him. “Get out,” she screamed. “Krin!” He kicked, desperate to untangle his feet from the blankets as a door slammed open somewhere down the corridor and footsteps fell on hall floor. The queen’s guard freed himself, scuffled up to standing. He stumbled to the doorway and reached for the handle as someone on the other side threw it wide. The wood jammed against his hand, bending his fingers back to add to the pain in his wrist. The bulk of Krin, the barkeep, filled the space. “What are you—” “Wrong room,” Strylor said, not waiting for the man to finish his question. He bulled forward, intending to push past him. “He put his hands on me,” the woman cried. The queen’s guard’s shoulder hit the barman in the chest, but Krin proved too big to be moved with such ease. He grabbed Strylor by the shoulders, spinning him around. By then, other doors along the hallway swung open, pale faces poking out to see about the commotion. He spied Ishla’s amongst them, peering at him from the chamber across from the one he’d entered. I didn’t even have the right side. Krin seized him by the front of his bedshirt, yelled into his face: “Get your stuff and get the hell out of my inn. Now!” He shoved him away, and Strylor stumbled along the hall toward his room, barely keeping his feet under him. He blundered against the jamb, the stares of the inn’s other guests raking his skin as he fumbled with the handle. It didn’t open on the first attempt, and the tip of his

nose banged against the wood with the failed effort. The latch released on the second try, and he lurched across the threshold, slamming the door behind him, thankful to find relief from the judging eyes of the others. But relief and thankfulness were short-lived. He’d just sunk his ass down on the bed and discharged a shuddering sigh before the door flew open, booming against the wall. Krin’s shape blocked moonlight from entering with him, but the queen’s guard needed no illumination to know the rage contorting his face. “Gather yer things right now,” he snapped. “If I get to ten and you’re still here—” He didn’t complete the threat—didn’t need to. Strylor eyed his sword but did no more than collect it in his arms the same as he did the rest of his clothes, his boots, and his pack. The big innkeeper stepped aside to let him past, but started following him as soon as he did. The queen’s guard made his way down the hall, doing his best to ignore the man trailing along behind him, counting. “Four…” Strylor’s gaze flickered toward Ishla as he hurried by, her stony expression outlined in the moon's glow. He looked away. What did she think happened? What should he tell Dansil when his friend found out he’d left the queen? What about the king? His bare feet thumped on the wooden stairs as he descended to the stone floor of the tavern, chilly on his soles. “Seven…” He hurried his pace, careful not to jam a toe on a chair leg or stool unnoticed in the darkness as he crossed toward the exit. When he reached it, he attempted to shift his belongings from both hands to one to grasp the handle and throw the portal wide, but he dropped a boot. He bent at the waist to retrieve it, imagining the barkeep’s breath on his neck as he did. While picking up the errant footwear, the door swung open, the edge knocking him in the side of the head—not sufficiently hard to stun him, but with enough force he knew it had hit him with intent. He straightened, boot hanging from his hand, ready to lash out, but the person holding the portal ajar turned out to be someone other than who he thought. “Ten,” Ishla said and waved for him to depart. Strylor glanced over his shoulder at Krin standing a few paces behind them, arms crossed over his barrel chest, his angry expression carved of stone. “And never set your foot in my establishment again.” The queen’s guard left Krin’s tavern, the queen following him out and shutting the door after them.

*** Ishla sat her horse, waiting for her companion to finish clothing himself and saddling his steed. It had been quick and easy to follow him out when she heard the yelling—she’d slept in her clothes, though the word sleep might be a generous description. Now she pursed her lips, holding in any comment threatening at the tip of her tongue. She wished she could have let him go on his own, made her way by herself, as she had wanted to when they left Draekfarren, but she knew the dangers of the road. Despite her misgivings and his shortfalls, he remained a sturdy arm with a sword. The barkeep no longer stood in the doorway watching, but she suspected he lingered by a window, peeking out of the darkness to be sure they departed. He might have had other reasons for spying; he’d kept a close eye on her from the moment they walked in and she wondered the entire time if he’d recognized her. If he did, he said nothing of it. “Hurry along, Strylor.” She resisted the urge to ask him how he ended up in the room, convinced he’d answer with a lie. Given his actions around her since the king had appointed him guard to the queen, she suspected she knew why he’d been in the chamber—because he mistook it for hers. She smiled to herself, thankful the lady of the house had been so accommodating when she asked to switch rooms. She bore some regret the poor woman needed to put up with even a small amount of the oaf’s advances, but it turned out right in the end. As the queen’s guard swung his leg over his horse and settled into the saddle, Ishla hoped for this to be the last she’d have to worry about him acting in such a way. But hope didn’t prevent things from happening. She must endure at least two more sunsets before they reached their destination; two nights of sleep with a dagger close at hand, if she slept at all. If he tried anything again, she’d kill him.

III Teryk – Healer Teryk found it difficult to take his eyes from the sky, even when a woman handed him a short sword. When she offered a weapon to Trenan, the most capable of every man in the kingdom of wielding a blade didn’t notice. He took it for the master swordsman, maneuvered himself around to slide it into the empty sheath hanging from his belt. When he raised his gaze again, the fireballs appeared far closer than he’d expected them to be. “Osis, what…” The sergeant-at-arms was gone. Teryk spied him farther down the column, speaking to each of the male soldiers individually as he made his way toward the rear. Did he rally his troops for a fight against mythical gods from the sky? Perhaps coordinating an attack against the women he’d seen as their captors from the moment they forced them to give up their weapons? The fireballs were close enough to notice the speed with which they moved, gobbling up distance at an incredible rate. At the front, Yoli called many of her warriors together, formed them into a strategic formation. When the balls of fire arrived they would be near their position, but why form up against what may be a hurtling rock? Did she intend to fight an inanimate chunk fallen from the sky? As they closed in, Teryk reached out and grabbed the bridle of Trenan’s horse, ready to steady the animal should it try to bolt. He glanced at his father, watched him raise his gaze to track the progress of the falling stars. “The Small Gods fall,” he whispered. A shiver ran along the young man’s neck at his words. Teryk redirected his attention in time to observe the first of them plummet to the ground. It hit with enough force to shake the earth beneath them. His own horse let out a panicked whinny and tried to rear, but he kept his steed under control. Trenan’s pulled against his grip, but not so hard he couldn’t keep it from escaping. It turned out a smaller mass than Teryk had thought, the glow surrounding it making it appear larger. But the light extinguished when it struck. It skidded across the plain, leaving a shallow trench in its wake. He watched as it rectified from what might have been a small round boulder to something more misshapen, then to a torso with limbs flailing as it tumbled. When it stopped, a naked man lay at the terminus of the furrow. Teryk stared, mouth open, shocked he remained in one piece after slamming into the ground with such force. His surprise increased when the fellow who should have been dead,

rent to bits, climbed to his feet. He stretched like someone waking from a long sleep, then directed his attention toward the phalanx. At the front of the column, Yoli raised her weapon skyward. Nobody moved for a heartbeat, two, then she lowered her arm, pointed the tip of her sword at the naked man. A cry rose and every one of the female warriors jammed heels into horse flanks. The beat of hooves rattled the earth as the women followed their leader. None of the men did. Teryk shifted in his saddle, pivoting to Trenan. “What should we do?” The master swordsman stared straight ahead. If he’d heard his son, he made no sign. The second shooting star impacted, but Teryk wasn’t prepared this time. His horse reared unexpectedly, and he let go his hold on Trenan’s steed to keep from being thrown from his seat. He grabbed the saddle horn, his eyes directed toward the sky before the animal set its front hooves on the ground. He counted four more stars streaking across the firmament. Frightened by the commotion, Trenan’s horse broke away. It galloped straight ahead, following the female warriors, the master swordsman bouncing in the saddle but keeping his seat. Teryk took a moment to settle his mount, glanced over his shoulder; the other men continued doing nothing. “Osis,” he shouted, thrusting a finger toward the sky. He didn’t wait for the solider to react or respond; the former prince prompted his steed forward, giving chase behind the master swordsman. The second falling star skidded to a stop and a man who resembled the first close enough to be mistaken as his twin climbed to his feet. Neither of them wielded axe or sword, yet the sight of both made him want to rein his horse around and flee for the hills. More so as the two naked men broke into a run headed straight for the warriors riding to intercept them. “Trenan!” One of the fallen leaped forward without breaking stride, covering the space between him and his attackers as though launched by a catapult. He slammed into the rider to Yoli’s left, knocking mount and warrior to the ground. The animal struggled to right itself and the man’s hand flashed out, ripping out its throat and sending a gout of horse blood spraying onto the yellow grass, splashing across his bare chest. The mare fell, pinning its rider under its bulk. Crushed beneath the creature, she waved her sword at the naked man. He sidestepped with minor effort and then stomped her head, cracking it open like he’d jumped upon an overripe melon. Yoli reined to a stop, slid out of the saddle and rushed the attacker.

The other warriors joined her and the second of the fallen reached the group. Teryk inhaled a shaking breath and turned his attention to Trenan, his mount beating its way across the plain, heading for the fortress of Ikkundana. Immediately ahead of it, a third star hit the earth, the impact throwing up chunks of dirt and grass. With it being closer, Teryk heard the sound it made—a high-pitched squeal mimicking the note of red-hot steel dipped in icy water. Or a scream of pain. Trenan’s mount skidded to a halt and reared, front legs pawing the air between it and its newest source of panic. The master swordsman tipped in the saddle, overbalanced, and tumbled from his seat, hitting the ground with the top of his shoulders, and the back of his head. The horse bolted in a different direction, leaving its rider behind. Concerned about the man who’d raised and trained him, Teryk didn’t notice the fourth falling star until too late. It struck the earth a few lengths away from him, spraying the prince and his steed with loose soil. A rock hit the animal, startling it, and its feet tangled. It toppled forward. Teryk freed his toes from the stirrups in time to keep from being pinned as it skidded on its chest, air knocked from its lungs with a grunting whinny. The young man tucked and curled, as his mentor had taught him, hitting the hard dirt with his shoulder and somersaulting, absorbing some impact. It hurt nonetheless. He rolled three times before coming to a stop, then lay immobile for an instant, ears ringing, assessing his body, trying to breathe and calm his pounding heart. He untucked himself, climbed to his feet. His muscles ached from the shock of the jolt, but nothing felt broken. He blinked, glanced to his horse struggling to reset itself; the animal hadn’t been as fortunate as him. Trenan knelt to his right, sword drawn. The naked man stood before him, black eyes fixed on the master swordsman, hands clasped into fists. The air wavered between them, like distant heat on a scorching day, and the fallen stepped forward, but the swordmaster didn’t rise. His blade’s tip quivered noticeably. “Trenan!” Teryk hurried two steps before a pained whinny interrupted. He whirled to face the spot where his horse stumbled in time to see the other naked man bring his fist down on the animal’s midsection. The horse’s belly burst and the poor beast screamed in pain. Stomach lurching, the former prince spun away, quickened his pace. A few paces remained between the master swordsman and what Teryk realized now must be a Small God from the sky. Trenan’s sword drooped, its tip touching the ground as if his arm didn’t possess the strength to hold aloft its significant weight. His shoulders sagged, chin wilted forward. His body bobbed and the naked man stood before

him, an expression reflecting both satisfaction and hunger on his lips. He brought his fists together, raised them above his head; Teryk thought he laughed. “Trenan!” The spear hissed through the air and struck the fallen in the chest, entering his flesh two fingers below his right nipple and continuing through him until it exited through his lower back. The impact sent him stumbling as Teryk reached the master swordsman. He stood beside him, short sword raised, ready to defend his father or die trying. The naked man turned his head toward where the spear came from, but had no time to act or move as the second spearhead entered his left eye. He fell over backward, the weapon’s momentum taking him off his feet. He hit the ground, bounced once, twitched, then lay still. “Teryk. Watch out!” He jerked his gaze away from the corpse; Yoli waved her arms, pointing. The other Small God finished eviscerating Teryk’s horse and crawled over the beast, covering most of his flesh with its blood, as though he’d painted himself for war. The blood-soaked man glared at the former prince and the master swordsman, set his shoulders and stalked toward them. Teryk swallowed hard. “Trenan. Get up.” He made no move to do so and, when the prince looked down at him, he noticed tears glistening on the man’s cheeks. “I can’t,” he said, his voice little more than a breath. “Can’t. I’ve killed so many.” Teryk’s heart shrank in his chest. Of all possible times, now the king’s ablest and most fearsome warrior had lost his nerve. He raised his chin and peered at the young man. “I’m sorry, son. I can’t.” Teryk clamped his jaw tight, forced his lips into a flat line. No help from Trenan, so it rested with him to save them both. He readjusted his grip on the short sword’s handle, spun around to face his attacker. His eyes widened at the scene before him. Osis didn’t slow as his horse galloped behind the blood-covered fallen. Sunlight flashed on his blade as he swung it with practiced aim born through season after season of practice. The sharp edge caught the naked man in the neck, the force of the blow and momentum of the steed carrying it clean through, separating head from shoulders. The man’s expression didn’t change as his skull tilted off his body, bounced on the grass, and rolled away. He took two additional steps before his muscles realized what happened; his knees gave out and the headless torso pitched forward onto the ground. Teryk gaped. Other riders followed Osis, men of the king’s army

joining the fray. Their horses thundered across the plain, carrying them toward where three more of the shooting stars hit. After they passed, the dust cloud they left hanging still in the air, he spied Yoli riding to him. “Are you all right?” she shouted. His lips moved, but no sound came forth. Blood hummed in his ears, numbness touched the surface of his skin. She halted her courser, slid from the saddle, and rushed to him. A moment later, she stood before him, one hand on his shoulder. She looked into his eyes, concern clear on her face. “Are you hurt?” He shook his head, realized he held the short sword at the ready, and let his arm go slack to avoid nicking her with its sharp edge, though he doubted she’d be so clumsy as to allow such a thing to happen. “And Trenan?” He redirected his gaze toward the master swordsman and shrugged. Yoli took her hand from him and crouched in front of Trenan. “I can’t,” he said again. “They’re watching.” She knelt for a few heartbeats, saying nothing, but Teryk saw more in her expression than he had in the entire time they’d ridden with her. Not disappointment, but something approaching worry, sadness. As she stood, her face returned to the stern countenance of the leader she was. “Take him to the tents. I’ll have a physician come by.” Yoli climbed onto her horse, leather armor creaking with her movements. The mount turned a tight circle, desperate to get moving, but she wouldn’t yet let it go. “Do not allow him to join the fray unless he returns to himself. He does no good if he spends his time fighting people the rest of us cannot see.” Teryk nodded, unsure if she expected any further reply. If she did, she didn’t bother waiting for it. With a flick of her wrist, she was away. She raised one hand to him as the horse’s hooves beat the ground, carrying her toward where naked men fallen from the sky clashed with her female warriors fighting alongside soldiers of the king’s army. He inhaled a deep sigh, the odors carried on the breath tinged with sulfur and blood, and turned his attention to Trenan. The master swordsman remained on his knees, head hung, the picture of defeat. How many times in his life had Teryk wished to be like him? As he grew up, Trenan represented everything a man should be: loyal, brave, trustworthy, strong. Training with him since his youth, he’d always nurtured a desire within himself to prove his worth. Wasn’t

this wish what had brought him here in the first place? If not for his hubris, his sister might be alive, Trenan himself, and perhaps none of the rest of this would have happened. Was it possible the prophecy on the scroll required his actions to trigger it? Did I cause the fall of the kingdom? Despite the warmth, Teryk shivered. His mind lapsed to a battle he had no way of being part of, one which took place before he ended Danya’s life, before he’d become the man from across the sea, before his birth. He glanced at Trenan, the sheath for his sword—now empty, the replacement lying on the ground in front of him—poked out awkwardly to the side. Teryk’s eyes settled on the place where once he’d had a second arm like everyone else. Had he severed it, or was that an illusion? I’ll never know. He looked across the grassy expanse stretching to where the forest began, the road splitting it and, if ridden, eventually leading to the Green. The short sword weighed heavily in his hand, so he slid it into its scabbard, the guard clinking against the brass locket. His feet carried him a few steps forward, he paused, then he strode a few more. How easy it would be to flee for safety, to save his own life and leave the fighting to those better suited to it. Two more steps, then he stopped. How could he desert them after everything? How could he run after the sacrifice Danya had made? After I sacrificed her. Furrows crossed the plain; bodies lay scattered around—a few of them the naked corpses of men fallen from the sky, others warriors of the Goddess and of the king. Teryk shook his head, wet his lips with the tip of his tongue and found them tasting of soot. He spat the acrid taste from his mouth and started toward the master swordsman—his mentor, his trainer, and his father. The man who’d raised him and also lied to him. Another heavy breath filled his lungs, further adding to the weight in his chest. Maybe he should have given Trenan to the healer in exchange for his sister’s life, after all. He wasn’t himself, anyway. “It’s not too late.” Though the volume and tone of the voice were neither loud nor harsh, its presence startled him. He spun around, hands raised as though ready to defend himself, doubting his ability to do so if the owner of the words wanted to hurt him. “I’m not here to harm you. If I desired your life, I’d have taken it when Bieta and Stirk invited me in. You know what I want.” The cowl of the healer’s robe hid the upper part of his face so Teryk saw nothing but his thin, pale lips moving as he spoke. As usual, the man called Stirk waited beside him, rocking from one stump of leg to

the other; his tongue lolled out of the side of his mouth like a thirsty dog’s on a sweltering day. The legless man’s gaze darted from Teryk to Trenan and back. The healer rested his hand on his shoulder, which calmed him slightly. “I gave you my answer,” Teryk said, attempting to keep the nerves from his voice. “Yes. But here is your chance to reconsider.” “Right.” He sidestepped toward the master swordsman. When the men made no move to stop him, he took two more steps, careful not to face away from them. “Are you enjoying having your legs again, my prince?” “Don’t call me that.” “Ah, yes, my mistake. What shall I name you, then? Former prince? Son of the queen? Brother of the firstborn child of the rightful king?” Teryk clamped his jaw tight, forcing himself not to speak. He moved two sidesteps closer to Trenan and glanced toward the swordsman, who raised his chin. His gaze found the healer and his pet, face contorting with seeming recognition. Teryk tried to catch his eye, but he jerked his attention away, staring at the ground again in search of relief and safety. Four paces separated them now. When Teryk looked back to the others, they’d gotten nearer, though he hadn’t noticed them move. Stirk’s hand rested atop the head of the dead Small God, rolling it around like a child playing with a ball. “And what do we call him?” the healer asked, nodding toward Trenan. “Liar? Adulterer? Traitor? I don’t understand hesitation in what needs be done.” “He is my father.” The robed man laughed, a melodious sound which under other circumstances might have been pleasant. It prompted a noise from Stirk which may have been a chortle or maybe a hacking cough; he kept at it until his companion stopped. “Father,” the healer spat when the laughing ceased. “Is this how a father acts? Lying to his son? Allowing him to kill his own sister? Stirk is more of a father to you—he gave of himself to save you when you teetered on the precipice of death. I am more of a father to you—I took your paralysis, gave you back your legs and your wits.” “Took my paralysis away? You caused it.” He crossed the last few steps to Trenan’s side, looked down at the king’s soldier; haltingly, he raised his gaze to meet his son’s, lips trembling as though he wanted to speak but couldn’t remember how. “You did this,” Teryk said, facing the robed man and his companion again. “You did this to him, like you paralyzed me. That’s why Stirk is missing so many body parts. He’s not your friend, he’s your sacrifice.” “My pet sacrifices of his own free will. Do not presume to know his

mind.” The healer’s tone held an edge Teryk hadn’t heard before. “As for this one, he deserves everything that’s happened to him. Don’t you see? He does. These days, he sees every sin he committed.” “I don’t understand. Why do you want his life so badly? What did he do to you?” “Do to me?” The robed man laughed—no, cackled. “It’s not what he’s done to me, but what he can do for me. A power resides in him, an energy, a force not even he is aware of, but I am. It will be mine. I am offering you a fair deal: your sister for the swordsman. I recommend you accept; if you don’t, I’ll take it anyway, and leave you with nothing.” “He’s my father,” Teryk replied, the words compressed as he forced them between his clenched teeth. The healer laughed again, the sound becoming harsher every time it happened; Stirk giggled along with him. “He may have fathered you. He was never your father.” “It doesn’t matter. He did—” “I tire of talking.” He took his hand from Stirk’s shoulder, waved it dismissively. The man with no legs teetered but stayed upright, leaning on the decapitated head. “If you don’t give me what I need, I’ll find another way. Perhaps your mother will be more willing.” His last words brought a chill across Teryk’s skin. He glanced away from the robed man, glimpsed the sword lying on the ground in front of Trenan. “She won’t help you. She wouldn’t—” “I liked it better when you neither spoke nor moved.” His lip tugged up into a sneer. “Stirk.” The legless accomplice pivoted toward him, the head rolling from under his hand. The sudden lack of support threw him off balance. His one arm pinwheeled as he attempted to maintain an upright position, but he overbalanced and tumbled. If he touches him, he’ll paralyze me again. In a single motion, Teryk bent, grabbed the sword’s handle, and hurled it toward the pair without taking his eyes off the healer reaching for his sacrificial pet. The weapon wasn’t meant for such a use, so his aim went askew. The blade cut through the air, missing its intended target, but the tip found a home in Stirk’s eye. It entered with a sickening pop, four fingers of steel lodging in his head. Stirk’s body jerked once, twice. His lips parted, but no sound came out. Blood gushed from his nose, flowed from his ears, the corner of his mouth twitched, then settled, his last breath a bubble of red fluid. “No.” The healer drew his hand away, faltered away a step. Teryk rushed

forward, yanked the sword from the dead man’s head, and rounded on the robed man. Droplets of Stirk’s blood flew from the tip of the weapon as he swung it at waist level, intending to cut the healer in two. The sharp blade sliced empty air. Gone. Teryk shuffled his feet, turning a tight circle to be sure his adversary hadn’t slipped behind him, but found no trace. He let the sword sag, gaze fixed on Stirk’s blood clinging to the tip. His attention drifted toward the legless man. Stirk lay on his back, eyes open and mouth agape. One socket contained an eyeball glinting in the sunlight, but a mixture of blood and jelly occupied the other. The sight of it tightened Teryk’s gut. He let his fingers go limp, and the weapon dropped to the ground with a dull thud. He turned his head and retched. “The first is the most difficult.” Trenan’s voice startled him and he jerked back a step, wiped his mouth on his forearm. The master swordsman remained kneeling on the yellowed grass, his haunted eyes fixed on his son. “I remember mine.” His gaze flickered away, as though the ghost of his first kill stood to his left. “How could I not, right now? I remember all of them.” “But he’s not my first. Danya was.” “That wasn’t you. Something possessed you. Not your fault.” The former prince refreshed his lungs and crossed the space between them, knelt in front of his father. “Do…do you still see them?” “I do.” His gaze faltered, found the ground again. “I hope he doesn’t come back to follow you.” Teryk nodded and resisted the urge to survey the dead man again. Staring at the popped eye and spilled blood wouldn’t soothe his conscience or his soul; he’d stared at his sister’s corpse long enough to recognize this truth. He hoped for time to heal it, but if what was happening to Trenan was any indication, then it wasn’t to be. “They won’t leave me alone.” “It’s the healer. He did this to you.” “No. I did this to myself. His magic makes me see them, but they’ve always been with me. I’m the one who killed them.” His voice caught on the last few words, and Teryk saw tears glimmering at the corners of his eyes. He couldn’t recall ever seeing such an expression on the man’s face, not until after the Green, and now it never left. The former prince found his way to his feet, hooked a hand under Trenan’s one arm. “Come on. Get up. We’ll find you help.” The master swordsman struggled to stand. When he made it, his

knees buckled, and he’d have fallen to the grass again but for his son’s aid. “There is no help for me.” Teryk held him for a moment, ensuring his balance returned. He ducked under his father’s arm, putting it around his shoulders to support him, and took three paces before the master swordsman stopped, his weight demanding the former prince do the same. “They’re burning.” Teryk’s heart jumped, and he raised his gaze from his feet, where he’d been watching to be sure they didn’t trip over the body of one dead fallen or another. Across the plains in front of them, flames engulfed the canvas tents at the foot of the fortress wall.

IV Horace – Travelin’ Horace gripped Ivy about the waist as they sat on the beast, movin’ faster’n anything the ol’ sailor’d ever seen. It bounded up and down, leapin’ o’er fallen trees, then jerkin’ this way and the other, findin’ its course around thick brush and rocks too big to jump. More’n once, branches came near to knockin’ him off, yet he kept his seat despite it all. He’d’ve felt proud o’ the accomplishment, but he understood it weren’t his physical gifts what saved him from bein’ bounced right off the antlered steed. Havin’ a Small God o’ the Green ridin’ along with him prob’ly had somethin’ to do with it. The ol’ sailor pressed himself as tight against Ivy as he dared. He’d seen enough o’ these little folk to realize he weren’t in danger o’ squeezin’ her too hard, yet he found holdin’ on looser’n he might’ve. It likely made for a more precarious ride but, no matter how high the stag leapt, or how quick it altered its course, Horace stayed put in his seat. Maybe it be my sea legs. He doubted it, but it’d be nice to think all his time on one ship’s deck or another gave him skills to use in the landlocked world. Gods or Goddess knew weren’t nothin’ else he gained from it. ’Cept an estranged—and now dead—son. Wind comin’ from the speed they travelled at buffeted his cheeks, stirrin’ his beard whisker. At first, when Ivy’d told him they’d be climbin’ on the back o’ the big stag and usin’ him for transport, he’d come up with a bushel o’ excuses why it sounded a poor plan. As often were the case, he got talked into doin’ so. It led him to wonder if the little gray creature might’ve used some sort o’ glamor on him to make him do what she wanted. To him, the whole idea o’ magic were strange, one he held no hope o’ understandin’. But he couldn’t deny the way her touch’d charged him up whenever he felt low. And then there were how they appeared to communicate with the animals. Nobody’d been left behind without a wild beast to ride, includin’ himself and the girl, Evalal. Course, they both shared with one o’ the Small Gods—him with Ivy and her with the fellow he thought they called Leaf. Doublin’ up didn’t slow the beasts, though, and he suspected the gray folk ridin’ on ’em might’ve helped their energy, too. He leaned closer to Ivy and twisted his neck around to get a look at Evalal. The buck she rode with Leaf—smaller than the one he found himself on with his co-rider, given he weighed more’n a girl what’d seen the seasons turn maybe twelve times—followed less than three beast-lengths behind. She wore a blissful expression, lookin’ to enjoy

the ride a damn bit more’n Horace, despite everythin’ she’d been through. And from what he’d heard and seen, she’d been through a load. Fuck me dead, seems we all been through a lot. He tipped her a nod and turned himself to the front again, dodgin’ an errant branch what decided it wanted to slap him across the face. He chuckled at it for missin’ the mark. “Are you all right, Horace Seaman?” The breeze plucked at Ivy’s query, tryin’ to throw it past the ol’ sailor before he heard, but his ears’d always worked fine, even when age threw his other parts into question. “Helluva ride,” he said, lookin’ to find a balance betwixt shoutin’ in her ear and makin’ sure she got his words. When he opened his mouth again, the wind took a string o’ his saliva and flung it against his cheek. “We’re gettin’ somewhere pretty damn quick.” He watched her head rock toward him and away, noddin’ her agreement. “Yes. This one is very fast.” “Not what I meant,” he grumbled under his breath, then said louder, “I meant where is the somewhere we’re goin’ so damn quick?” “Ikkundana. To join the fight.” He’d already known what her response’d be, but gulped anyway. He knew little about the place, other’n some people callin’ it the City o’ the Sick. Didn’t know why they called it such, but didn’t sound like the kinda town he’d want to go. Havin’ said that, trapped behind the Green weren’t nowhere he’d ever wanted to be, neither. And if you went deeper, ain’t never been a time he especially loved standin’ on the deck o’ one ship or another, but there you have it—an entire life spent in places he’d rather not’ve been. The thought left a foul taste on his tongue, so Horace turned his head and spat, forgettin’ about the other beasts racin’ along so close behind. “Sorry,” he said, raisin’ a hand as the wind tore the apology from his lips. If anyone comin’ up the rear cared about apologies or bein’ spat upon, they made no sign. Thinkin’ about how much o’ his life he’d wasted—pretty much the whole damn thing—caused him to ponder what’d happened to everyone he’d liked even a sliver. Rilum, Thorn, Ailyssa, not to mention ev’ry man what’d been on the Devil—not that he’d cared for all o’ them, but some. What did his history mean for Ivy? Or poor young Evalal ridin’ up behind them? If somethin’ befell one o’ them, too, he didn’t know what he’d do. He held on tighter around Ivy’s thin waist as the stag bounded and danced through the forest, not because fallin’ off scared him, but because he feared losin’ her the way he’d lost her brother.

As long as I got breath in these ol’ lungs, I ain’t losin’ no one else. He gritted his teeth and gave a brief nod what he alone experienced, reinforcin’ the promise. Only he didn’t have any idea what they was goin’ to be in for once they reached this City o’ the Sick —Ikkundana. He leaned a mite closer, held onto Ivy even tighter.

V Erral – On the Road Where is Ishla? Erral gripped the reins in his right hand, his left resting on his sword, holding it from banging against his thigh or the horse’s flank with the bounce of its gait. He pressed his lips together, his teeth unconsciously ripping tiny pieces of flesh from the inside of his bottom lip. The tang of blood made him realize what he was doing, so he forced himself to stop. As far as he knew, she’d been gone since before the sun rose on the day the rider arrived with the news of the capture of Osis and his men. Her guard had disappeared, too. Whether good because he was with her and keeping her safe, or something altogether different and bad, Erral didn’t know. But he was the king, and she his queen, and no matter what, someone would pay for her disappearance. He released the tension in his face, let his lips part to lessen the inclination to ravage its interior. A deep breath filled with the musk of his mount and the oil on the joints of his riding armor brought him a measure of relief; he turned his attention to the muddled thumps of hundreds of hooves striking dirt behind him and his mind settled. Much time had passed since he last rode at the head of a column with a battle to come. The thought rested well with him—a war was always a suitable way to reacquire the support of the people. In the distance on the road ahead, a smudge of dust caught his eye. He leaned forward in his saddle, squinted. A rider—or riders— approached. The king sat his ass down and motioned for the nearest soldiers. One of his standard bearers increased his pace and pulled his horse up to the king’s right, two paces behind. “Find Dansil,” Erral said without looking from the distant cloud. “Bring him to me.” “My liege,” the color bearer replied, then retreated. The king heard him relay the message to someone else, where it got passed on to another, then another, until it reached the proper ears. The former queen’s guard must have been close behind because it didn’t take long for him to reach the king’s side. “Your majesty?” Erral inclined his head toward the horizon without looking at him. “Do you see?” “A rider.” “Take two men and find out who approaches.” “Yes, my king.” He fell back, his departure followed by a scuffle of horses moving aside to make room. Three riders went past the king, Dansil in the lead. They broke into a gallop as soon as they got ahead of the rest of

the column. Erral settled in his saddle and waited. *** Dansil curled his hand into a fist; the empty fingers of his glove pointed out awkwardly. He and the men with him had covered half the distance to the approaching riders—close enough now to recognize they numbered two. The former queen’s guard’s innards knotted at the sight. Could it be the healer coming to get him, Stirk lashed in the saddle at his side? He put the possibility from his mind. He had nothing to fear with the other soldiers with him. An unarmed man in a robe and a fellow with no legs and one arm would be no match for three men of the king’s army. Or would they? Wind buffeted his face as the distance closed and he saw both riders possessed all their limbs. He uncurled his fingers, releasing the tension in his sword arm, and sighed his relief. Soon they drew close enough to recognize the lead rider as a scout sent ahead on their trek to Ikkundana; the other bore the features of a woman. Dansil slowed his steed, the men with him following his lead, and raised his hand to the scout. He and the other didn’t slow until they reached them. When they came to a stop, the former queen’s guard opened his mouth to speak, but the king’s man interrupted, his sweat- slicked horse prancing and pulling against the reins. “Move aside. I must see the king.” The tone of the man’s voice—like he was in command and expected Dansil to do as told without question—irked him. He raised his hand, gesturing for the other riders to hold their ground. “His majesty has sent us to meet you. What is so important, scout?” He spat out the last word as if it a bug he’d found on his tongue. “An army of black priests and their followers.” He angled his head toward the woman, whose horse stood placidly, fully in her control. “The women need our help.” Dansil threw his head back and laughed. “The same females who captured Osis and his men? The same ones harboring the traitor Trenan? I hardly think the king—” “Out of my way, oaf.” The scout put his heels to the flanks of his mount and the animal shouldered past the former queen’s guard’s steed. Both the actions and words surprised him, and they passed by before his anger settled in, otherwise he’d have drawn his sword and stopped them in their tracks. With no other choice, he turned his horse about. “Move aside,” he growled, and pushed between the other two soldiers, both of them looking as astonished by the scout’s actions as

he’d been. He dug his heels in, prompting his mount to its fastest pace. Despite the other riders’ horses having been traveling for an extended time, he didn’t catch them before they reached the king. *** Erral watched the modest dust cloud grow closer, wondering why the riders were in such a hurry. When they’d drawn close, he reined his horse to a stop and held up his hand, halting the column behind him. He sat in the saddle, reins gripped loosely in his fingers, the sound of steel on leather echoing nearby as the surrounding soldiers drew their weapons, prepared for the worst. One of the front riders approaching wore the king’s colors—a scout, he presumed—the other was unknown to him; Dansil and his men trailed behind. What does it take to find a capable man? The two in the lead pulled up short of the king. The scout slid from his saddle before the horse had halted, crossed the three steps to Erral, and dropped to one knee. “My king. I come with news.” He barely heard the man’s words, so distracted was he by the second rider. A woman. His upper lip curled, and he released his hold on the reins, reached for his sword. He wrapped his fingers around the grip but did not free his steel. “What is she doing here?” he growled. “What have you done with my men?” The woman made no move to respond. Instead, the king’s man stood facing his monarch. Dansil arrived, horse’s hooves beating the ground as he jumped from his saddle and ran to the king. He bumped the scout with his shoulder, pushing him aside. “My king. I—” “You have already let me down. Get out of my sight.” The former queen’s guard slumped but did as he was told. He walked to his mount, feet dragging like a child’s after finding out he’d be sent to bed without a treat. Erral scratched at his head and turned his attention to the other man. “Scout. What is the meaning of this?” He tilted his head toward the woman. “An army, my king.” “Yes, yes. I know of their so-called army.” He waved his hand at her like shooing a fly—she didn’t react. “But what challenge to the king’s company are a bunch of women? They will kneel before me…if they don’t flee when they see us coming.” The female rider stared at him, expressionless. He found her lack of

reaction more infuriating than if she’d cried out or pulled her weapon. “No, my liege. Another army. Black priests and their followers.” Erral blinked twice, looked from the woman to the scout. To this moment, with the female sitting a horse in front of him, he still found it difficult to believe an entire army of them might be within the boundaries of the kingdom without his knowledge, but a second battalion, as well? “Impossible. She is telling you lies to manipulate you, to lure us into a trap. They have already captured some of my men. Now they aim to ensnare the king.” He shifted n his saddle, hardened his expression, and stared hard at the woman. “Tell the truth, harlot.” She made a clicking sound with her mouth and her horse carried her forward three paces before stopping again; her face remained calm despite his epithet. “It is the truth. We have no desire to capture you or any of your men. My commander sent me to warn you and to beg your assistance in protecting the kingdom from the return of the Small Gods.” “Oh, you’ll beg.” He loosed four fingers of steel, jutted his chin toward the woman, but she didn’t flinch as he hoped. She watched him, waiting for a response to her request. She spoke to me as though she is my equal. Annoyance warmed Erral’s cheeks, but he pulled no further measure of sword from his sheath. Instead, he released it, let the weapon drop into the leather holder. He glanced around at the soldiers nearest him, every one of them waiting for the merest of twitch from their king to launch at her and rend her limb from limb. If the bitch understood the danger, she didn’t show it. “How did your commander know you’d find me on the road to Ikkundana?” “The Goddess’ followers are everywhere. Often words travel faster than horses.” Her horse shuffled its feet, and she leaned forward, stroked its neck. “Why should I believe? An army of black priests can’t exist, let alone be on the march, without my knowledge. And the Small Gods aren’t real.” “My liege.” Erral had forgotten the scout standing on the hard-packed dirt road before him. He spoke quietly, with reverence, hesitant at interrupting his king. The woman could learn from him. “What is it, man? Speak up.” “I’ve seen the army she speaks of.” “What? How? You’ve not been gone long enough to see another

army and return.” The scout inclined his head toward her. “They showed me, my king.” Erral raised an eyebrow. “Showed you?” “A vision.” The king barked a sudden laugh. “A vision, is it? Some magic?” He shifted his position, faced the female rider. “Let’s have it, then. Show me this vision of an army.” “That is not my role. I am a warrior, not a priestess.” “Right. A warrior. Of course you are.” Erral snickered and his men laughed along with him. The woman showed the first hint of reaction with the bulge of muscles in her jaw, but she made no threatening move, no sign of rebuttal. The laughter died away leaving king and Goddess soldier to stare at each other. Erral’s horse shifted its feet impatiently. “My words are all I have to offer,” she said, breaking the extended silence. “You have the message. What say you? Will you help us save your kingdom?” The king’s right hand curled into a fist; he tapped it on his thigh three times. “You have the traitor Trenan?” She nodded. “The master swordsman is with us. As are your other men. They understand the danger.” “Then take me to your commander.
