But if this is a lie, your blood will be the first to spill.” The woman ignored his threat, prompted her mount around, and put her heels to its flanks. Erral watched her for a few heartbeats before turning his attention to the scout standing before him. “Don’t stand there, oaf, you’re blocking our way.” “One more thing, your majesty.” The king frowned, did his best to glare a hole in the man’s face. “Out with it. Did you not just tell me the kingdom is in danger?” The pronounced lump in the scout’s throat bobbed as he swallowed. “It’s the queen, my liege. We saw her on the road to Ikkundana.” “By herself?” “With a soldier.” He first thought Trenan had come for her to make their escape together, but the idea was ludicrous. The queen’s guard rode with her. Strylor. The idiot was too stupid to realize he answered to the king, not Ishla. Any other man would have the sense to tell him of her plans to flee. Flee to find her lover. Erral flicked his hand, dismissing the scout. He offered a shallow bow and hurried to his horse, scuffled steps kicking up dust from the dry road. When he’d climbed into his saddle and started off to catch

up to the woman, the king waited a few moments longer before prompting his own steed into action. Her story of black priests must be a lie. Even her own so-called army must be blown out of proportion, but they had the traitor with them. The man who fucked his wife, killed his daughter, spent season after season lying to him. He saved my life. No matter anymore. Too many pebbles filled the scale on the opposite side for losing his arm in defense of his king to be the determining factor. Whether black priests, Goddess whores, or Trenan, his sword ached to taste someone’s blood.

VI Mother of Death – Passing The Mother of Death woke with a start. Not an unusual happening. Sometimes her own loud snore startled her into wakefulness, the result of always sleeping on her back. Often, the cry of a babe disturbed her slumber, drawing her out of sleep several times a night. But the culprit wasn’t either snoring or crying this time. She gazed at the babes resting on her ample bosom. Neither of them suckled anymore, both having dozed off themselves; the Mother craned her neck and found the usual complement of attendants around the room awaiting her needs. “Come,” she said to the nearest. “Take them from me.” Two girls approached, one on either side, and took the sleeping little ones from her. The Mother of Death sighed with their absence— few times did she find herself with no contact to a small, new life, and fewer still when no fetus grew inside her. She pushed herself to sit up in the semi-reclined chair in which she spent most of her days. After a moment to notice the oddity of not having a noticeable belly inhibiting her movements, she swung her legs to the side. Immediately, another pair of attendants came to her—these a few turns of the seasons older than the previous, bigger and stronger—and grabbed her at the elbows. “Thank you,” she said, nodding first to one, then the other. The old woman slid forward on the seat until her feet touched the floor. The chilly stones caressing her soles delighted her, as did all sensations. She sat for a few moments, a girl holding her on each side, while she waited for the tingling of the nerves in her waking limbs to pass. “Have you been outside?” she asked the daughter on her right. “What is the day like?” “Warm. The sun shines bright as Goddess smiles upon us.” “Good.” The prospect of feeling sunshine on her cheeks slanted her mouth up at the corners. “Take me, please.” The girls clutched her arms as the Mother of Death leaned forward, shifting her weight from her backside to her feet. Her joints creaked, her knees popped and wavered; her helpers held her steady. They’d become used to the process, the same two helping her whenever the time came for the old woman to exercise. Exercise, she thought, chuckling to herself. If I can consider dragging these tired bones around dark corridors exercise. Always the same route, as much a temple inspection as a way for her to bend her joints and stretch her muscles. She loved those forays, when she got to see more of her daughters. Not every one of them had

emerged pink and screaming from her belly—though most had. She thought of each the same, nonetheless, as if they all belonged to her. They led her from the room into the hall, bare feet padding on the stone floor, and turned left instead of right as they normally did. The Mother sighed. She knew the staircase lay at the corridor’s end and, as much as she anticipated the sun’s warmth on her skin, she dreaded climbing those stairs. No other way, though. “Have you two been doing your schooling?” she asked as they guided her along the dim corridor, them standing straight and moving smoothly, her hunched over, shuffling. “Yes, Mother.” My own life once filled me instead of the lives of others, she thought and sighed again, breath rattling in her chest. So long ago. “Good. Always listen to your teachers. Goddess speaks through them.” “Yes, Mother,” they answered together. The old woman smiled. How she loved her daughters. It saddened her whenever one left to go to another temple, though she understood it the will of the Mother of Mothers. Faith eased grief, never extinguished it. She knew all was for the best; her offspring worked hard to fulfill their destinies and save the kingdom, and her heart swelled with pride—Yoli, Ishla, Ailyssa, and all the others. How she missed them. They arrived at the bottom of the stairway and paused. The Mother of Death raised her chin, peered up to the nearest landing—the first of four before they’d reach the roof. She inhaled a shuddering breath, looked from one helper to the other, then up the stairs. Air escaped through her nose and she nodded. “Best we get going,” she said. “The roof won’t come to me.” She lifted her foot and placed it on the first riser, felt the grips of her aides increase ever so slightly and lift, then she was up. Now to repeat it a hundred more times. “Not a hundred,” she said aloud. “Just one at a time.” “Mother?” the girl at her left elbow asked. “Oh, child, my old bones ache at the thought of the steps ahead, more so for all those behind. The key to arriving at any destination is to take each on its own. Don’t worry about the next, or the next, until this one is complete.” “Yes, Mother.” The elderly woman became quiet and concentrated on her footing. No good would come of her falling, though she had confidence her attendants wouldn’t allow such to happen. With no child in her belly, she was light enough for them to handle with ease. When they reached the first landing—a square step the size of two

normal steps where the stairway took a turn to the left, following the temple’s outside wall—they stopped to rest. The youth at the Mother’s right elbow plucked a skin from her belt. She pulled the cork with her teeth, then held it up to the Mother of Death’s lips, leaned it toward her. Cool water flowed into her mouth, refreshing her and returning energy to her tired muscles. She smiled at the girl who’d given it to her, raised a quaking hand and touched her cheek. Hers had been a hard birth; she’d twisted around and wanted to come out feet first and they’d worried she might not survive, worried the Mother might not survive. And now the seasons have turned, and she’s becoming a healthy young woman while I can’t keep from shaking. She leaned against the wall while the girl released her arm to return the stopper to the water skin and hang it on her belt again. When she finished, she took the Mother of Death by the elbow again. “Ready?” “Yes, yes. Let’s get this done with.” They carried on, repeating the rest at each landing. By the time they reached the third, sweat dampened the mother’s smock under the arms and along the middle of her back; droplets ran from her forehead, following the lines of her wrinkles down her nose and onto her cheeks. The girl at her left elbow pulled a soft cloth from under her robe and dabbed the old woman’s face. “Oh, thank you,” she clucked, the words bouncing on a good- natured chuckle. “I’m not sure when I got to be so ancient.” The aide with the cloth stared at her, eyes wide. “You are the Mother of Death. You’ve always been old.” “To you I have always been old,” she said, the chuckle becoming a laugh. “Once I was as young as you. Younger once, believe it or not. Time passes though, for all of us.” “So one day I’ll be as old as you?” “Mmm, perhaps. I am older than most. Goddess’ plan for me lasted longer than even I expected.” The aide with the waterskin rubbed her arm. “It’s all right, Mother. You will be around for many more turns of the seasons.” Once, I would have remembered her name. All of their names. “No, child. My time nears its end.” Both the girls’ faces showed shock and sadness at her words. “Tut, tut. Everyone leaves their body sometime to be with Goddess. It may be I’ve nearly reached the final reward, but I will not leave you without a Mother. I promise.” She smiled, perhaps a bit sadly, and stroked first one girl’s cheek, then the other’s. They both gazed upon her, unmistakable love gleaming in their eyes, strongly enough for her to notice and bring

gladness to an old woman’s heart. “No more dilly-dallying. We’re almost to our destination. Shall we race the last bit?” They laughed and supported her by the elbows again, guided her up the final flight of stairs. There was no hurry, of course; the Mother of Death’s racing days were far behind her. Most of my days are behind me. They reached the top step—a platform bigger than the landings by twice—and the waterskin aide offered her one more drink. The Mother of Death declined. What she wanted was the warmth of the sun on her face, to hear the chirp of birds, smell the bouquet of the gardens, and finish with this. She leaned while the two of them used their combined strength to open the heavy door. As they did, the old woman peered back to the last landing, regarding the riser edges worn smooth by so many feet, the dark line on the wall where uncountable fingers touched the stone. She remembered climbing them herself as a child, making her way to the roof with her sisters for ceremonies, for lectures, or to play and enjoy a third-season day. If she examined them closely enough, she might find where her soles had rounded the stair, where her touch stained the rock. The door swung open and sunlight streamed onto the final landing. The old woman raised her arm, shielding her eyes until they became used to the brightness; her two aides waited until she nodded, then they returned to their posts at her elbows. They guided her forward, one careful step at a time, out of the shadow and into the light. When the sun touched the Mother of Death’s face, she stood straighter. They crossed the threshold onto the roof and she immediately detected the aroma of the gardens though four floors separated her nose from them in the courtyard below. How she’d loved it up here when she could get around on her own, before Goddess had proclaimed her Mother of Death. And now those days are coming to their close. A stiff wind rose out of nowhere, stirring her sparse hair and flapping the sleeves of her robe. She halted, stooped a little, though she knew she needn’t. She listened to the ruffle and flutter accompanying the breeze, closed her eyes against any dirt and dust the disturbance might stir up. When the current dissipated, she opened them again. The black bird loomed over her, half again her height, and stood only three paces distant from her and her aides. She smiled upon seeing it and stepped forward, the girls at her elbows more following now than guiding. She raised her hand and stroked its neck. “Hello, Father Raven,” she said. “It’s so good to see you, old

friend.” The bird clacked its beak twice, jerked its head sideways so one eye faced her. She patted him and took a step to the side to peer beyond it. “And it’s wonderful to see you, too,” she said. “Both of you. Come, we have much to discuss.”

VII Strylor – Prince and Queen As much as he cherished her, and knew she loved him, Strylor thought the decision to ride ahead of the queen the right one. ‘Decision to ride ahead’ might not have been the most precise of descriptions—Ishla suggested he scout the way. Insisted it the best course of action. Encouraged him to do it. Finally, she’d invoked her power as queen and commanded him to go on before her. He didn’t think it the wisest of ideas—she always needed his protection, as she’d proven repeatedly —but after careful consideration, he’d seen the prudence in her recommendation. After the incident at the inn, the discussion about scouting was the extent of the words they’d exchanged. Though riding by himself left him no one to talk to, it was a more comfortable lack of conversation than the awkward silence he’d endured with her at his side. To pass the time, he hummed to himself an off-key tune enjoyable to no ears but his own. He understood what upset Ishla. How might he react if he discovered her crawling into bed with another man? A simple misunderstanding, but his mistake embarrassed him too much for him to tell her the truth of it. Her love for him brought her jealousy over the incident, his tenderness for her left him hesitant to admit he’d erred and risk diminishing his stature in her eyes. It would sort itself out; these things always do. Destiny meant them for one another. Ahead, he noticed the road widened and the trees on either side ended. Difficult to discern much beyond the end of the tree line from his vantage point, but Strylor suspected he spied a plain. A change in scenery was all the news he needed to swing his horse around and return to the queen to give her a report. The corners of his mouth tilted upward at the thought—it had been too long since they enjoyed each other’s company. He ended his hummed tune and reined his mount to a stop, stood in his stirrups for a better look rather than approaching any nearer. With the ditty finished and the hooves no longer clacking against the track, he noted sound emanating from the clearing ahead, a veritable hubbub of indiscernible noises. He clicked air through his back teeth and nudged his mount’s flanks, urging the horse forward, but not too fast. The gentle clip-clop of its steps rose again but, now he’d noticed the other sounds, they didn’t disguise the hullabaloo. He gripped the reins tighter, squeezed his knees against his steed. When they reached the end of the track where the forest ended, he stopped again. Without the trees to block the noise, it grew louder, but no more recognizable. He prompted the horse forward a few more steps and paused once more, this time sucking a breath between his

lips, tasting the dried grass, the dirt beneath it, and another flavor, like a joint of beef hung over the fire too long. To his left, soldiers clashed, some ahorse, others on foot, a mish- mash making it impossible to tell who might belong to what army. To his right, the plains appeared less congested. Deep furrows cut across them, soil and grass pushed aside in their wake like after a farmer dragged a massive plow but gave up before completing the job. At the center stood a fortress with intimidating gray walls, a place the likes of which he’d never seen. Strylor sucked his bottom lip into his mouth, nibbled it absently, then prompted his horse to the right. He followed the edge of the forest outside the clearing, sticking closer to the area with fewer people where he might be safer. His mount trotted along the fringe while he turned in the saddle, striving to make sense of what lay before him. He hadn’t gone far when he spotted the flames burning at the base of the citadel wall—tents set alight, though he neither cared who’d started the fire nor why. If not for the flickering background, the two figures making their way across the plains would have been lost against the backdrop of the featureless fortress. He wouldn’t have noticed one of them lacked an arm. Trenan. He stopped his mount, leaned out and squinted, as though either promised to help him be certain. But who else might it be? One arm, draped over the other person’s neck, a younger man, as they crossed away from the furrows toward the inferno. Younger man? He scratched his cheek, wet his lips with his tongue. Prince Teryk! With no more thought about them, he reined his horse around and urged it into a gallop back the way he’d come. Here was his opportunity to make up for his mistake. Once he told her he’d found her son, and the bastard responsible for her daughter’s death, she’d forget about the mix-up at the inn. She might even offer to show him her appreciation. He leaned into his steed and pushed it to go faster. *** When the first streak of light slashed across the sky, it caught Ishla by surprise. She spotted it out of the corner of her eye and reined her horse to a stop, raised her head to survey what showed of the clear blue between the boughs of the trees overhead. A trail of smoke remained, evaporating before her eyes, breaking up and drifting away. Before she lowered her chin to ride again, a second one came into view.

It whizzed past at an incredible speed, a fireball with a tail of fog. Ishla gasped, her mind jumping to stories told by priestesses about the end days of the Small Gods, the destruction wrought by Goddess in her efforts to banish them. Was this her work, then? She coaxed her mount along the track again, faster than before, the breeze created by her movement cool against her cheeks. Little distance had disappeared beneath the horse’s hooves when the third fireball flew overhead. She dug her heels in, whipped the reins, and bent forward. The animal’s gait ate up the road. So much time had passed since she last sat a galloping horse. The rhythm of it refreshed her, the cadence bringing her a peace she hadn’t felt in too long; it dissipated when another ball of fire cut across the sky before her, this one close enough she heard it, but not just the sound of flames buffered by the wind. It moaned with the tone of a man’s voice. Ishla shuddered at what it might mean and tried to coerce more speed out of her mount. Hooves pounded ground sprinkled with spots of grass struggling for life, each impact throwing up clods of earth in its wake. She didn’t know how much distance remained to arrive at Ikkundana, but she desired for her horse to carry her as fast as possible, aware of how alone she was. For the first and likely last time, she wished the oaf Strylor was with her. He may not be any good as a protector—or anything else—but at least he’d be company. After a while, she slowed her horse’s pace, worried she might tire the animal before arriving at her destination, forcing her to walk the rest of the way. The queen breathed heavily. Her heart beat fast, as though she’d been the one to run all this distance, not her mare. She inhaled a deep breath, forced herself to loosen her grip on the reins and collect her thoughts. Why am I rushing toward the place where these fireballs are falling? The Mother of Death once told her destiny awaited her at the City of the Sick. What other choice did she have? Ahead on the road, she spotted someone approaching. She reined her mount to a stop, then turned it sideways so her sword arm faced the person coming toward her. She laid her hand on the weapon’s grip, realizing the last time she’d wielded a blade lay farther in her past than when she last galloped on horseback. The speck of rider and horse grew larger as he neared until she recognized it as the queen’s guard. He halted in front of her, both animal and man sweating noticeably. “Did you see them?” she asked before he spoke. He stared at her, eyes wide with surprise. His shoulders sagged, like someone let the air out of him. “How did you know?” “What did you mean ‘how did I know’? Did you not spot them

streaking across the sky?” She wanted to ask him how he got to be so stupid, so out of touch, but resisted. His expression shifted to confusion. “Trenan and the prince?” Ishla’s heart jumped in her chest. “What? No. I meant the fireballs.” She swallowed hard. “You’ve seen Teryk?” “Fireballs?” He tilted his head, jerked it side to side in an exaggerated movement that might have otherwise been funny. “What fireballs?” “Fuck the fireballs,” she snapped. Her tone snatched his attention from the sky. “You saw my son?” He nodded. “And Trenan.” Her chest fluttered, and she pressed her lips together. Her son yet lived, thank Goddess, but Trenan… “Where?” He turned awkwardly and pointed over his shoulder. “Near the City of the Sick.” “Take me.” She whipped the reins and put heels to horse without waiting for a response. Her mount took off at full gallop, hooves pounding out their cadence on the packed dirt road so she heard nothing else but the wind in her ears. Behind her ribs, her heart beat fast, excitement, fear, worry, and so much more setting it racing. Her son, alive! Thinking of it made her want to push the horse faster, but it was at its limit, carrying her swiftly to reunite with her boy. And with the man who killed her daughter. Tears streamed from the corners of her eyes, streaking the side of her face and disappearing into her hair. Whether the wind caused them or the ache in her heart, only she knew. *** By the time he caught up with her—he did so because she stopped —they had reached the end of the track where it opened onto the plain. Strylor brought his horse to a halt, huffing and puffing and wiping sweat from his face as he pulled up beside the queen. From what he saw, not much had changed since he withdrew from this spot, but Ishla hadn’t seen it before. She sat in her saddle gawking at the furrows cut across the space, the fire burning against the backdrop of the imposing fortress wall, the battle raging. “What in Goddess's name?” she whispered. Strylor looked the other direction, to his left, and realized one thing had changed—the size of the skirmish. He squinted, held a hand up to his forehead, less out of a need to block the sun and more because he thought it what you do when you want to see a long distance. To his mind, it helped, but what he observed made no sense. Fighters in

armor and also ones in robes, armored and topless women, each of them swinging weapons. Naked men strode amongst them, taller than the rest and more noticeable; above the heads of all snapped the standards of the Windward Kingdom. He sat straighter in the saddle, pleased about the arrival of the king’s soldiers—they represented the best chance of putting down whatever rebellion this turned out to be. On the other hand, if they spied him, they’d likely enlist him to aid in the fight. He sank back in his seat. “Where are they?” Somehow, he’d forgotten the queen—his love—sitting the horse right beside him. He faced her, recognized strain and concern etched in the lines of her face and his heart swelled. It did him good to realize she didn’t want him to join the fray, either, because she feared losing him. He swallowed, slanted his lips into a smile and readjusted his posture. “What are you smiling at? Does something strike you as happy or funny?” A crease appeared above her nose and her eyebrows did their best to touch in the middle. “Where did you see my son?” Shaken by the abruptness of her words, Strylor couldn’t respond with anything more than raising his arm and pointing to their right, in the direction of the fire. She twisted around to follow his gesture, stood in her stirrups. “Follow me,” he said, finding his voice, cheeks hot with the vehemence in her nature. Not in all their time together had she used such a tone with him. He started along the edge of the forest like before, the hoof prints of his earlier passing visible as a path in the beaten grass. The queen’s horse fell in behind him, following close. He heard the animal’s steps, separate from those of his mount, and its tired breathing as it attempted to catch its breath, but the rider remained silent. The urge to glance over his shoulder forced itself upon him, but he resisted. If her expression had shifted to the admiration and love he’d become accustomed to, it would be worth the chance, but what if she wore those other emotions on her brow? The ones that—dare he think it— made her ugly. Ahead of him, the previous path angled to the left, into the grassy plains and toward the conflagration against the fortress. He stopped his horse and pointed once more. “They were that way, making for the city.” He stole a glimpse of her from the corner of his eye, sufficient to recognize her expression fell somewhere in between the two extremes he’d imagined. It gave him slight relief, and he understood—after surviving the confusion at the inn, their love for each other had grown

strong enough to withstand anything. Ishla urged her horse forward and past him, moving more slowly than before as she realized the need for care. He gulped a breath to fill his lungs and calm his nerves; given the decision between fighting with the rest of the king’s army or keeping the queen safe—his job, after all—he’d take the second choice every time. “Wait, my love. Let me lead the—” She spun her horse and fixed him with a look that stopped his words in his mouth. “What did you call me?” His eyes widened, mind reeling as he shook his head numbly side to side, trembling lips opening and closing though they produced no sound. His action appeared to enrage her further, but he failed to make himself stop. “You deluded oaf.” Her lip curled up in a sneer like a dagger in his heart. “I’ve dealt with your touches and advances, your stupid fantasies. Enough. I am your queen, and you are nothing but a guard I neither wanted nor needed. Trenan and my son are out there; I will find them and you will leave me be.” She turned her back on him, prompted her horse out into the plain. Before she rode out of earshot, she said one more thing to him over her shoulder, “I never want to look upon your face again.” Strylor stared after her, his mouth hung open. When he realized his head still moved, he made it stop. Where did he go wrong to deserve such treatment? Hadn’t he always held her best interest in mind? He’d wished for favorable outcomes for her, even when she didn’t understand what that looked like. He snapped his jaw shut, huffed breath out through his nose. His own forehead creased with anger as the words she’d spoken settled into him and realization dawned. Trenan. How many times had he heard her defend the one-armed swordsman, both to the king and others? Even after Dansil told her he’d killed the princess, it appeared she didn’t believe him, though everyone else knew it the truth. He’d wondered why she’d been so resistant to the obvious. Strylor stuck out his bottom lip, forced air between his teeth, then sucked it back into his mouth over and over. After everything I’ve done for you. He recalled Dansil hinting at something between her and the master swordsman, but he never thought much of it, especially with the devotion and care she’d shown him. But it was gone now, shattered on the ground like a lump of shale struck with a hammer. He spat the saliva from his mouth, aiming in the direction the queen had headed when she’d deserted him, when she forsook their love for another. Leaving him alone. Empty. Angry.

Strylor turned his horse, urged it back the way he came, but he’d not be taking a left turn onto the road to the Horseshoe. Instead, he’d carry on toward the battle. Not intending to join in the bloodletting, of course, but he hoped to find Dansil, who’d surely be amongst them and interested in what he now knew. As would the king. *** He stayed to the edge of the forest as he made his way toward the tangle of warriors fighting on the plain, glancing over his shoulder often in hopes he’d discover her coming up behind him, her mind changed. She didn’t. For a while, he saw her horse in the distance, then it became a speck until he could no longer tell her from any other rider or bit of wreckage. Despite her fading away, he kept peering over his shoulder for her, expecting to catch sight of her again. Hoping against hope she’d pursue him. These backward glances made him almost ride over the bald man in the black robe.

VIII Dansil – Arrival Dansil hung back, staying near the king. Erral hadn’t asked him to stay close, to act as his adviser or guide, but he chose to himself and the regent had yet to tell him any different. The uncommon battlefield laid out before them gave the former queen’s guard pause. He’d seen plenty of skirmishes in his day, though not so many recently. Once he got himself assigned to protect the queen, rarely had his duties sent him to put down rebellion or add his weapon to the defense of the realm. He’d missed it. His sword arm was as strong as ever—as anyone’s—and readying for a fight brought a tingle of sensation along the surface of his skin. The battle engaged before him lacked sense: no lines drawn, no formations held. Instead, hundreds of bodies clashed, some on horseback, some armored, some in robes. Many of the women fought topless, a spectacle that would have had Dansil licking his lips and chuckling under his breath, perhaps rubbing the outside of his clenched fist along the inside of his thigh. Not today. Those female warriors swung swords and wielded halberds, wore splashes of blood across their tits. His groin and his brain struggled to reconcile the sight. Even when the king gave the order to engage, Dansil kept out of the fray, though he was unsure why. His majesty’s soldiers thundered onto the battlefield, bright standards flapping, armor clattering. He’d given instructions not to harm the female warriors, but as the first wave intersected the fight, swords swung without care cut down women and men alike. Dansil clucked at the corner of his mouth and prompted his steed to back away, leaving Erral and his close advisers overseeing the battle. They leaned closer together to speak, occasionally raised an arm to point at some happening or other, but none of them noticed him sneaking off. This ain’t my fight, he told himself. The words rang false, but he lacked any other explanation as to why he retreated. After a moment, the answer came; he realized some extra sense gave him warning of what was about to occur. At the far end of the clearing, a mass of bodies boiled out of the forest. Any closer and he’d have heard the collective battle cry of those men who did not belong to the ranks of the king’s army. Who they sided with, he didn’t know, for they flew no standards, wore no colors, though he spied flashes of black amongst them like the robes worn by the priests. And the healer. He shuddered, but the shiver caught halfway along his spine. The

last one out of the forest stood taller than all the others by more than half, sunlight gleaming on his bare dun flesh as if covered with a sheen of sweat or dew. Dansil pulled on his horse’s reins, turning the animal away from the battle, but stopped when he spotted another rider waiting behind him. “Dansil?” He shook his head, blinked. It took him a few heartbeats to recognize Strylor sitting before him. “What are you doing here?” “Came looking for you.” Dansil frowned, craned his neck to look past the man. “Ain’t you supposed to be taking care of the queen? If Erral sees you, he’ll lop your melon off himself.” The expression on Strylor’s face drooped, whether due to his mention of Ishla or the beheading, he couldn’t guess. Either way, he hesitated before he spoke again. “Wasn’t able to stop her. You remember what she’s like.” Dansil shrugged. “Gone off to find Trenan.” The name of the one-armed swordsman brought tension to the muscles in his shoulders. “He’s here?” “And the prince, too.” Dansil shifted in his saddle, glanced toward the king and his advisers. They hadn’t moved from their spot, watching the turmoil, nor did they care about his absence. His lip curled; their lack of interest should have made him relieved, but he couldn’t help seeing it as a slight. But if anyone desired to give Trenan his dues, Erral was the man. He returned his attention to Strylor. “Where are they?” “Somewhere over there,” he said hiking his thumb over his shoulder. “Don’t know for sure. Been a while since I saw them. They headed toward the fortress. Might be inside by now, for all I know.” “Damn it.” “If it’s important to find him, I met a fella who says he can help.” Dansil had enough time to raise an eyebrow before Strylor reined his horse to step aside and reveal the robed man standing behind him. With his hood thrown back, the sun reflected on his bald head. He likely did it to avoid being mistaken for one of the black priests, he presumed. No single-limbed cohort stood with him. “What the fuck?” Dansil squeezed his hand into a fist, hating the space left by two missing digits. The healer raised his hand, sleeve falling away to expose a pale palm and long fingers with knots where knuckles should have been. He surely meant the gesture to stop Dansil’s words and thoughts, but

the sight of him brought rage the former queen’s guard fought to control. If he made a commotion, he’d attract the king’s attention, and who knew how the monarch might react to his sneaking away, or to the man in the black robe. He pressed his lips together and lowered his brows. “Fear not, Dansil. I’m here to offer assistance. We both strive for the same goal.” “I am familiar with the cost of your help.” He glanced to both sides of the healer, making his survey of the area obvious. “But where’s your pet?” “Alas, I lost him to a flash of the former prince’s ire.” Strylor raised an eyebrow. “Former prince?” “Never mind.” Dansil waved a dismissive hand without redirecting his attention. “If I wanted your help—which I don’t—who’d be paying the fee, I wonder?” “Oh, you need my aid, good sir. When you have accepted it of your own accord once, it’s difficult not to accept it again. But if you think you can convince the king into letting you desert his army, please go ahead. As for the cost,” his gaze flickered to Strylor atop the horse beside him. The man didn’t realize the predatory eyes had touched him. “I expect we can come to an agreement equitable for both of us.” Dansil flexed his hand open and closed, open and closed. Each time he felt the space where the two fingers should have been, he cringed. He’d never have them back but, if he didn’t see Trenan punished as he desired, he’d have lost them for nothing. He glared at the robed man, then looked at Strylor. The queen’s guard peered at him, unassuming, unaware. Dansil nodded. “Take me to the traitor.” The healer moved toward Strylor, the robe hiding his feet and making it appear he floated across the space—or maybe he did. When he drew close enough, he reached up and laid his hand on his forearm. The man glanced at the bald fellow and Dansil saw his lips part, heard the first note of a shriek of pain before the world swam into darkness. *** Dansil returned to awareness on his hands and knees, the ground tilting and spinning. He opened his mouth to draw breath, but his guts took the opportunity to empty themselves of anything they found inside them—the remnants of breakfast, last night’s wine. He knelt for a time, a string of saliva hanging from his lips and sweat cooling on his brow. The sound of the fight drifted across the plains to him, mixed with the crackle of fire; beneath it, the dull groan of a man in pain. He blinked, raised his head. Five paces away, Strylor lay on the ground, rolling back and forth

in the dry grass, flattening it to the dirt. He held his left arm cradled against his body, empty space where his hand should have been. Fucking healer my ass. He dragged himself to his feet, spied the robed man halfway between him and the queen’s guard, watching them both. When he sensed Dansil’s gaze upon him, he leaned his head toward the fortress. Against the backdrop of the conflagration, Dansil recognized the two figures—one standing, a hand on the other’s shoulder, the one short an arm. A few of the female soldiers milled about, too. He frowned, growled in his throat. Saliva filled his mouth, his body understanding what he needed to do and reacting to it before it happened. “I need more men,” he said, then turned his head toward the healer. “Take me back.” He floated across the ground, the grass bending but not flattening with his passing, and laid a hand on Strylor again. The queen’s guard jerked at his touch, cried out. Dansil closed his eyes this time, hoping to avert the effects of the healer’s dark magic.

IX Trenan – Battleground They didn’t gather in a line as they had along the side of the dirt track, or crowded him like those nights in camp, but the blood-streaked faces watched. They spied on him from the top of the wall; their eyes pierced him from within the flickering flames, and from amongst groups of female warriors making their way to the battleground. Trenan did his best to keep from looking at them, fixing his gaze toward the ground or on Teryk’s feet, but he sensed their glares upon him. Their stares may as well have been daggers poking his flesh. Each accusing stare, each hating expression chipped one more piece off his soul, leaving his body exhausted. He maintained awareness of everything around them—the distant battle, the clamor of women attempting to extinguish the fire started when a fireball falling from the sky crashed into them. They’d put down the fallen man it brought, but now they had to douse the flames it left behind. Everywhere, soldiers needed his assistance, the kingdom demanded defending. Like so often before. And look at the results. He shook his head to loosen the thought. A battlefield was no time or place for doubt. How many times had he spoken those words? More than he could count, the youth standing beside him amongst them. And how many men did he see lose their lives out of hesitation? Too many. Despite the guilt and grief weighing on him, he struggled to his feet, using his son’s arm to help him. “Are you all right?” A dead man lurched toward him, half his face cloven off to expose bone and muscle beneath, teeth missing from his grisly grin. Trenan jerked away, sidestepping the phantasm. Teryk noticed, squeezed his shoulder. “Yes.” Trenan nodded but didn’t gaze directly at him, worried his expression might reveal the fear gnawing at his gut. This trepidation may cost him his own life—maybe he deserved the result—but he wouldn’t let it end Teryk’s. “We need to join the others.” He took a step away from his son’s steadying hand, knees wobbling under him, and stopped to keep from losing his balance. The world tilted, his stomach lurched. If Teryk hadn’t reached out and grabbed him, he’d have found himself on the ground again. “You’re in no shape, Trenan.” “But I must.” He raised his head and a man with his innards draped from his belly took a swipe at him with an axe. The master swordsman flinched. “Yoli said not to let you unless you returned to yourself.” He lifted his chin to peer at his son, lips pressed together, ready to administer an admonishment, but he stayed himself. Or perhaps the

throng of dead men gathered behind Teryk stopped him. “I have to try.” The younger man nodded once, then took his father by the arm, guided him away from the fire at the base of the fortress wall. With each step, the scabbard of Trenan’s sword bumped against his thigh, something he’d once found a source of encouragement, but not now. Every time it touched him, he thought of it as a register of the men, women, and children whose lives he’d ended during campaign after campaign to protect the kingdom, as duty drove him to do yet again. He wished he possessed two arms to have one with which to grab the sword’s pommel and stop it from tap, tap, tapping against him, hoped stopping the tally might make the empty, dead eyes watching him disappear. Teryk stepped around a body lying on the ground—a woman who stared at the sky, the pale skin of her chest painted red by a wound to her belly. How she clamped her hands over the gash made Trenan assume she must have been injured elsewhere and was making her way to the fortress when she succumbed to the injury. He glanced at her face but didn’t recognize her from his time with the women in Ikkundana’s training yard and wondered if her ghost would soon haunt him. I didn’t kill her. A shiver quaked along his spine. Trenan faced Teryk, found his son pulling his sword to hold out in front of him as though he thought someone might attack at any instant. A sliver of worry lanced the master swordsman’s chest. Had he taught him well enough for him to survive a battle? During his training he’d expected the boy to live as prince, and eventually king to a peaceful kingdom, likely to never have to test his steel in combat. He’d allowed him to get away with sloppier form than anyone else, and to skip lessons of no interest to him. He’d let him believe himself a better fighter than he really was, and it already almost cost him his life once. “I’m sorry, son,” he said, overcome by regret. Teryk raised an eyebrow. “For what?” “Never mind.” He allowed the young man to lead him as they made their way toward the skirmish. Women rushed past, fighting to extinguish the fire, while others hurried to join the fray. Trenan scanned back and forth, watching for threats, but to him perils lay everywhere; wherever he looked, he gazed upon the faces of the dead. As he turned his head to look left again, he saw a man break through between two of the female warriors. This fellow showed no fatal wound, no missing limb or hanging entrails. His leather chest piece, steel-banded buckler, and broad-bladed short sword suggested a soldier of the king’s army.

He spotted Teryk and Trenan, amended his course toward them and increased his pace. “Watch out,” the master swordsman said, stepping out of the path behind his son. He made the familiar movement of reaching across his body to pull his weapon, but his fingers found the hardness and texture of the grip uncomfortable. When the steel rubbing against the scabbard’s hard leather sang its song, it sounded the lament of a dying thing to Trenan’s ears. His stomach lurched, his last meal threatening to find its way up his throat and out into the world. The distance between himself and the attacker shrank; the man held his shield in front of his chest, raised his sword. Trenan lifted his arm, but his muscles quaked under the effort. The man’s shaggy beard hid his mouth, but his eyes gleamed with an unnatural light of hatred. The master swordsman thought he recognized the fellow but didn’t have the opportunity to figure out where from as the space between them disappeared. He struck at Trenan, swinging his weapon in a downward arc he caught with his own sword. It sent a shock up his arm and into his shoulder and chest. The strike wasn’t well considered and his buckler dipped with it, leaving the side of his neck exposed. The master swordsman saw this clearly, recognized how he should move to wield his blade and take advantage of the mistake, but nothing more came of it than the recognition. He didn’t make the killing blow. Instead, he turned his head and vomited on the yellow grass. The soldier laughed and struck again. Trenan twisted his body, and the strike went wide, the miss throwing his opponent off balance, spinning him around and giving the master swordsman his back. The opportunity screamed at his honed fighting instinct and he brought his weapon up this time, but his arm lacked the energy to thrust. The expression on the man’s face changed from hatred to fearful surprise. He jumped away, attacked again. Trenan caught the strike with his steel, but the force pushed it toward him so the sharp edge of his own sword scraped against his armor. A hand’s-breadth higher and it would have found his throat. His opponent made no mistake this time, following up by thrusting his buckler forward, catching Trenan in the chest and forcing him backward. The master swordsman stumbled away, feet tangling uncharacteristically, and he fell to the ground, vaguely aware of landing in his own vomit. The impact jarred his spine. His eyes closed for a heartbeat; when they opened again, the faces of the dead leered at him—broken teeth, dangling eyeballs, sheets of flesh hanging from cheeks. He let go of his sword and threw his arm up in front of his face, a scream threatening at the back of his throat, but it didn’t

surface. Instead of the sound of his voice, he heard the clang of steel hitting steel. He opened his lids to find his son standing over him, weapon extended, the attacker’s blade having glanced off it, deflecting its path intended to end his life. The soldier redirected his attention toward the young man, but Teryk didn’t hesitate; he put his foot hard against the fellow’s buckler, sent him stumbling, and then pounced on him. The tip of his sword found a spot under his chin and sank into his flesh, running up through his mouth into his throat. The fellow gagged, spit blood, went limp. Teryk removed the blade, scanned the surrounding area for any further threats, then rushed to Trenan’s side. “Are you all right?” He laid his steel on the grass, the spots of red clinging to its tip obvious against the yellow backdrop, and put his hand under his father’s head for support. The faces of the dead crowded around Teryk, many of them seeming to press against him without his notice. Trenan’s eyes flickered from one to the next. Despite his attempt to stop them, tears spilled onto his cheeks. “I…I can’t.” He found his son once more, and he held his gaze on him, though he wanted to divert it, to hide this uncontrollable display of weakness. “I’ve already killed so many.” “It’s okay.” Teryk slid his arm down and under the master swordsman’s shoulders. “Let’s get you up.” The young man helped him sit up, then offered his hand to aid him getting to his feet. Trenan accepted it, scrambled to standing without grace. Light-headed, he wobbled, and Teryk held his arm to keep him from falling. When he regained his balance, he wiped away the tears on his forearm, but more replaced them. He tried not to look at his son, but the alternative of peering at the crowd of the dead pressing in on them left him cold. “I’m sorry.” “This isn’t your fault. It’s the priests, or the healer. They did this to you.” Trenan nodded to appease his son, but he remained unconvinced. He suspected the souls had always been with him, but he hadn’t been able to see them before. Why now didn’t matter and wouldn’t change the fact he’d ended these lives. He bore the responsibility for so much death and couldn’t bear any more. Teryk bent at the waist and retrieved his father’s sword, holding it in his right hand while his left steadied him, guiding him as they withdrew toward the fortress wall again. Trenan peered at his feet, boots crunching the dry grass under their leather soles. Each step squeezed his heart—once before he’d retreated

from a battle, and it had taken the loss of his arm to pull him from the fight. Never had the possibility of losing his nerve occurred to him. Yet here he was, being led from the fray by his son who, not so long ago, could barely sit a horse by himself. He’d worried the lad might never be himself again, and now he’d saved his life. How quickly things change. His legs didn’t want to carry him, but he forced them to as Teryk steered him around the corpse of the Goddess warrior. Trenan looked into her dead eyes as they passed, thankful they lacked the accusation of the other faces populating his days and nights since the day on the hilltop outside the Green. The sickness he’d felt had been bad, but he’d have traded the ghosts haunting him, the doubt they caused, for physical illness in a heartbeat. He longed to be himself again; he couldn’t imagine anything he’d rather more. They got as close to the fortress as they dared and Teryk held his arm as he sank to his knees. He stood beside him, put his hand on his shoulder. “It’s okay. Rest. I’ll take care of you.” The master swordsman nodded, let his chin sink to his chest and closed his eyes to avoid the ghosts stalking the surrounding space. *** “Trenan.” The hand gripping him gave him a brisk shake as he made his way back toward consciousness. “Trenan.” His eyelids fluttered open, the world around him blurred, but not from smoke. “How long did I sleep?” he asked, mouth dry and tacky. “Not long. Men approach. They wear the colors of my…the king.” The master swordsman blinked hard three times to clear the haze of slumber from his eyes. His head spun, left him feeling woozy, but Teryk’s hand remained on his shoulder, steadying him. When his bearings returned, the young man raised his arm and pointed. Eight of them. He squinted, trying to recognize any of them, but the brief, unexpected nap kept him from seeing clearly. And an army of the dead gathered around them distracted him with entrails hanging in the dirt, headless torsos blundering their way alongside men missing limbs. A gray fog tickled the edges of his vision as though he’d stood too fast. Instinct made him reach for his sword, but touching the grip brought about the same nausea as the last time he’d pulled it. A knot rose in his throat and he fought to keep from gagging on it. “Teryk, I…” “I’ve got this. Will you be okay?” Trenan nodded and his son took a step away, taking his hand from

his shoulder. The master swordsman leaned against the ground, maintaining his balance though his head spun like a child’s top. How did I sleep? He watched the young man go toward the soldiers, a flare of pride igniting in his chest, but it proved short-lived as a wall of the dead inserted themselves between them. The phantasms ignored everything going on around them, each staring at him as though he was the last person in existence. They shuffled his direction, one slow step at a time, obscuring Teryk, the king’s men, the Goddess warriors. The master swordsman set his jaw. They’re but ghosts. Remnants of the past. “Trenan?” The word floated to him from across a distance, from behind him, its tone familiar. He raised his head, scanned the expanse of open grass to his right, the burning tents, and then the gray wall beyond. Nothing. He scuffled around, turning his back on the specters and his son; it took but two heartbeats to spot the figure of the woman approaching. She wore no armor, instead clad in a robe of the Goddess, clothing he was unaccustomed to seeing her in. When he saw her, his heart missed a beat. “Trenan!” She started running toward him and he froze; chilly sweat formed a line on his forehead. Ishla.

X Ishla – Finding Trenan Ishla let herself become distracted from the simple task of guiding her galloping steed. Without her encouragement, it leapt a furrow left by a fireball, but misjudged the distance. Its front hoof clipped the edge on the far side, taking its legs from under it. The horse lurched forward, chest hitting the ground and skidding in the dirt. It twisted to protect itself, a pained whinny issuing from the injured steed. Surprised, Ishla reacted without thinking, pulling her feet from the stirrups and pushing herself away from the falling beast. She hit hard, but took the jolt on her shoulder, rolling over and over to absorb the impact until she came to a stop. She lay unmoving for a few heartbeats, pain flaring along her arm and into her spine, her face turned down into the grass. Behind her, she heard the animal struggling to return to its feet, chuffs and whinnies interspersed with the sounds of its hooves pawing the earth. Ishla rolled onto her back, groaned, and let out a long breath of her own. The blue sky hung above her, and she thought she might have laid there the entire day, looking at it until another fireball streaked by overhead, leaving a smoky tail in its wake. With an effort, she sat up, her muscles protesting against her doing so. She tested her shoulders, bent her elbows, flexed her hands. Painful, but seeming to lack real injury. She shifted and climbed gingerly to her feet, taking care with her joints, aware of how each movement affected her. Standing, she sighed her relief at the relative absence of damage she’d suffered. Her mount hadn’t gotten off as lucky. The poor animal lay on its side, inhaling and exhaling heavy breaths, one front limb twisted beneath it, but it must have sustained more injury than merely a broken leg. Empathy squeezed her heart. The horse should be put down instead of being left to suffer, but times of war demanded sacrifices. She closed her eyes, said a quick prayer to Goddess to grant mercy on her steed, and turned toward the fortress of Ikkundana. She’d been here once, a very long while ago. So long, she wondered if it was a memory of a true event, or if it might be the echo of a previous life. And she remembered the Mother of Death, though whether the same person as the one she recently visited at the temple in the city, she didn’t know. Your time has come to take up the fight. The Mother of Death’s words had stayed with her since she left the old woman. But what did it mean? Ishla wasn’t a fighter, despite the sword hanging at her side provided by the sisters. If they meant her to contribute to this battle, she knew not how.

She forced thoughts of the temple visit from her mind and took three tentative steps toward the fire burning at the base of the fortress wall. When Strylor had pointed out Teryk and Trenan fleeing across the plain, she’d picked them out easily. Now, after the ride and the fall, and with more people having found their way onto the grassland to engage in battle or fight the blaze, she’d lost track. She peered over the yellowed grass beaten by hooves and boots, searching for a recognizable shape. Medics, warriors—both male and female—women passing buckets of water along a chain to douse the flames. She inventoried them but she spied no one she recognized. Her gaze fell on a figure who stood out amongst the others like a rotten tooth in an otherwise pristine smile. He knelt alone on the ground, head hung, paying no attention to anything transpiring around him. She squinted, increased her pace, watching her footing more closely than she had her horse’s—a lesson hard learned. The sword at her waist bounced against her thigh, uncomfortable. Any other time, she’d have removed it, cast it aside; the rough wool of the robe chafed her skin, made her sweat as she put forth more effort. Her hand settled on the weapon’s grip to stop its annoyance; her fingers curled around it, grasped the soft leather wrap. She was too distant to make out his face, or markings on the armor, though she recognized it as higher quality than that of most of the other men she’d seen. Her steps grew quicker, boots whispering through flattened grass. Until then, the stink of the fireballs fallen from the sky had marred the air, a charnel stench now overwhelmed by the clinging odor of burning canvas. As she drew closer, the angle at which she regarded the man shifted and she realized he possessed only one arm. “Trenan?” Her muscles filled with aches and pains as she broke into a run, oblivious to the fight, the tents, the fortress. A thousand daggers poked at her shoulders, her thighs, her neck. Her legs wobbled beneath her, but whether because of the fall or the shock of seeing him, she couldn’t have said. “Trenan!” He faced her, and she pushed herself faster. If he was here, Teryk must be close. Her vision narrowed to the man before her—the man she’d loved, the man she’d been told murdered her child. She skidded to a stop two paces from him; Trenan made no move. He neither greeted her, nor retreated, merely gawked at her with a look of stunned disbelief. She stared back, unsure what to say. During the ride from Draekfarren, she’d imagined this reunion repeatedly, each time with different beginnings and distinct resolutions, but none

of her imaginings began with this…nothing. He stared at her as though he didn’t know her. “Trenan.” His gaze flickered from her eyes to her lips, over her shoulder, from one side to the other, before finding her face again. Not so long ago, standing this close to him would have set butterflies fluttering in her stomach. Now, her gut twisted into an uncomfortable knot, her fingers curled into fists. He continued looking at her without recognition. As though my daughter wasn’t dead. The tangle in her belly climbed into her chest, threatened to become a lump in her throat. She swallowed it and took one step nearer to the man who fathered her son. He wavered, leaned away like he thought she might hit him. His cheeks quivered, tension evident in his face as he refused to meet her eyes. “Is it true?” He tilted his head, brought his gaze up to hers; it flitted away and back, away and back. His lips pressed tight together, the bottom one sucked into his mouth, his jaw moving as though he chewed upon it. It wasn’t an expression she recalled ever having seen on him—fear, worry, anguish. Perhaps he’d worn a similar aspect once, the night she went to him after he lost his arm, but never since. She’d loved him for it then; she hated him for it now. “Say something,” she snapped. His mouth opened and closed twice. His tongue moistened his lips in preparation to speak, but he said nothing. Each action he took without explanation or communication became a nail driven into her heart. When he glanced away again, she stomped her foot to attract his attention to her. “Did you kill my daughter!?” His bottom lip quivered. “I…” His throat worked as he swallowed awkwardly. “I…” “You what?” The quiver in his lips turned into a shake. Wetness rimmed his eyes lids. “I didn’t.” “Who did, Trenan? Dansil said he saw. He claimed you killed her. Why? Why would you hurt her? Why would he lie?” Tears clogged her throat, made speaking difficult, but anger forced them through. His gaze stayed on her, but she recognized his difficulty in maintaining eye contact. Each time he wanted to look away became to her an admission of his guilt despite his words. “Not me,” he sputtered. “It was…it was…” “Who, damn it!” “Teryk.” The word came out a whisper, so quiet she wouldn’t have heard if

not standing so close. But he couldn’t mean Teryk had killed Danya; she was his sister. For their entire lives, they’d been thick as thieves, playing together, adventuring, getting into trouble. Surely, in his addled state, he meant to tell her something about her son. Their son. It’s not possible. Her legs wobbled, the energy sapped from them by the single word he spoke. She let herself sink to kneel in front of him, eyes wide with disbelief. “What are you saying?” He shook his head, tears spilling along his cheeks, caught in the stubble of too many days without shaving. He glanced over her shoulder again and this time she turned to find out what he peered at, hoping she might glimpse Teryk nearby. Nothing. She reached forward, put her hand on his cheek and angled his face toward her. It bore lines which didn’t exist the last time she saw him, and his eyes seemed haunted. Despite the tightness binding her chest, her heart ached for him, too. So many nights she’d lain awake, sometimes with the king beside her having deposited his seed, imagining what her life might have been. So many times she’d watched him and brimmed with love like she’d never known for anyone else before or since. “Trenan, what’s wrong with you?” His face pinched, and he flinched as though she’d slapped him rather than spoken to him. He raised his arm and gestured at the surrounding area. “I killed them,” he said, words squeaking. “I killed them all.” His head sagged to his chest and his shoulders slumped, rising and falling with sobs too savage to hide from the world. Ishla stared at him, wondering what he meant, the firm grip on her heart loosening with his tears. She’d never seen him act in any way approaching this manner, and it reminded her of the love she held for him. She leaned forward and slipped her arms around him. He collapsed against her, face buried against her robe, ragged sobs muffled by her shoulder. She put her hand on the back of his head, fighting against her own tears—for him, for them, for Danya. His body shook, and he wrapped his arm about her, drawing her tight against him. She closed her eyes, drew a deep breath in through her nose, nearly gagged on the stink of the burning canvas. She let it out again in a lengthy sigh between her lips meant to bring her a measure of control. “Where is Teryk?” she asked, fighting to keep it level. Trenan leaned back, his gaze finding hers for an instant. In that brief time, she recognized so much in his eyes: yearning, regret, sadness, fear. Things she’d never expected from him but so often experienced herself. He snuffled, blinked, turned his head with what appeared a significant effort—not like it weighed too much, but

because he didn’t want to look away from her. She waited the interval of four heartbeats, and then he raised his arm and pointed. Ishla looked to where he indicated, saw a man who stood the same height as her son but wore longer hair, more unkempt. Is it him? She straightened but, at this distance and with him facing away from her, she couldn’t be sure. As she stared, three men stalked toward him with bared steel, and she realized she had no choice but to trust the master swordsman, no matter his state. Ishla turned, kissed him on the forehead, and used him as leverage to gain her feet, the pain in her muscles incurred when her horse fell forgotten until then. She groaned aloud, gritted her teeth, and ran toward the man who might be her son.

XI Dansil – Opportunity “And they’ll do what I say?” “You have my word.” The healer’s assurances meant nothing to Dansil. In his heart, he believed in his ability to best the master swordsman on his own, but he had to consider the damned women. On their own, they posed no challenge, but he was one man if they tried to overwhelm him and defend Trenan. He couldn’t take the chance. He stood tall and raised his arm, waved it side to side. Behind him, he heard Strylor moan and realized the healer must have laid his hand on him again. His gut twinged at the possibility of his compatriot losing another body part, but the cause demanded it. Dansil dismissed the morbid curiosity making him want to find out what the robed man might take from him this time. A group of six soldiers yet to join the fight noticed him and made their way toward him. That should do. They gathered in front of him, mumbling amongst themselves, but none of them addressed him directly. Strylor whimpered. “I need your help,” Dansil said. They stared at him, making no motion of dissent or agreement. He felt a pressure against his back, as though someone laid a horse blanket on his shoulders, but it didn’t merely enshroud him, it moved past him. “By order of the king, you’re to come with me.” They nodded, glanced at each other, then waited. “Come closer,” a voice intoned from behind him. They did as he said, the six king’s men crowding Dansil. The air crackled and their eyes widened. “Please, no,” Strylor whispered before the world around them turned to gray. *** Teryk strode away from Trenan, his gut twinging at leaving him. Never in his life did he imagine he’d see the master swordsman in this state. Even before finding out the man was his father, he’d looked up to him in every regard—for his ability with a sword, his way of demanding respect, the fact he lived normally with one arm. Strength, loyalty, honor; these things Trenan instilled in him as being hallmarks of an exemplary soldier, attributes he himself swore by. And now his fear of ghosts left him incapacitated. Too simple, but it tucked it in a tidy little nutshell. Ghosts might not be the correct term; maybe guilt. Either way, it rendered the king’s most daunting fighter useless to the kingdom when it appeared

it needed him most. Teryk raised his hand to the soldiers of the king, but none of them responded in kind. He frowned, considered perhaps they hadn’t noticed, or didn’t realize who approached them. They don’t know I’m not their prince. He faltered. Do they? A group of Goddess warriors neared the men, adding to their numbers, and bringing Teryk a measure of relief. The tension in his shoulders let up and he adjusted his pace to be less hurried. Until one of the king’s soldiers lashed out at the nearest of the females, impaling her with his sword. He stopped without meaning to, his skin gone cold. The other warriors of the Windward Kingdom attacked the rest of the women, blades flashing. Three of the Goddess’ fighters fell, taken by surprise; the others defended themselves, though outnumbered. When the men swarmed them, Teryk spied two more figures hidden behind them: a fellow missing his left arm and part of his right, and a bald man clad in a robe. His eyes widened and tension returned to his muscles; his lips pulled up in a snarl and he snatched his sword from where it hung on his belt. “No,” he cried, and broke into a run. *** Dansil laughed aloud when he noticed the prince running toward them. Killing the whelp had never been his plan, but he was the lone soul who knew the truth of who’d killed the princess and might tell. Justification for a change in strategy. The former queen’s guard bounced his sword in his hand and smiled. For so long, he’d kept the secret of the prince’s true lineage and gotten nothing. Trenan had shown no appreciation, in no way aided him to climb the ranks or make him wealthy. It left him with the knowledge of the queen’s transgression, a fact he alone knew. His smile faded. The only thing he’d get from it was knowing he’d ended the life of the master swordsman’s son. “Guess it’ll have to do.” The prince—former prince—loped toward him with the alacrity of an amateur, someone determined to find himself dead on the end of Dansil’s sword. Seeing him returned a smidge of the former joy. “Come on then,” he yelled, gesturing for Teryk to attack him. The young man obliged with a wide, arcing swing of his short sword. Dansil caught it on the flat of his blade and stepped to his right, allowing his adversary’s momentum to carry him past. He could have retaliated with a blow of his own, taking out the tendon in the

back of the leg or slashing painfully across his spine, but he did neither. He saw this an opportunity to show the lad he was the greatest swordsman in the kingdom, not Trenan. Maybe he’d let the whelp live to tell him so. He spun around and raised his sword, facing away from Trenan, and awaited the youth’s next attempt. The boy didn’t disappoint. With his face pinched in a snarl of rage—an excellent indicator of a fighter without experience—he launched himself at Dansil, bringing his short sword down from above. This time, the former queen’s guard need only take a sidestep for the swipe to miss him. The tip of Teryk’s blade hit the ground, jarring his arms, and throwing his balance into doubt. Dansil responded by raising his boot, placing it against his adversary’s shoulder, and sending him sprawling backward. He tipped his head and laughed toward the sky. “Get up, lad. Is that all you’ve got? I expected your daddy would’ve taught you better.” He watched Teryk’s eyes widen as his own narrowed. He snorted, spat on the ground between them. “Yup, I saw the truth of who sired you. Last question is: which one of you will die on my sword first?” The former prince scrambled to his feet; this time he didn’t lunge at Dansil. Instead, he held the weapon out in front of him, kept his eyes on his adversary as he circled, searching for an opening. “Ha! Fucker didn’t teach you how to use a blade properly. Maybe I can do it before I open you up and spill your innards out onto the grass.” Teryk’s eye twitched, but he refused to take the bait. As he continued his slow circle—crossing his feet instead of sliding them, a mistake Dansil allowed him to get away with for now—the one-time queen’s guard noted the other soldiers had dispatched the warrior bitches. Not without casualty, though; two men lay dead or near to it while a third rolled on the ground holding in his guts. More would be here soon, so it might be time to finish the whelp. They’d turned around from where they started and, as Dansil raised his sword, he glimpsed Trenan over the shoulder of his son; the so- called master swordsman wasn’t alone. The person with him was a woman garbed in the robes of the Goddess, but he’d guarded her long enough before Strylor took over to recognize the queen. “Fuck me. What’s she doing here?” Teryk seized the opportunity afforded by the distraction and leapt forward, lunging with the tip of his sword. He almost caught Dansil off guard. Almost. The veteran soldier swiped the blade aside and put his boot to the former prince’s backside, then spun around and darted toward the healer.

“Take me to the king.” The bald man gripped Strylor’s shoulder, who jumped as though stung by a hornet. Dansil had an instant to see tears shining on the queen’s guard’s cheeks before the world winked out. When it reappeared, they’d returned to where they’d started. Dansil shook his head, orienting himself and appreciating the fact he didn’t need to vomit; he spied Erral seated atop his destrier, prominent between the coursers of his advisers. Their backs were to them and the former queen’s guard wasted no time. “Come,” he said over his shoulder while gesturing for the healer to follow without waiting to find out if he did or not. He stalked across the compressed grass, sword gripped tight in his fist, the missing fingers reminding him of what he’d been through to get here. A pace behind the king, he stopped, opened his mouth to speak but one of the adviser’s horses lifted its tail and sent a clutch of manure thumping to the ground, interrupting. Dansil sneered, cleared his throat. “Your majesty.” The regent either didn’t hear, or ignored him. Dansil took a step closer, spoke louder. “Your majesty.” Erral didn’t move, but the adviser to the right glanced toward him. When he noticed the former queen’s guard, he leaned toward the monarch and whispered. Erral raised his arm, flicked his fingers in the air like a man with a ball of snot stuck to the tip. The gesture might as well have been a slap to the face. Dansil darted forward, grabbed him by the wrist, and wrenched himself around, facing the healer standing a few paces behind, hand on Strylor’s shoulder. Tears streaked his cheeks, his expression twisted by sobs. “What are you—” Erral blurted but didn’t get a chance to finish. “Take us back,” Dansil demanded. He swallowed hard and readied himself for the world to disappear. *** By the time Teryk righted himself and got turned around to accept whatever attack his mother’s guard might launch at him, they were gone. “What?” His shoulders sagged and the short sword hung limp at his side as he stared at the empty space the healer and a man who wasn’t Stirk had filled a heartbeat before. It was as though they, along with Dansil, hadn’t been there at all. The other of the king’s soldiers, however, remained. The three remaining men wore confused expressions reflecting Teryk’s own feelings. They looked from their downed companions to the lifeless Goddess warriors, then to the spot where

Dansil and the others had been. When they also found it vacant, their attention shifted to Teryk. One of them raised his sword and pointed. “Get ’im!” The tone of his words suggested they’d rush Teryk; instead, they stalked toward him, wariness in their steps. Did they assume he’d dispelled their compatriots? If so, he might use it to his benefit and, considering they numbered three to his one, he needed every available advantage. He gripped the hilt of his sword tighter, brought it up in a defensive stance, then raised his other hand, palm out facing his aggressors. “Stop or I’ll banish you as well.” To his mild surprise, they halted. The leader glared at him, then glanced at the others. When his gaze returned to Teryk, he burst out in harsh, humorless laughter. “You think us idiots, boy? How is it you s’pose we got here?” They started toward him again, gleeful savagery shining in their eyes, and Teryk felt a sinking from his chest into his gut. He lowered his arm, gritted his teeth, and thought through the lessons Trenan had given him through his youth. Did he give advice on what to do when facing multiple opponents at the same time? He believed so: avoid at all costs. Three of them. That’s all. He swallowed around a lump in his throat, dropped his hand, and took a step away from the soldiers. As he did, Trenan’s lessons popped into his head: never walk backward, always sideways or you’ll risk tripping; don’t cross your feet when you move. Teryk readjusted, sword arm toward them. A drop of sweat rolled from his forehead into his eye; he blinked it away rather than wiping it on his sleeve. If they attacked at once, he’d have little chance of survival. If he had any hope, it was either one-on-one or talking them out of attacking. “Do you know who I am?” he demanded, lowering his voice and doing his best to instil in it the tone of authority he’d heard used by both the man he’d considered his sire and the one who truly was. “Aye, we know.” “As prince of the kingdom, I command you to stop where you are. What will my father do to you if he finds out you threatened my life?” He shuffle-stepped away, the way Trenan taught him. “Why don’t we ask him?” the leader said, angling his chin at a point behind Teryk. “Looks as though he and your mother might be talkin’ ’bout you right now.” Teryk sucked a breath between his teeth, tried to resist the temptation to peer over his shoulder toward where he’d left Trenan. He did so for a moment, then gave in. He planted his feet, turned his

head; the queen knelt beside Trenan, looking into his face while he stared at the ground, her hand on his cheek. This he saw in the space of four heartbeats before the three men of the king’s army rushed him.

XII Erral – Trenan Pain flared in Erral’s gut, and he was vaguely aware of hitting the ground, but all remained dark around him. The man, Dansil, must have pulled him right off his steed, but what of the injury? Did he stab him? The king rolled onto his back, forced his eyes open. Instead of looking up at his horse, or the concerned faces of his advisers standing over him, billows of smoke blotted out the sky. He blinked hard twice, untrusting of what his vision showed him. It didn’t disappear, so he put his hand to his belly, brought it up in front of his face, expecting to find blood on his fingers. They were clean. “Are you okay, your majesty?” He recognized the voice as Dansil’s and rolled over, pushed himself up to his knees far too fast. His head spun and his stomach lurched; a hand on his shoulder kept him from toppling to the grass. As soon as the wave of nausea passed, he shrugged it off and climbed unsteadily to his feet. The former queen’s guard stood in front of him, two other men behind him and to his right. Erral glanced at them. One he identified as Ishla’s current escort and the sight of him brought him instant rage; he’d have acted on it but for the fact the fellow looked to have been through a battle and come out of the wrong end. The other man wore a black robe which instilled a different reaction in him despite his hood being thrown off to reveal a gleaming bald pate and hungry eyes. Erral reoriented his attention to Dansil. “What’s going on here?” he demanded. “What have you done?” “I’ve brought you here to show you something. You wanted to find Trenan, did you not?” The king frowned but didn’t answer; the question deserved no response. “And the queen, too, I presume? Would it surprise you to discover them together?” “What are you talking about?” Erral snapped. His hands curled into fists. “I don’t have time for your games.” “I think this will interest you.” The man’s mouth contorted into a lopsided smile dripping with a cocky confidence Erral desired to slap away. The urge didn’t dissipate in the slightest when he crossed the few paces between them and draped his arm around the king’s shoulders. “What—?” “You’ll want to see this.” Dansil exerted pressure against him, prompting him to shift. Erral did so grudgingly, unused as he was to being touched or spoken to in such a way. He’d find out what this man wanted for now but, when

this concluded, he’d face consequences for his actions. Repercussions awaited many people. They completed the turn, putting the burning tents and the fortress to their left, the plains to their right. He’d seen the fire from atop his horse before finding himself here, but distant enough not to cause him worry. He used its proximity to calculate how far he’d—traveled? Been moved? He glanced toward the grasslands and noticed the fighting had spilled farther this direction than he realized. “There,” Dansil said, pointing at a spot ahead of them and to the right. Erral stared. It proved easy enough to identify Trenan, as no other one-armed men would ever be allowed on a battlefield, but it took him a moment to recognize Ishla. She wore a near-colorless cloak and her hair hanging loose—not the way she normally dressed. But her appearance meant little as she raised her hand and lay it against the master swordsman’s cheek. The king growled and tried to shrug Dansil’s arm from his shoulders, but the former queen’s guard held him tight to keep him in place. Erral cocked his head to look at him. “Let me go.” “But there’s more than just what you see, my liege,” Dansil said, enjoying the drama. “Not only did Trenan kill your daughter, he is the father of the boy you call your son.” Erral’s lip curled, exposing his teeth, and his cheeks warmed. Had he a weapon at hand, he’d have used it to end the soldier’s life. “Speculation,” he spat, but he knew it to be more. For many turns of the seasons he’d suspected them, often spotting the way Ishla and Trenan gazed at each other when they thought nobody around to notice; he recognized how Danya bore a resemblance to him, yet Teryk did not. And he’d seen how the master swordsman treated the boy. These and more hints added up to a conclusion he’d done his best to avoid. Dansil leaned close. “I saw,” he said, his stale air brushing the king’s ear. “I was but a lad, adventuring in a part of Draekfarren forbidden to me. Where your good queen didn’t expect me to be. I watched her go to Trenan during his recovery, more than once, I did.” The king clamped his jaw tight, huffed a hard breath out through his nose. He turned his attention to the couple kneeling in the grass in time to spy his wife kiss his friend on the forehead. He took half a step; Dansil continued restraining him. “Give me your sword,” he growled. “I can do better,” the man replied. He cocked his head and said over his shoulder, “Strylor, fetch the king his axe.” A whimper from behind them lasted a moment, then cut off. Erral

paid it little attention as he watched the queen embrace the master swordsman once more then get to her feet. She turned and ran off another direction. He opened his mouth to call out, but changed his mind. If she noticed him, came to him, she’d surely beg his forgiveness, his mercy. He had neither to offer her and her lover. An instant later, the robed man and the queen’s guard appeared before them, startling Erral; he jumped, heart beating faster in his chest. Black priest. He glared at the bald fellow, realized he not only lacked hair on his head, but anywhere else on his face, and it left the king wondering if he was male at all.
