The smug expression he wore on his countenance gave no hint of his gender. With a flutter of his fingers, he gestured toward the queen’s guard. Strylor rested on hand and knee—he had but a single arm and one full leg remaining—in front of his monarch. His head hung like a man exhausted, a string of saliva hanging from his mouth and sweat or tears or both dripping from his face. He grasped the haft of Erral’s battle axe, the flat side pressed against the ground. The king sneered, bent at the waist, and snatched the weapon away. “Give it to me,” he said. Strylor toppled over, his support ripped from under him, a sound like the mewling of an enraged kitten issuing from him. Erral ignored it, shrugged off Dansil’s arm, and started toward the traitor kneeling in the grass. *** It didn’t take long for Teryk to realize the three men toyed with him. One pranced in, took a couple of blows and pokes at him, then dodged away to allow another of his fellows to do the same. Until he caught on to their fun, he thought himself doing an outstanding job in defending. Then he understood their game—their laughter gave it away. A man leaning toward portly with a pencil-thin mustache lunged. Teryk spun, the point of the king’s soldier’s sword catching his sleeve and cutting a hole in it. He swung in return but his attacker, despite his girth, danced aside. The next—a craggy-faced fellow with apple- red cheeks—aimed a two-handed downward blow at the blade of Teryk’s weapon, driving it down. The tip hit the ground, setting him stumbling forward a half-step. He recovered, but realized the soldier could have struck a devastating follow-up stroke. Instead, he stepped away, and bellowed a laugh skyward. “Magnificent work, prince,” he said, emphasizing the title like an epithet. They only gave him enough time to recover before the third man—

this one not much older than Teryk himself, with a baby face sprinkled with wispy whiskers and hair sticking out from the sides of his helm looking too small for him—lunged at him. But Teryk had seen this move before and, instead of dodging the wrong direction like before, he parried the attack with his blade, then brought his sword up. The sharp edge of his steel dragged along the young soldier’s forearm. He jumped back with a screech, free hand going to the wound. Teryk noted with satisfaction blood leaking through his fingers. “He fucking cut me,” the injured king’s man shrieked. “Enough playin’,” portly soldier growled. He took a pace toward his prey while craggy face maneuvered himself to get behind him. The former prince turned, taking care to shuffle his feet and not cross them up. When the two soldiers stood one to his left, the other to his right, he caught sight of someone unexpected as he glanced between them. “Mother?” “Your practice-yard trickery ain’t gonna work on us, boy,” apple cheeks said and spat on the ground at Teryk’s boots. Teryk looked away again out of necessity, keeping his eyes on first one threat, and then the other. Each time his gaze slipped between them, he saw the woman getting closer, her hair flying out behind her as she ran. How is she here? “Ain’t no trick,” the young soldier with the cut on his arm said, his tone filled with amazement. “It’s the queen.” Teryk took a last look at each of the other men as they lowered their weapons, and he backed up three paces away from them. As she approached, he let his own sword down. When she reached him, she wrapped her arms around him. “Oh my Goddess, you’re alive.” She squeezed him tight, then leaned back, brushed the hair out of his face to get a better look at him. “Are you all right?” Shocked, he could do nothing but stare at her, the last person he’d expected here. He hadn’t prepared himself for what he must tell her. He blinked and shook his head. “How—?” She ignored his reaction and pulled him close again. A hard object under her cloak pushed against him and he realized she was armed. How could the king allow her to join the fight? Had he lost his mind? Emotion welled up in the former prince, threatening to spill out in the form of tears, a torrent of words. But what to say? He murdered his sister? Knew they'd lied to him his entire life? His father couldn’t operate because the ghosts of everyone he’d killed haunted him? It

barely made any sense to him, and he’d lived through it. As she held him, he heard the men who’d been attacking him shuffling away, no doubt hiding their faces and hoping for neither of them to remember them and report them to the king. Teryk didn’t care; being reunited with his mother offered the first bit of relief he’d experienced in longer than he dared recall. He closed his eyes for two heartbeats, enjoying the respite for the briefest of times for, when he opened them again, another shock ran through him. “No,” he whispered and grabbed her by the shoulders, pushed her away. “Teryk? What is it?” “The king,” he said and bolted from her, headed for the man stalking toward his father, axe in hand. “Trenan!” *** The world narrowed to the path leading to the traitor. Erral no longer saw anything else around him, the fire diminished to naught but an annoying smell, the lone sound the whoosh of his own blood in his ears. His heart thumped against his ribs; he squeezed the haft of his weapon, muscles in his forearm knotted and ready to dole out the punishment due. No reason to save the job for an executioner when he had the opportunity and desire to do it himself. His heavy footsteps hammered the ground, flattening grass and leaving impressions in the dry soil. When he’d reached within ten paces of the man he once called friend, he stopped. “Trenan,” he roared. The leather of his gauntlet creaked as he flexed his fingers against the doeskin-wrapped handle of his weapon. The master swordsman appeared distracted; he neither looked toward his regent nor responded. His lack of attention and respect stoked the rage burning in Erral’s chest. “Have you nothing to say for yourself? After fucking my wife and killing my daughter?” More silence from him. He approached one step closer. “Trenan.” The traitor finally raised his chin, brought his gaze to bear, though it appeared he peered right through him. His mouth opened and closed twice; no sound emerged. “I command you to rise and face your king.” Trenan’s head jerked like someone had hit him, then it drooped and he stared at his hand resting in his lap. No further response, no following the order issued by his commander. “Insolence,” he spat and resumed walking toward the liar kneeling on the ground ahead of him. Anger flooded blood into his limbs; his vision grayed at the edges. “Murder. Lies. Adultery. Of this and more, you stand accused. What do you have to say for yourself?”

Five paces remained between them. Trenan stayed hunched forward, as though ready to accept the punishment he deserved. And Erral was fit to dispense it. He halted with one pace left separating them and stood, legs spread at shoulder width, scowling down at his general. If the master swordsman knew of his presence, he did nothing to show it. Blind rage filled the king, blocking out everything around him as he shifted his hold on the axe’s haft to grip it with both hands. Blood roared in his ears, his lips peeled up in a snarl, baring his teeth. Erral inhaled through his nose, raised his weapon, and held it aloft momentarily to give the traitor an opportunity to offer an excuse, beg his forgiveness, admit his wrong-doing. He continued staring at his hand, resigned to his fate. The king released his breath and brought the axe down with all the force in his body, eyes closing with the effort. The blade contacted flesh, but too soon by his estimation. A cry battered his ears, but not in the master swordsman’s voice. Something wrenched his weapon sideways, jerked it from his grip. The unexpectedness of it spun him. He snapped his lids open and saw a man fall to the ground, skidding in the grass and leaving a trail of blood in his wake from where Erral had separated his arm from his body. The king stared, confused, until he heard a voice from behind him. Ishla’s voice. “Teryk!”

XIII Teryk – Fade to Black It hurt more than he’d imagined. Teryk had spent little of his life wondering what it might be like having his arm sheared off, but he’d probably done it more than most, given who’d mentored him. He didn’t notice the pain until he hit the ground and skidded to a stop. His nose and chin scraped in the dry grass. Bits of the yellowed blades and dirt got in his mouth, the soil grating against his teeth. He tried to spit, but the effort proved too great. He drew his arm under him and pushed hard enough to roll over, but something underneath him made it uncomfortable. He wanted to shift, to reach over and pull it from behind him; when he did, he realized what had happened, because he had no arm. The pain from his shoulder flooded into him and he cried out again. Tears overflowed onto his cheeks, smearing the smoky sky into a blur of gray. A blob of a face hovered to his side, and he blinked to clear the water away and find out who stood beside him. The king waited two paces distant, eyes wide and mouth agape, but he did nothing more than stare. Seeing him, Teryk’s mind flashed to the times the man he’d assumed his father had the opportunity to offer him aid and chose not to. When he found out the truth of his paternity, he understood why—he must have known at some level that Teryk wasn’t his son. But would he stand back and let him die? It appeared so. It might have been a moment later, or perhaps considerably longer —time didn’t matter so much to him anymore—when his mother fell to her knees beside him. She knelt close enough for him to make out her features through the blur of tears, but was it getting darker, too? She leaned in, put her hands on his face, her palms so warm on his skin. Her lips moved, but he found following what she said troublesome. A tear rolled along her nose, dropped onto his forehead, then she turned away and yelled over her shoulder. At the king, he suspected, and it amused him to imagine her hollering at the monarch. He’d have smiled were his mouth capable. Someone rocked him up a bit and pulled the uncomfortable thing from under him; enough wits remained for him to recognize it as his severed arm. Seeing it made his head spin faster until pressure against his wound sent a jolt of agony through his entire being. It brought his voice out of hiding and he let out what he intended a scream but which may have been nothing but an exhalation of breath. They lowered him again, and the compression continued on his shoulder, but the pain faded as his body numbed. The strain gave him a flash of clarity and he perceived other faces

looming behind the queen; besides the king, he recognized Dansil, who was his mother’s guard, and the hairless moon of the healer’s face. But he wasn’t really a healer, he realized now. Teryk didn’t know what other name to give him, what other label suited. What the creature did was far removed from healing. He wondered if he could have brought Danya back from the dead, as he claimed. If he’d been willing to sacrifice Trenan’s life, would his sister live again? He inhaled a shuddering breath as the queen leaned forward and pressed her face against his. She spoke as she did so, her words no more than a jumble of sounds to him, as indecipherable as the noises made by an animal. When she leaned away and their gazes met, he realized how much she and Danya looked alike—the line of their noses, the set of their cheekbones, the shape of their eyes. How did he not notice before? They shared the same features as he and his sister. I’m so sorry, Danya. He’d heard it said a man close to slipping into the realm of death sees clearly his successes and mistakes. If such was correct, then Teryk decided he either must not be near to the end, or the murder of his sibling outweighed every other occurrence in his life. But of course it did. Any other blunder paled beside it; any success became irrelevant. During his time, the king had dealt with him as though he wasn’t his son—rightly so, it turned out—while Trenan, his true father, held him at arm’s distance. His mother had treated him well, but her duties as the queen kept her busy and often unavailable. Through everything, it was always his sister at his side—good times, bad times, adventure, heartache. Always him and her; always them. Teryk blinked, attempted to lick his lips with a tongue dry enough it might better be used to freshen the edge on a knife. His mother saw this and issued an order over her shoulder. Dansil shifted and moved, produced a skin he handed to the queen. She uncorked it, tilted it toward her son’s mouth. Cool water touched his tongue, splashed over his chin and onto his neck. His throat worked hard to swallow it, each spasm of his esophagus squeezing a few drops down. If only he could drink, he’d feel better; the liquid would refresh him, force out the gray haze overtaking the edges of his vision. He opened and closed his mouth, trying to use the action to squeeze more of the fluid into his throat, but it spilled out, ran along his cheeks. At least he could employ his tongue to wet his lips now. He did so, though he lacked the ability to sense if he’d found success at the venture. Thinking about it, he didn’t seem in touch with any part of his body. He attempted to wiggle his toes, to flex his fingers, shift his head. None of them responded. In some places, he sensed a vague tingling, but even it faded with the sunlight.

Sound muffled into indistinguishable pulses. His nose ceased identifying or recognizing odors. The world dwindled to a pinpoint of light. Teryk gazed up at his mother, did his best to shape his mouth into a smile, and closed his eyes. *** Strylor finished dragging himself across the space, his palm raw from sharp-edged grass chafing it and unnoticed rocks pressing against his skin. He halted beside the healer, his shoulder brushing the bald man’s leg. Given a choice, he’d have crawled the opposite direction to get himself as far from him as possible. Unfortunately, freewill had left the queen’s guard after the first time the robed man took a part of him. When he stopped, he hung his head, panting from the exertion and the toll taken on his body by the loss of various parts. He coughed, spat an unpleasant mixture of phlegm and blood on the ground in front of him, then attempted to raise his chin. Dansil and the king stood ahead of them, both regarding the figures another stride or two beyond them. Strylor peeked through their limbs to discover what held their attention. The master swordsman knelt to one side, head hanging and paying no mind to anyone near him. Beside him, he spied the legs of someone sprawled flat on their back; on the ground nearby lay a severed arm. Strylor gulped a mouthful of saliva. Is it mine? The possibility the healer might leave a limb he’d taken lying around seemed unlikely; Strylor shuffled forward, anyway. He stopped a half step closer to Erral and Dansil when the robed man put a hand on his shoulder. He exhaled a breath bearing an unintentional moan, squinted at the arm, then cocked his head to survey himself. The sleeve on the severed limb didn’t match the color of his own tunic. It wasn’t his, but did that mean it couldn’t be? Maybe the healer could make it his. He craned his neck and looked up at the hairless face. The black-robed being paid him no attention, instead staring at the others in the same way as the king and his friend. Strylor returned his concern to what interested everyone else, doing his best to put the stray and available arm from his mind. He glanced at it, slurped a string of saliva into his mouth, then averted his gaze to the people on the ground. The figure kneeling in front of him blocked him from seeing to whom the legs belonged. He saw the back of the individual, their shoulders hunched forward as they leaned in to the other. They wore a nondescript cloak, the color of which niggled at his mind. He knew he should recognize it but didn’t.

No one but the stooped-over person moved for a lengthy time. Strylor’s shoulder ached from holding himself up with his remaining arm; he tilted his head side to side, stretching the muscles in his neck to relieve the fatigue. Once, not so long ago, he’d have stood beside the others. How did he get in this place? Dansil. One of the few people in his life he’d called friend. It took little for him to volunteer bits of Strylor’s body to the healer for whatever he needed for himself. Not the actions of a comrade, the way Strylor saw it. He cocked his head and glanced up at the man who’d been the queen’s guard before him. Like the others, he stared straight ahead; from his angle so close to the ground, Strylor couldn’t make out his expression, didn’t have any idea what he thought about the events unfolding before them. When he turned to look for himself, the hunching figure had stood, head still hung. Between the person’s stature and the hair tumbling down the shoulders, he drew the conclusion he looked at a woman. A flicker in his chest made him draw a sharp breath as puzzle pieces fell together in his foggy mind. Trenan, the king. It was Dansil’s plan to put them in the same place for Erral to punish his confidant, an aim which necessitated the loss of Strylor’s bits and parts. Why his so-called friend wanted the master swordsman punished, he didn’t know, but his actions showed it to be true. And since they assumed they’d find Trenan in the prince's company, was it Teryk lying on the ground? If so, the woman hunched over him must be only one person. She turned, and the queen’s guard’s pulse beat faster, his eyes widened. Ishla. My love. His muscles tightened with the desire to go to her, embrace her to the best of his capability, ask forgiveness, offer her his, but he forgot everything when she raised her head. Tears streaked her face; grief tugged her mouth down at the sides, drew lines across her forehead. Strylor’s heart shriveled at the sight. “He’s dead,” she said, voice deeper than usual, half-choked. “And you stood by and did nothing.” They went on doing nothing. Strylor’s gaze flickered from one to the next as Erral, Dansil, and the healer viewed her; Trenan continued staring at his hand in his lap. He looked to the queen and watched emotion after emotion cross her brow: pain, grief, shock, and finally anger. She directed her scorn on the king, eyes narrowing. “You killed him.” The torment in her voice, the fresh tears leaking down her face, tore at Strylor’s insides. His heart curled itself in a ball and rose into

his throat. He inhaled a shuddering breath; another time, it might have turned to sobs, but now he fought them, for an idea occurred to him. He understood how to relieve his love’s pain. Strylor pushed against the ground with his hand, tilting himself. He did so hard enough to topple over backward but caught Dansil by the sleeve before he tipped. Surprised, the former queen’s guard and erstwhile friend attempted to jerk away; Strylor’s grip held fast, strengthened by his resolve for what he must do. “The healer…” he croaked. Strylor stopped, enticed some spit into his mouth and sloshed it around. “The healer can bring him back.” All eyes turned toward him and he sneaked a glance at Ishla; her expression softened the slightest amount. The sight of her slight relief gave him strength. He pivoted on his two stumps, switched his hold from Dansil’s sleeve to the bald man’s robe, canting precariously. After straightening himself and drawing a breath, he inclined his head and glared at the hairless face. The healer’s smooth, pale skin nearly glowed in the sunlight, but not a drop of perspiration glimmered anywhere on his flesh. “Take my life for his,” Strylor said. “I give it freely for you to return him from the realm of the dead.” The healer gazed at him, a look nearing bemusement twitching the corner of his mouth. He stared at him, rocked his head back and forth, then titled it to the side. “No,” he said, sly smile canting his lips. “I am nothing without you, Strylor.” His expression, the tone of his voice; both cut the queen’s guard as though he’d swung a blade at him. Strylor returned his attention to the queen, his love, and opened his mouth, intending to apologize. What he saw stopped him. Ishla’s face went red with rage. She reached under her cloak, pulled out a weapon longer than a short sword, but thin, her thick robe muting the sound as she yanked it from its sheath. As they gawked at this unexpected reaction, she shrugged the coat from her shoulders. It fell to her waist, where the rope belt wrapped around her held it, revealing her bare chest beneath. Strylor gasped. In the first instant before she crossed the space between her and the healer, he didn’t understand why she might expose her breasts here, now. Then he remembered. She thinks he’s a black priest. He gulped, wondered why he hadn’t considered the possibility. The thought fled his mind as she stood in front of the bald man, practically bumping against him with her blade held at the perfect spot near her waist for the tip to brush him under the chin. “Is it possible to bring him back?”

Strylor had never heard her use such a tone before, not even at her angriest with him. If he possessed legs, he might have backed away a step. “It is.” “Then do it,” she snapped. The healer made a clicking sound with his tongue—once, twice, three times—then shook his head. He appeared unconcerned with the knife tip tickling the underside of his chin. “That is not how it works, my queen. To revive a life, you must offer one in return.” She glanced at Strylor and, though he hadn’t been doing it this time, he felt the same as every other instance she’d caught him ogling her breasts. There they were, in front of his eyes—and bared—yet he dared not so much as peek. This is what love is. Ishla returned her gaze to the healer, glaring at him. “My guard offered himself to resurrect Teryk.” “So he did,” the robed man drawled, seeming to enjoy dragging out the drama. “But I can’t be the one who takes a soul to return a soul. It must be proffered to me by he or she who desires the restoration. The death realms are particular about their souls.” To Strylor’s senses, the air grew thick. Maybe a breeze rose, blowing the smoke of the tent fires toward them. He tested it with his nose but noticed no more fumes than before. No, it wasn’t smoke, but his own reticence, or her expectation. The queen diverted her gaze to him again. It touched him like the caress he’d desired from her from the first instant he saw her, dispensing the haze in his brain, the heaviness of the air. His heart filled; he imagined a bird singing somewhere nearby. He tilted his mouth up in his best proximity of a smile and nodded. Ishla nodded too, took a step away from the healer, relieving his chin from the point of her narrow sword. He inhaled a breath through his nose he’d have sworn carried the bouquet of spring flowers, then released it slowly. He closed his eyes and waited to give her his life in return for her son. The thin blade whistled through the air and Strylor tensed, awaiting its sting. It hissed again, and this time he heard it strike; he experienced nothing. The world went quiet but for the beat of his heart as it pumped lifeblood through his veins once, twice. Is this what it’s like to be dead? A gurgling pulled him from the silence; the sound hadn’t originated with him. He opened his eyes in time to watch the king sink to his knees and then pitch forward, blood gushing from the open wound in his throat.
“Now you have your sacrifice,” Ishla said over her shoulder, voice icy. She spun, brought the sword tip to bear on the healer again. “Give me back my son.”

XIV Ishla – Resurrection Ishla concentrated on holding the sword steady, keeping the tip trained on the strange person in the black robe. After a long while, the healer nodded. His expression didn’t change from the mild bemusement he’d been wearing as he crossed the space to where Erral lay, blood pumping in a decreasing stream from the wound in his throat, painting the yellow grass red. The king drew occasional ragged, wet breaths, the time between each lengthening. Ishla turned as the healer passed, keeping her weapon pointed at him. What have I done? When she’d realized it was she who must take a life to retrieve Teryk from the realm of the dead, emotion controlled her before she thought. Her blade flickered through the air, slicing across Erral’s throat and sending droplets of blood spraying with no concern for consequence. The only things her rage allowed her to see was his axe lopping off Teryk’s arm, his moments of anger, his unwillingness to put real effort into finding their children. The healer laid a hand on the king’s forehead and Erral’s body jerked as though someone struck him. Ishla gasped a breath, held it. A sound emanated from the bald man, a low hum perhaps with words hidden in it; if so, they were too quiet or too foreign to understand. She let the air from her lungs and glanced away at the other two men observing the proceedings. If she’d taken time to think, she’d have accepted Strylor’s offer of giving his soul for the prince. He’d been a constant source of annoyance to her from the time Erral had appointed him her guard, but his exposure to the healer had left him ravaged, physically half a man. And Goddess knew how such manipulation by a black priest affected him mentally. Taking his life might have been a relief for him, a release from torment. In the end, though, he’d shown willingness to sacrifice for her when Erral did nothing. Easy to understand why, when emotion ruled, she made the choice to spare him and kill the king. She turned toward king and healer. Blood had ceased flowing from the wound and he lay unmoving; any of the king’s exposed skin had gone as white as the healer’s flesh. Ishla shivered at the thought. Did it mean the man himself wasn’t alive? The hum continued, deep and steady. It caused a shimmer in the air; it vibrated in her chest. What will happen when it is discovered I killed the king? The question flashed through her mind, though the answer meant nothing. If sacrificing his life brought back her son, she’d willingly do it again, no matter the cost to her. Part of her wanted to grieve—he’d been her husband all these turns of the season—but that part was a mere sliver, for it wasn’t true. She’d

been his wife while he was being the king and no proper partner to her. Husbands care for their wives, fathers mentor their children. Erral had done neither, preferring to spend his time embroiled in the affairs of the kingdom rather than those of his family. The healer stood and Ishla took a step away, keeping the tip of her sword pointed at him. She noticed her shoulder ached. The robed man flashed a glance in her direction and she watched his expression change. Instead of bearing the countenance of someone entertained by what went on around him, his features shifted into something trance-like—eyes hooded, mouth slack, cheeks empty of color. He reoriented his attention toward Teryk and made his way to the prince, kneeling beside him when he arrived, though whether he possessed legs with knees and feet hidden beneath his robe, Ishla did not know for sure. She swallowed, adjusted her grip on the sword’s hilt without lowering it. A droplet of sweat ran from her neck and down her front, tracing a wet line between her breasts. Her heart throbbed, each beat bumping it against her ribcage; she sucked her bottom lip into her mouth and bit on it. The healer laid his hands upon Teryk’s chest. The hum she felt as much as heard continued, shifting to a different quality, atonal—harsh to her ears and resonating unpleasantly in her being. Her muscles tensed to thwart its distasteful nature. Beyond the disagreeable thrum, nothing appeared to happen. And then, all at once, it did. The prince drew a sudden breath, air whistling in between his lips, and energy jolted through her own body. She resisted the urge to rush to him, take him in her arms and cradle him against her. It took every bit of her resolve to keep from going to her son. The healer got to his feet, pivoted toward her, the catatonic nature of his features returned to their normal state of beguilement. “It is done.” He waved one arm in Teryk’s direction, as though giving her permission to visit, then slipped each hand into the opposite sleeve and floated to where Strylor and Dansil stood. Ishla stared at her son, enthralled by the uneven rhythm of the rise and fall of his chest. His eyes remained closed. Every fiber of her being wanted to go to him, to offer succor to her boy. She didn’t. I have more than one child. The queen faced the robed man again, stretching her sword arm toward him, renewing her threat. “My daughter,” she said, forcing the words between teeth clenched with determination. The healer dipped his head and laughed. The sound contained no

joy or mirth; if it carried on too long, she might have slit his throat to make it stop. The appalling moment of levity ceased, and he trained his gaze upon her again. “It cannot be.” Her eyes narrowed. “You said that before.” “Indeed, but this is different.” “I have another life to give.” She flicked the tip of her sword toward Dansil and the former queen’s guard raised both hands, palms facing her, and faded back a step. Did he only have three fingers on the one hand before? Not that she recalled. She trained the weapon on the bald man. “Oh, I see,” the healer said, the voice’s tone equally likely to belong to female as male. “You don’t know.” A pace closer to him, the sword tip floating half a hand’s breadth from his face. “Know what?” “It’s not the life you offer, my queen, but the one your request.” Her frown deepened, the nerves in her body firing and bringing a tingle across her flesh. “What do you mean?” “The princess is not dead, Ishla. Not all of her, at least. She is at a place where even I cannot go.” “Not dead?” “You’ll find out soon enough, I suspect.” The tension in her loosened, the sword tip drooped away from the healer’s face. Ishla’s eyes darted from him to Strylor and Dansil, to the fire burning at the base of the fortress walls then back. Though she gazed upon it, she recognized none of it. She didn’t know if she should believe his words. Did he have any reason to lie? The healer shook his head, amused expression shifting to impatience. “Since I am apparently not going to get what I wanted,” he lifted his chin, gesturing toward Trenan behind her. “My time here is done.” *** Emotion wrestled in Strylor as he watched the proceedings. The queen had chosen him over her husband, and she’d gotten back her son, both of which elated him. But then he saw her confusion and disappointment over the healer not having the ability to return the princess. Finally, and most relevant, he noticed the way she looked at him, with pity and sadness. And why shouldn’t she? No legs, one arm. Though he couldn’t regard his own face, he sensed its disfigurement— certainly no nose; if he put his hand to the sides of his head, he was certain he lacked ears. If she no longer loved him, the blame didn’t rest with her. It belonged on the shoulders of he who made him this way. Lost in his thoughts and concern for his love, he’d missed the

healer’s words, until he spoke the last few. “My time here is done.” The bald man shifted toward Strylor, pulling his hand from his opposite sleeve and extended long, thin fingers, reaching for him. Memories of pain and torment flashed through him—through his body and his mind. Every muscle and joint suffered the agony of his touch again. Parts of him didn’t disappear when the healer used him, he tore them away, flesh and tendon ripped by invisible hands, bitten off by unseen teeth. He never wanted to experience it again, considered no reason to, now she wouldn’t want him. Their love might live forever, as great loves like theirs always did, but he wouldn’t force her to look upon the hideous monstrosity the healer created of him. As the robed man reached for Strylor, he kept his gaze on Ishla. The queen’s guard used this distraction to his advantage. Before the deathly white fingers found his flesh, he grabbed the healer’s loose and dangling sleeve, and pulled. The sudden jerk and the pale man’s inattention tilted him off balance. Strylor coiled, yanked on the robe again, and launched himself as best he could. He struck the surprised healer, throwing him to the ground, and landing on top. Before his hand found him, Strylor scrambled up the wicked man, the scrawny body under him poking into him, then he leaned forward and sank his teeth into his neck. The healer screeched in his ear, a high-pitched sound like an animal in pain. The queen’s guard closed his eyes and bit as hard as his aching jaw allowed. His incisors pierced the pale skin and a thick and bitter ichor oozed out of the wound. He fought the urge to gag on it, to release him and spit the foul taste from his mouth. Instead, he thought of her, of how proud of him she’d be for ridding the world of this loathsome being. Strylor widened his jaw, bit harder, piercing his esophagus with a pop and a whoosh of air quickly becoming a gurgle. He shook his head like a dog with a rat, refusing to relinquish his hold. The healer’s screeches filled with his version of blood. He coughed, thrashed and squirmed. Then the pain came. It shot out from Strylor’s shoulder, where the bald man’s hand must have found a grip. Like a river bolstered by flooding, it flowed into his body, occupied him until he thought he might burst. Still, he didn’t let go. The sticky liquid overflowed his mouth, choking him. He bit harder, shook more vigorously, until it became too much. Energy drained from him and he sagged forward, teeth embedded in the healer’s throat. He forced his eyes open, hoping for one more view of the woman he loved, but the vile blood seeped into them,

stinging, forcing them closed. His breathing slowed along with his heartbeat; pain deepened, then dissipated. As the world slipped away, he hoped Ishla realized he’d done this for her. He’d done everything for her. *** Shocked, the queen lowered her sword and stepped away. She barely recognized her queen’s guard as he slumped, finally motionless after moving furiously, as though possessed by a wild beast. Blood so dark it appeared black covered his face, splashed down his body, as it also discolored the grass in a half-circle an arm’s length around him. Beneath him, nothing but the woolen robe remained of the androgynous bald creature they’d called the healer. Ishla looked aside, about to ask Dansil what happened. He was gone. She watched him as he lumbered across the plain away from them, going as fast as his boot-clad feet would carry his armor-bound body. Her gaze returned to Strylor. The man was deceased, no doubt about it. For the best, given the shape in which the healer’s manipulations had left him. The bald creature, though… Did it survive? Could it have used Strylor’s life to save its own? She took one pace toward the dead queen’s guard and stopped, a clatter of sound behind her disrupting her thoughts. Teryk! She spun around, sword slipping from her grip and falling to the grass. She managed a half-step forward before stopping again, mouth agape in surprise. Trenan stood before her, their son thrown over his shoulder. The cloth she’d pressed against the prince’s wound fell away and she spied blood oozing from it. “We have to get him help,” Trenan said. “Hurry.”

XV Evalal – Ikkundana From the direction they approached the fortress, few hints gave away the battle raging on the other side. Smoke billowed above the wall from a fire and, upon closer listen, one might hear an out-of-place noise muddled in with the song of crickets hidden in the long grass. Nerves bundled in Evalal’s stomach; somewhere she couldn’t see, her sisters—the warriors of their Goddess—fought to save a kingdom full of people who cared little about them. If Goddess’ followers were the only ones threatened, would the kingdom stand for them? The question required no answer. Not simply because of the obviousness of it, but because it didn’t matter. From as far as her memory went, she recalled teachers telling her: what we do for others does not depend on what they do for us. Our own truths and values—given by Goddess—guide our choices. And so she sighed as Leaf helped her off the buck. As soon as her feet touched the ground, the gray fellow climbed onto his mount. “You’re leaving?” “We all are. Ivy will stay with you and the man of the sea.” He lifted a hand, turning at the waist to remain facing her as his steed reoriented itself to carry him to the far side of the wall. “Your role is not in the fight, young one. Goddess be with you.” “And you.” She nodded to him. The animal-mounted Small Gods left together, urging their deer and elk, moose and bear toward the corner, leaving Evalal behind with Horace and Ivy. She watched them for a time before facing her companions and finding a door open in the face of the imposing stone wall where none had been before. If she hadn’t visited the City of the Sick as a child for combat training, its appearance might have surprised her the way it did the old sailor. “Fuck me dead,” he whispered. Before, his casual use of foul language would have shocked her, but different times force a change of values. The fate of the kingdom depended on them, no matter how small their roles, so the time for taking offense had long passed. “Hurry,” she said, grabbing Horace by the hand, “come with me.” Evalal rushed through the doorway, the old sailor dragging after her; hurrying didn’t seem a task he excelled at. He scuffled his feet, raised his eyes to peer at the massive wall. He crossed the threshold, Ivy close behind, and the door swung silently closed, controlled by an unseen person operating an unseen mechanism to which Evalal gave little thought. They passed through into a narrow alley, the walls stretching high

overhead. Fifteen paces brought them to its end, where it opened onto a broad avenue lined with leafy trees at regular intervals. She paused, looked one direction then the next, the street empty of people. “Which way?” Horace prompted. He stood close enough behind her the breath of his words stirred her hair. She shrugged, took a hesitant half-step forward, stopped. Her lids slid closed, she bent her head, waiting for Goddess to give her guidance, breathing slow and steady despite the sailor’s nervousness pressing against her. A moment later, something touched her. She opened her eyes to find Ivy pushing past into the avenue ahead of her. “Ivy says the infirmary,” the Small God said. She inclined her face toward Evalal. “Which way?” The girl thought for a few heartbeats, then nodded to herself. “This way.” She headed left, the sailor in tow. Her boots clopped on the pristine flagstone street, and she wondered how surprised people would be if they knew the Sisters kept the so-called City of the Sick so immaculate. If the general populace experienced the gardens maintained by the Goddess followers, saw the way they looked out for each other, how they cared about the world, the knowledge would change everything. Instead, the kingdom viewed them with suspicion and unearned animosity. Knowledge is power, she remembered the Mother of Death telling her. But so much more, too: understanding, compassion, empathy. Everything is born of knowledge. Yet, from the time she and Danya left the temple, feelings rather than knowledge had guided her, trusting Goddess to lead her, allowing her to do what needed doing. The Mother of Death’s voice whispered in her ear again: When we have no knowledge, we have faith. They rounded a corner onto a wider but equally empty street. Their footfalls echoed off the walls—the click of boots she and the old sailor wore, the slap of the Small God’s bare soles. Horace’s breathing grew more labored with each step, but they didn’t have far to go. The stairs to the infirmary building lay ahead on the left, visible from where they were. “Almost there,” she said over her shoulder and gave the older man a quick smile. Horace nodded appreciation, his cheeks ruddy. He blew air out between his lips in an explosive puff and wiped a trickle of sweat from his brow on his free arm. For all his foul language and occasional bluster, Evalal found she liked him. She’d encountered few men in her life; so many of them looked down on her for being a sister. She thought if more of them behaved like the sailor, the world might be a

better place. They reached the foot of the stairs to the infirmary, hurried up them and through the door, passing from the warmth of the sun into the cool of the building. More than just the temperature changed, though. The noise level increased, from the rustle of wind in leaves and the chirp of birds to a bustle of activity, voices calling out, cries of pain, the creak of armor and the clank of weapons. Horace halted, nearly pulling Evalal from her feet. “How?” he whispered. “Where’d they come from?” “There are other entrances to the infirmary,” she said. “Some face toward the battle.” The old sailor let out a sad breath and shook his head as Ivy pushed by them. She hurried along the corridor, leading them past rooms the young girl did her best not to peer into. She knew what she’d see: Goddess warriors injured and dying after taking up the fight to defend a kingdom that preferred they didn’t exist. Evalal pressed her lips together, swallowed the thought. We are all of Goddess; some just don’t know it or won’t admit it. Ivy turned through the last door on the right before the corridor opened into an enormous room, and Evalal followed, Horace trailing behind, hand in hers. As she rounded the corner, she glanced into the hall, saw white cloth stained red, a woman’s face pinched with pain, a nurse working to suture a wound. Then they thankfully crossed the threshold, and she focused her attention to the chamber they’d entered. She didn’t know the two Sisters within, but the other three people were familiar to her, one of whom she’d only seen from afar. She stared at Teryk lying on the table as the nurses worked on him, applying sutures and poultices. Her mouth dropped open at the sight of his missing arm. The other two in the room looked to them as they entered. Trenan’s eyes fell first on Ivy, then Horace, before finding hers. “You,” Trenan said. He left his spot at the queen’s side and crossed to her, put his hand on her shoulder and crouched so their gazes met. They peered at each other for the space of three heartbeats. Though she didn’t know why, she desperately wanted to look away. Behind her, Horace’s hand slipped out of hers and he stepped up beside her. “Hands off the girl, fella, else you’ll be answering to me.” The master swordsman’s eyes flickered to Horace and then back. “I said—” “It’s okay.” Evalal rested her touch on the old sailor’s forearm, then returned her attention to Trenan. “Danya?” He spoke the name in a low voice, as though he meant to keep it from the others. If such was his intent, he failed.

“You know of my daughter?” Queen Ishla stepped up behind the master swordsman, concern in her tone, perhaps hope. Evalal peered into her face, saw the pain etched in her brow. How much this poor woman had been through in such a brief passage of days. The girl first thought to tell her everything would be all right because Goddess had a plan. She didn’t. While those words often offered solace, sometimes they weren’t enough and caused aggravation. She sensed this the case this time and shook her head. Ishla shouldered Trenan aside and leaned closer. “The healer couldn’t save her the way he did Teryk. He claimed she wasn’t dead.” “Ishla, that’s not what—” the master swordsman began. “Let the girl speak.” Evalal looked from one to the other, swallowed. “The Seed of Life,” she said. “And the Barren Mother.” The one-armed soldier raised an eyebrow, his upper lip curling, like he’d bitten into a sour fruit. Ishla’s expression softened, and she nodded once. “Goddess has a path for her.” The corner of Evalal’s mouth quivered, and she suppressed the smile threatening; this wasn’t the time. “Yes, Sister, she does.” The queen pivoted away from them, returned to her son’s side as the medics attended him. His eyes remained shut, the Goddess mercifully taking his consciousness from him while they did what needed doing. Trenan stayed put, gaze shifting to first the sailor, then Ivy. The Small God looked up at him, smiled. “Have the dead ones left?” The master swordsman’s eyes widened. His mouth opened, closed, opened again. “How did you—” “You must come with Ivy. We need your sword.” She turned to the girl. “Evalal can stay with the prince.” She glanced from the Small God to Horace, then to Teryk lying on the table being tended by the medics, and experienced another of those moments. No desire to fight lived within her, but what good did tending to an incapacitated young man do? Faith when knowledge is absent. The Mother of Death’s voice spoke the words in her mind, dispelling any hesitation. She looked to Ivy and nodded. “Of course.” Taking a step nearer the table, she released her hold on Horace’s hand, approached the nearest medic. “How can I help?” The woman bent her head toward a bowl of water, a cloth floating on its surface. Evalal went to it, plucked the square of soft fabric out, squeezed the excess liquid from it, and touched it to Teryk’s forehead. Ishla caught her eye as she did and offered a pained smile. “Take care of my son as you did my daughter,” she said.

A sliver of guilt twinged in Evalal’s chest. Had she really done well watching over the princess? Destiny made what happened necessary. She nodded, faced away from the queen, casting her eyes on the comatose son lest tears begin. From the corner of her eye, she watched Ishla cross the room to Trenan. She put her hand on the master swordsman’s shoulder. “Best get me a sword. I’m coming with you.” *** The one-armed swordsman made a sound o’ protest, but it took no more’n a single glance from the queen to shut him up. A bit o’ an unusual happenin’ what caused the ol’ sailor to raise an eyebrow and wonder if somethin’ more between them two, suspicion he set aside for another time, or maybe not at all. “I be in need o’ some weaponry, too,” he said, the words intended but surprisin’ him, nonetheless. “I think you should stay, Horace Seaman. A battle is no place for a man of the sea.” Truth be, weren’t no argument against Ivy’s proclamation. Didn’t stop him from crouchin’ in front o’ her, knees poppin’ and hips achin’ as he did. He gazed into her big, dark eyes, seein’ his own face reflected in them, all the while thinkin’ about how much she resembled his friend Thorn. “I lost ev’ryone what were ever important to me, and a bunch who wasn’t, too,” he said. “I can’t promise to keep you safe and alive, but I’m goin’ to do my best to make it so.” Ivy nodded and smiled a smile what made her appear more like her brother than usual. It gripped his heart in a fist o’ remorse; he inhaled a deep breath through his lips, tryin’ his hardest to calm the feelin’. Here were his chance to atone for ev’ry time he failed. “I understand, Horace Seaman. And I will do my best to keep you safe and alive.” “It sounds like we had better get you a sword, too,” Trenan said. The ol’ sailor glanced at Evalal, saw worry written plain across her face. She looked away quick, pretendin’ to concentrate on the injured prince. “Aye, you be right.” He reached up, holdin’ his hand open. “Now help a fella up, would ya?”

XVI Horace – Golem When they stepped through another door similar to the one what gave them ingress to the fortress—’cept on the opposite side, near as Horace suspected—the ol’ sailor lost his breath, necessitatin’ a stoppage to find it again. Bein’ a man o’ the sea for his entire life, he’d never seen anythin’ like what lay before him. The fire what’d been belchin’ smoke they saw before still smoldered, the result o’ tents what someone’d set ablaze. The stink o’ burnt canvas tickled his nostrils, but he ignored the scent because his eyes distracted him by bein’ busy tryin’ to process the first battle they’d ever seen. A bit o’ space lay between where they emerged from outta the wall and the fightin’, though not so much it didn’t leave him fillin’ with awe and dread. The metallic clash o’ weapons, although quieted by the distance, sounded harsh to ears used to the creak o’ boards and the flappin’ o’ sails. The yellow grass stretchin’ out before them were mostly pressed flat but for a few patches stickin’ up. How those escaped gettin’ trampled by the wall o’ people and horseflesh beyond seemed a miracle. He might’ve marveled at the sight for longer, ‘cept Ishla and Trenan started out toward the fight, Ivy trailin’ behind as she waited for the ol’ sailor. “Come on,” she said, gesturin’ with one hand for him to follow. “Stay close to Ivy.” He forced his feet to get movin’, a feelin’ o’ mild concern risin’ in him since he found himself followin’ a small creature what carried no weapon. Mind you, if someone required him to speak the truth aloud, he’d’ve admitted to havin’ no actual idea how to wield the spear-like thing the master swordsman’d provided him. Better’n gettin’ up close and personal with a sword, but the prospect o’ killin’ anyone caused his tackle to shrink to the size it were when he were a babe. Already killed one man. S’enough for me in this lifetime. But it might not be as simple as makin’ a decision. If for no other reason, he’d do whatever needed done to keep Ivy from harm. As they hurried across the compressed grassland toward the swirlin’ chaos o’ fight, he did his best to distract himself with the master swordsman’s story. He’d related the account to the queen as they navigated hallways and then streets while gettin’ outta the City o’ the Sick—a name he didn't understand. A sad tale, to be sure, but they all carried with ‘em some sort o’ tragedy. He’d watched Ishla struggle with what she heard, sometimes holdin’ back tears, at others lookin’ like she’d burst out in anger. Horace understood; havin’ lost his own son, he knew pretty well what she suffered with.

No one did much talkin’ after he finished tellin’ his story. They crossed toward the battlefield with no sound from any o’ them but their feet trompin’ on grass, makin’ sure them blades possessed no chance o’ bouncin’ back. After not too long, they began passin’ by bodies lyin’ on the ground. Some fellas, some women. Horace knew which the Goddess warriors was; he couldn’t tell the good guys from the bad when it came to the men wearin’ armor. Suddenly it seemed it might be an outstandin’ idea to get it figured out. And how are they gonna know what side I’m fightin’ for? He gulped a mouthful o’ saliva, then voiced his concerns to the Small God trottin’ along beside him. “Stay with Ivy, Horace Seaman.” The ol’ sailor frowned and nodded once. He thought the world o’ her, and her brother Thorn before her, but were havin’ trouble seein’ how stayin’ with her’d help. The ground rumbled beneath his feet, the way a ship’s deck might’ve if it ran ashore. “Fuck me dead,” he spat. Ivy raised her arm, pointed skyward as a streak o’ light whizzed by o’erhead. “The gods of the sky return,” she said, not near enough surprise or awe in her voice, Horace figured. “Thorn’s death allowed it.” Her words tugged at his chest. He considered sayin’ somethin’— apologizin’, pleadin’ forgiveness, tellin’ her it weren’t his fault. He didn’t, because he knew it’d make no difference; not to her, not to him. Ivy’d say things needed to go such a way. No amount o’ sorry- sayin’d bring him back—the only chance o’ healin’ that particular wound in the ol’ sailor. More fireballs shot past o’er their heads; the ground shook again and again. Horace wondered what might’ve been hittin’ the earth, then changed his mind and decided he didn’t care to know. “Stay away from the fallen,” she said. “The Small Gods will attend to the Small Gods.” “No need to tell me more’n once.” About stayin’ away from them, he thought. The rest is just damn confusin’. When they neared the fray, Trenan—who led them—veered to his right. The queen and the Small God followed along, givin’ Horace no choice but to do the same. He didn’t have an issue doin’ so, because it took ‘em around the fight rather’n into it as he’d expected. The longer before he needed to figure the use o’ the spear thing, the better, in his mind. A man broke from the fray when he spied them tryin’ to sneak by.

He ran at them, sword raised high, threatenin’ to chop in half from head to asshole anyone who got in his way. Trenan stopped, waitin’ for him to arrive, and the rest o’ them gathered in behind him. Horace stayed close to Ivy, like she said. He held the tip o’ the spear out in front o’ him, careful not to put it anywhere it might prick the master swordsman in the back. The angry-lookin’ soldier reached them and launched his attack, swingin’ his blade downward in a mighty arc while hollerin’ somethin’ unintelligible. Trenan side-stepped with an ease and grace what Horace never would’ve expected, but which explained his title of swordmaster. The fella completed his charge off-balance after cuttin’ nothin’ but air and buryin’ his weapon’s tip in the soil where Trenan’d been an instant before. His eyes went surprised when the one-armed man’s swordtip found its way in through a space under his chin and out again through the top o’ his head. Horace looked away before Trenan pulled it out again. He’d seen some atrocities in his life, most o’ them accidents where a man lost a limb or got crushed by unsecured cargo, rarely out o’ anger. Course, one time four nitwit sailors’d mutinied and ended up hung from the yardarm with hooks through their necks—an example for anyone else thinkin’ the same way. Took them longer to die than this fella, their legs flailin’ under them while the cap’n made the entire crew watch. When he heard the body hit the ground, he turned around. The master swordsman wiped his blade on the dead man’s sleeve and moved a step before the queen stopped him with a hand on his arm. “Are you going to ask for mercy on him?” she asked. Trenan shook his head. “I have discovered mercy doesn’t exist.” He started out again, but she held on. “Do you still see them?” “No, I don’t. But they are always with me.” This time, her touch dropped away, and she followed him. Horace hesitated, then hurried to catch up to Ivy, who scurried along three paces behind the warrior and the queen. When he got to her, the ol’ sailor leaned o’er so she’d hear him. “What the fuck were that about?” Ivy gave him a quick sideways glance and shrugged, her face expressionless. Horace realized these little folk was generally only in possession o’ two expressions: smilin’ or none. They skirted their way around more o’ the battle. At one point, he overheard Ishla askin’ the master swordsman about his plan and he said somethin’ about findin’ a fella called Osis. Who that were, the ol’ sailor lacked any idea. He kept followin’ along, takin’ regular peeks o’er his shoulder makin’ sure nobody sneaked up behind him with a mind to chop off his noggin while he weren’t lookin’. So far, so good.

And Ivy stayed safe, too. They climbed through a trough cut into the ground by one o’ them fireballs he’d seen flyin’ through the sky. The already dark dirt looked charred, the grass along its edges singed from yellow to black. He shivered at the image o’ what kinda thing might fall amidst a fireball, then climb outta the ditch to overthrow a kingdom. He forgot his worry when he saw the clay monster. His pace slowed. It towered o’er ev’ryone else, standin’ a full head taller’n the next tallest soldier, and near as tall as most o’ the mounted ones. Bigger’n he remembered it. For an instant, he considered it might not be the same one what’d taken his friend Thorn, but he knew. Couldn’t be two, for a start, but his bones told him it were the same brute. The thing were close enough Horace spied the dents in its head where he ought to have eyes. Regardin’ the near-featureless, dun- colored face reminded him o’ the creature Rilum’d become. As if it weren’t enough, it’d stolen Thorn from him, taken the little fella to his death. He pinched his lips together tight. “Fucker,” he said in a tone he meant for bein’ under his breath. Without thinkin’, Horace Seaman’s legs turned him abruptly left, carryin’ him toward the golem at a faster clip’n he’d managed in a long time. Movin’ at this quickened pace, the ol’ sailor needed to take care with the unfamiliar weapon he carried. If he didn’t watch the tip, he might poke someone undeservin’ o’ bein’ stuck; if he angled it too far the other way, the end dragged on the ground. He adjusted his hands, the left in front nearer the blade, the right closer to the tail. Awkward, but it gave him more control, enablin’ him to worry less about it and concentrate more on the shit-colored bastard what’d killed his friend. “Horace Seaman. Come back.” Ivy’s voice sounded small behind him. With the space he’d created between him and them, it’d taken some time before she noticed his absence. A sizeable chunk o’ him wanted to heed her, stop his foolish courage and return to them before anythin’ bad happened to him. A much bigger piece desired to see what’d happen if he sank the spear’s tip into the mud monster’s guts. The people fightin’ around him thickened, slowin’ him. Outta the corner o’ his eye, Horace saw a bare-chested woman slash a man across his belly, blood spurtin’ out from the wound. Before she reset, another fella slashed her forearm. The ol’ sailor tried to block the things goin’ on from his mind. Got pretty good at it until a big bastard with crazy eyes and wearin’ a leather chest piece stepped in front o’ him. Horace skidded to a halt, glanced from the man’s matted beard coverin’ his face right up to his eyeballs, to the axe he held in the one

hand and the shield strapped to his other arm. The ol’ sailor gulped, wishin’ he’d paid attention to the smaller chunk wantin’ him to return to Ivy and the others. Too late now. His gaze flickered past his foe to the livin’ sculpture, and his rage flooded in, not quite extinguishin’ his fear, but doin’ a splendid job o’ quashin’ it. His jaw pulled tight, mashin’ his teeth together, and he lashed out, intendin’ to poke a hole in his adversary with the pointy end o’ the spear. The soldier not only had a different idea how things should go, he also possessed a bushel more skill’n a man used to riggin’ a ship’s sails. The big, bearded fella took the jab on the flat o’ his buckler, turnin’ it at an angle so the tip slid off and past him. He followed up by swingin’ his axe, makin’ Horace jump aside to avoid it. Its sharp edge struck the spear’s shaft, sunderin’ it in two. Right then, the ol’ sailor’s legs remembered the exhaustion they’d forgotten upon seein’ the golem, and he toppled o’er backward. His ass hit the ground, jarrin’ his teeth together with a loud click, bringin’ a smile to his adversary’s face. He said somethin’ what sounded to Horace’s ears like a growl amongst the din o’ battle ragin’ around them, then raised his axe. If someone’d asked in advance how he’d feel watchin’ a soldier about to claim his life, Horace would’ve declared he expected to experience enough fear to end up shittin’ his pants. But he weren’t. Instead, he lay lookin’ up at the sun glintin’ on the sharp-edged the blade and thinkin’ maybe the time’d come for an ol’ man who’d lived a questionable history to meet his end. Turned out Ivy felt different. He didn’t see where she came from. At first he thought a gray cannonball struck the soldier in the chest. She knocked the wind outta him in a loud huff, sendin’ him topplin’ o’er backward, the way Horace’d done himself. The axe flew up then tumbled down, bouncin’ on the grass beside him. Ivy’s fist rose and fell quicker’n the ol’ sailor’d ever seen a hand move, and the man shrieked. Didn’t take but a few heartbeats before each time she pulled back to hit him again sent a shower of blood droplets sprayin’ through the air. Horace’s heels dug into the ground, leavin’ shallow furrows behind as he pushed himself away. Ivy finished pummelin’ the poor fella—killin’ him, Horace thought likely —as he felt a touch on his shoulder. He jumped in surprise, raised his hands defensively until he realized the queen’d laid her fingers upon him. “Get up,” Trenan urged from his spot beside her. Ishla offered a hand and Horace grasped it, lettin’ her help him

struggle to his feet. His joints protested, creakin’ and groanin’. While he climbed to upright, Trenan took the time to push away someone who got too close to them, then slashed his sword out at another combatant. The ol’ sailor didn’t see if he contacted anyone, but you don’t get called master swordsman for missin’. When he made it to his feet, the queen’s hand on his shoulder steadyin’ him, he looked at Ivy standin’ in front o’ him, her right arm covered in blood to the elbow. He shuddered at the sight. Better him’n me, though. “What was Horace Seaman thinking? He almost killed you.” Her face wore the no-expression, and he knew it meant he’d upset her. Didn’t matter. He peered past her, glimpsed the hulkin’ clay figure swingin’ its arms and sendin’ soldiers, both male and female, flyin’. Horace swore he smelt the stink o’ the thing even this far away. He watched it pick up one unfortunate man in both hands and break him in two like a stick. The ol’ sailor swallowed hard and raised an arm. “He be the creature what took Thorn.” He directed his gaze to the Small God; she peered up at him despite his pointin’ somethin’ out to her. “The clay bastard killed your brother.” “Then that thing is the key,” Ishla said. Out o’ the corner o’ his eye, he saw her take a peek toward Trenan. The one-armed swordsman continued fendin’ off anyone what got too close, but he took her meanin’ and gave a nod. She faced Ivy and Horace. “If he dies, so does the rebellion.” The ol’ sailor raised an eyebrow, wonderin’ how the queen might assume such a thing, but he didn’t say nothin’. Slaughterin’ the fucker for what he did to Thorn were what he wanted, too. It appeared Ivy concurred, for she bent at the waist, plucked the axe what once belonged to the man she’d killed from outta the grass, and handed it to Horace. He took it from her, the grip sticky with blood what’d transferred from her fingers, and bounced it in his hand. The weapon weren’t much more familiar to him than the damn spear’d been, but at least it’d be easier to carry. Ivy spun on her heel and started out toward where the golem were killin’ people left and right, not waitin’ for the others, like Horace’d done before. He followed along close behind, Ishla after him, and Trenan protectin’ the rear. Another fireball flew by overhead—there’d been a few o’ them while ev’rythin’d been goin’ on, now he reflected upon it. The thing crashed to the ground somewhere up ahead, throwin’ chunks o’ sod up in the air and leavin’ a trail o’ smoke in its wake. And so an ol’ sailor what’d spent most o’ his life on the deck o’ one

ship or another followed a Small God from the Green toward an animated clay man, the queen and the general o’ the king’s army in tow, with the intent o’ hackin’ it to pieces and endin’ the uprising o’ the Small Gods from the sky. “Fuck me dead,” Horace muttered and gripped the axe tighter.

XVII Osis – Yoli Osis didn’t see the man who took his horse from under him. In his head, he used the word ‘man’ but the way his mount crumpled as though its bones had turned to dust made him suspect the perpetrator may have fallen from the sky at the fore of a fireball. He threw himself clear, hitting the ground hard and wincing with the impact. Rolling with it, he came to rest on his belly, immediately climbed to hands and knees, blinking to regain his equilibrium. He’d lost his sword in the fall and raised his head, searching for it. A fellow who looked more farmer than soldier rushed him, a three- tined pitchfork extended toward him. Osis reached for the dagger at his belt, fingers wrapping around its hilt, and waited for the man to close. At the last instant, the sergeant-at-arms rolled to his left, simultaneously pulling the weapon free and slashing at his attacker’s leg. The points missed him by a hand’s breadth, and the sharp blade sliced through the tendon at the back of the man’s calf. He took a step with the other foot, then tumbled to the ground as his weight settled on the injured one, screaming with pain. Osis launched himself on top of him, a slash across his throat turning the pained sound to naught but a gurgle. The sergeant climbed to his feet, plucked the pitchfork from the dying man’s hand, and returned his attention to the battle raging around him. In front of him, not twenty paces away, stood the one responsible for killing his mount. As with the other fallen, he loomed taller than the others on the battlefield, noticeable by his lack of not only armor, but clothing, too. Their eyes met, and a grin tilted the mouth of the being who fell from the sky. Osis frowned at him. “I was fond of that horse,” he said, transferring the pitchfork from left hand to right, swapping his dagger the other way. He bounced the unfamiliar farm implement against his palm as he started toward the naked fellow, testing its weight and finding its balance point. He’d never been partial to polearms of any sort, but the preference hadn’t stopped him from training with them as much as he did sword and axe. His soon-to-be adversary stalked toward him, matching his pace. Osis wet his lips, spat the taste of battle from his tongue. Each step with his right leg caused him pain—he must have injured it when he tumbled from the horse. He ignored it, concentrating on the enemy approaching him. Normally, he’d have spent the few paces looking for a weakness in his armor, somewhere to strike and cause the most damage. One spot might be as good as another when fighting an unclothed combatant. When he got close enough, he extended the pitchfork toward him with a quick thrust; his enemy jumped to his right, avoiding the

pointed tines as Osis hoped. The sergeant-at-arms dropped back, raised the farm tool and, spear-like, launched it at the man standing three paces away. Incredibly, the fallen caught it with one hand, halting its flight the width of a finger from his face. Osis had never seen a person or animal move so fast. “Shit.” The naked man gave him just enough time to shift the knife from his left hand to his right and raise it in a meager gesture of defense before he swung at him. The sergeant twisted, taking the brunt of the strike on his shoulder and back. The force of it picked him off his feet and threw him through the air, the crunch and pop of bones noisy to his ears. Pain exploded through him and he hit the ground, his cheekbone chafing through the grass, leaving behind a channel in the dirt. He came to a stop, groaned, kicked to twist himself right side up so he might look into the face of his killer. The man fallen from the sky took his time approaching, as though he savored each heartbeat leading to killing Osis. If the thing has a heart. The sergeant-at-arms tried using his feet to push away, but each movement sent fresh pain through his shoulder and spine. He inhaled a pained breath, realized he’d broken his ribs, and let it out again in a rattling sigh. As a career soldier, he’d always assumed his life would come to its end on a battlefield, but how could he have foreseen this? Bested by a remarkable swordsman, or the victim of a stealthy dagger he didn’t see coming, but crushed by a man long ago banished to the sky? He continued holding the knife in his right hand, for what little good it might do. No matter, a real warrior never gave in to death. He flipped the weapon over in his grip, holding it by the blade, and hurled it at his attacker, forcing another shock of pain through his torso. It came as no surprise when he flicked it aside like an annoying fly. Osis tensed, waiting for the killing blow, hoping for it to be quick. He doubted this man—this thing fallen from the sky—possessed any capacity for mercy, but perhaps he realized a field of battle was no place to dally. Based on his languid pace approaching, the sergeant thought maybe he’d made no such realization. The ground rumbled under him, and Osis assumed it the result of another fireball crashing to the earth. An instant later, he needed to wonder no more. A horse leapt over the dead farmer and thundered toward them. He saw it over his enemy’s shoulder, but did his best not to divert his gaze as his opponent didn’t appear aware of it. At the last instant, he

did, and he spun in time for the topless warrior seated atop the steed to sink her blade deep into his neck. She rode past, pulling the sword free as she went, and the naked man stumbled, hand reaching up for his throat. Blood squeezed between his fingers and he yelled in anger, more of the red liquid spraying from his lips. The woman’s horse reared up on its hind legs as she turned it about and charged him again. This time, instead of staying seated as her adversary might have expected, she leapt from the saddle as she approached. The move caught him off-guard. Leading with her weapon, she landed atop him, skewering him on the blade as she did. Despite the pain, Osis twisted to watch her ride the man to the ground, landing with her sword through his chest and her knees on his gut. The impact forced what breath remained from his lungs; a spurt of blood shot up in the air and splashed across the Goddess warrior. She jumped to her feet, wrenching the blade from him, then inserted it through one of his eyes until the tip came out the back of his head. The fallen’s body jerked twice, then stopped moving. She pulled her weapon free and hurried to where the sergeant-at- arms lay. She stood for an instant looking down at him, bare chest shimmering with sweat-streaked dirt and fresh blood. A deep sigh rose and fell in her, and she offered her assistance. “Yoli,” he said. “Are you all right, Osis?” He grabbed on to her hand and allowed her to pull him to his feet, wincing at the pain it caused. He drew his own shuddering breath, taking it in with care, trying to avoid causing more agony in his broken ribs. It didn’t work. “No,” he replied when he’d finished. He bent at the waist, laboring air into his lungs, before straightening with a grimace. “We need to get me a blade.” *** They stood back to back, fighting off whatever attackers came. Whenever Osis swung the sword they’d acquired for him, she heard him grunt with effort and pain. With anyone else behind her thus, she’d have worried for his and her safety; though she didn’t know much about the sergeant-at-arms, she sensed him cut of the same cloth as Trenan. And herself. “We can’t stay here,” she said after cutting down a man who looked more suited to tending counter at a general store than bleeding on a battlefield. “They keep coming.” Osis swung his sword, grunted. “What do you suggest?” With a reprieve to draw breath, she cast her gaze across the plains. Bodies clashed; some in armor, others topless, still others in robes.

Small, gray folk scampered amongst the fray, mostly engaging the black priests. The Small Gods of the Green had shown up unannounced and with no trumpeters to blare their arrival. She appreciated their presence. Without them, she worried her warriors might not have held off the priests. Several men strewn throughout the battle stood taller than the rest —those who fell from the sky. One other of greater height than those loomed over all, his gray pate visible above all others. Yoli glowered at it, eyes narrowing. “We must cut off the head. Come.” She left without waiting for him; she knew he’d follow. Truthfully, he should have found a medic to tend his injuries, but she already recognized Osis wasn’t the kind of man to leave a fight as long as he remained standing. Yoli focused on the clay skull bobbing above the others, striking out at any enemy who strayed too close as she went. Though enemies of Goddess, it pained her to injure or kill these men who obviously lacked training and were here for…what? Their beliefs? Or did something compel them to fight for the return of the Small Gods? As she paced toward him, the tacky blood on her chest made her skin feel too tight, and she wished for a chance to wash it from her flesh. Every time she breathed, the scent of it filled her nose with the cloying, coppery odor of lives she’d ended. She took no pride in ending them like some soldiers did; their deaths gave her no comfort or peace. She’d heard of men who kept tallies—pieces of parchment with marks the way the Sisters counted the days between their moon times, or belts or sticks they cut notches in to keep track. None of this appealed to her. She killed in the name of Goddess, doing her will, and for no other reason. When this was done, she planned to put aside her sword and never touch it again. If the Mother of Mothers allowed her to live so long. Without looking, she felt Osis at her side. His labored breathing gave her concern—he must have injured his ribs or something in his chest when he clashed with the fallen—but his sword arm seemed unhindered. So far. They weaved through the fray, avoiding conflict whenever possible, keeping it short when they couldn’t. Yoli kept glancing toward the golem, seeing it swing its thick arms, brushing aside all who stood in its way. Men and women alike hacked at it with no effect, their blades slicing through the clay only to have it close up the instant the steel passed through. “How do we stop it?” Osis asked breathlessly, watching alongside her. She shook her head. “I don’t know.”

They pressed on, their progress hindered by a thick throng of fighting. They amended their course, circling wider, only to realize it brought them into the path of one of the fallen. He stood before them, blood gleaming on his skin, part of someone’s arm dangling in his grip. When he saw them, he dropped it, started toward them. Yoli set her feet, held her sword in both hands in front of her, tip pointed toward the sky. “Are you ready?” Osis drew a halting breath and sighed the air out between his lips. “Always.” The first of the small, gray folk jumped out of a knot of people to its right, grabbing its forearm. It hung from him and the fallen swung its arm, attempting to flick it off. While distracted, another grabbed one of its legs, a third leapt onto its back. The naked man roared in anger, or pain, perhaps both. He turned a circle, reaching over his shoulder with his other hand to grab the Small God with its bite now lodged in his spine. Five more enveloped him and in the space of three heartbeats later, he crumpled to his knees. Tiny fists rose and fell, yellow teeth gnashed. Yoli watched, mouth open, until the little ones finished beating him to death. They climbed off, wiping blood from their faces on forearms covered in more blood, the action accomplishing nothing more than smearing the foul liquid. The Goddess warrior didn’t ease her stance; from what she’d seen, these Small Gods of the Green fought on the right side of the affair, but she knew little of them or their demeanor. Did they come here to protect themselves and others from the threat of the fallen? Or were they merely animals driven by a thirst for death? One of them saw her and walked away from the others, approaching. Yoli tensed; she felt Osis ready himself beside her. The gray creature—a female—stopped eight paces from them, a smile upon her bloodied lips. Without looking away, she raised an arm and waved, as though prompting someone to join them. Yoli quickly realized that was exactly what she did. Of the three people who ducked out of the crowd and hurried toward them, she didn’t recognize one—a man with gray hair and beard, a shamble to his walk. Neither of the others did she expect to see. She opened her mouth to speak, but Osis got words out before her. “Trenan,” he exclaimed, then his feet shifted, his armor creaked. “My queen.” They approached and Yoli saw the blood spattered on their clothes, the grim bits clinging to their weapons. She struggled to find her voice. It continued eluding her when Ishla stood before her, put her
hands on her shoulders. “Yoli,” the queen said, looking into her eyes. “My sister.” She pulled her close and embraced her.

XVIII Vesisdenperos – Fight Instinctively, he knew the clay he’d used to create the golem healed itself from every nick, cut, and slash, yet each one touched Vesisdenperos as though the blades nicked his own skin. He watched through the creature’s eyes, the world made dull and gray by the veil of mud. Men attacked and were rebuffed, many of them left in shattered heaps by the strength of the beast, others broken in two, split wide open. Appalling. The sculptor wanted to look away, but the spectacle held his gaze. Somewhere in whatever remained of him inside the living statue, a spark of pride blossomed. Despite the terrible things it did—most notably killing Kuneprius—Vesisdenperos had created this unstoppable monster. He’d fashioned it with his hands, contributed to it with his sweat and blood, imbued it with his soul. If his creation acted thus, did it mean this way of being lived in him, too? The way sons are born with traits of their parents, the golem retained part of him. No. I couldn’t slaughter innocent men and women. No sooner did the thought complete in his head than a second followed it. Couldn’t or wouldn’t? Another warrior fell under the beast’s crushing blow. The force of the impact sent a vibration up its arm, into its body, shaking the sculptor. He heard the muffled scream of the man dying under the golem’s fist. The tip of a sword or spear sank into the clay man’s side. Though the beast experienced no pain, it burned in Vesisdenperos as if a brand freshly pulled from the fire had touched him. The shock proved short- lived, diminishing as the mud healed itself, but its memory continued on. The statue swept the attacker aside. Another soldier confronted the living sculpture, approaching from in front. Vesisdenperos recognized the fear in his eyes. Here came a man doing his duty, wishing to be anywhere else but here. The sculptor empathized with his misery. But not the same pain as when the golem grabbed him by the top of his skull and twisted until a loud pop sounded and he slumped to the ground. The thing tilted its head and roared toward the sky. Vesisdenperos heard himself in the tone of hatred and defiance, tried to make it stop without success. “What’s wrong, sculptor?” the voice around him said. “Do you not enjoy what you have wrought?” He didn’t. He didn’t revel in people dying. He didn’t want his mentor to be dead. How was it possible for such a stupendous piece of

art to wreak such atrocity on the world? A laugh rumbled through the beast as another soldier fell. “Your clay creature is but a vessel, sculptor, a lump of earth fashioned to resemble a man. Do not give yourself too much credit. It is the god within who is deserving of your awe. When I have claimed my rightful place, this container will return to the mud whence it came, and you along with it.” Another blade cut into the golem’s leg, sending heat through Vesisdenperos. He cringed, fought the urge to cry out. No one heard. Nobody cared. The laugh again, reverberating inside with him, shaking his being, rattling his soul, if such a thing remained.
