Through the muddy eyes, he spied a group of warriors approaching; this one appeared different from any other. An air of determination preceded them. A soldier who looked as if he’d been beaten and survived, two women, a gray-bearded man, a fellow with one arm. And a Small God. Vesisdenperos noticed the evenstar’s attention shift to them. A smile flitted onto the golem’s face, though the sculptor knew it would not appear mirthful if he saw it from the outside as these six did. It would resemble pain, torture, and death. The golem took a step toward them. *** The earthy scent of clay and mud overpowered the stink of the battlefield—the smoke of the fire, the odor of spilled blood, of men voiding their bowels and bladders in death. Trenan’s nostrils flared. The muddy smell might have reminded someone of a warm summer day; today it stirred nausea in his gut. He let his gaze flicker from the hulking dun-colored man, surveying the surrounding area. Since Strylor had attacked the healer, he’d seen no sign of the dead, other than those freshly killed. Regardless, he suspected they remained unseen. Watching. Waiting. Two black-robed figures appeared to the left of the golem, and the master swordsman’s heart jumped. Despite their drawn up cowls, he realized neither of these were the creature who tortured him with ghosts of the dead. He opened his mouth to make Yoli and the others aware of their presence, but the small gray person with them stepped out in front first. “Ivy will take care of them.” She leaped away, covering far more distance in one jump than the master swordsman thought possible given the shortness of her legs. Her feet barely touched the ground before she sprang up again, appearing to bounce toward the black priests. “Ivy. No!” the old sailor shouted and made like he’d give chase. He progressed half a step before Yoli stopped him with an arm held

out, blocking his way. “Do not approach the black priests. Leave them to me or the little one.” “She be more’n a little one to me,” Horace growled. His tone surprised Trenan, and he glanced at the man. His face had gone hard, eyes narrow and the grooves on his forehead creasing into fleshy furrows. The sailor’s gaze flashed to meet the master swordsman’s. “This fucker already killed my friend. I ain’t gonna stand by while he kills another.” “And my daughter,” Ishla intoned, her voice low and filled with hatred. “You stay here,” Yoli said, directing her attention toward the queen. “Be safe. Someone needs to take care of the kingdom.” The queen’s eyes widened. “How do you—?” She stopped, and Trenan was glad she did. Not everyone here knew what had happened to Erral, and best to keep it so. He looked to Osis, saw how the sergeant-at-arms listed to one side, a pained expression on his face every time he sucked air into his lungs. “Osis, stay with your queen. Protect…” He hesitated, scanned the set to her features. “Protect each other. We’ll take care of the beast.” He turned away and took his first step toward the monstrosity before they objected. Yoli and Horace came right after him, both of them hurrying to catch up, one on either side. He changed his grip on his sword, which fit more naturally in his hand now than it had in a long time. He looked to Yoli. “What do we do?” he asked. The woman’s shoulders rose and fell, though her focus remained on the clay monster thirty paces away. “Trust in Goddess.” *** Horace cared not a damn for this Goddess the woman with her tits out talked about. What mattered to him were makin’ sure nothin’ happened to Ivy. He hadn’t done muchuva job takin’ care o’ her brother—somethin’ he couldn’t go backward in time and change nor ever forgive himself for—so keepin’ her alive meant ev’rythin’. Even if it cost his own existence. Never thought o’ givin’ up my life for no one. But this weren’t just about her. He needed to make up for Thorn, for Dunal, for Rilum, and for a life what he wasted. Truth be told, no amount o’ bloodshed or revenge were goin’ to atone for any bit. Maybe if he passed, the guilt’d go away. He didn’t want to be dead, but it’d turned out livin’ weren’t muchuv an upgrade. They stalked across the grass what’d started out tall and yellow sometime earlier in the day or the one before, but what were now

trampled, mucky brown, and bloody in spots. Horace watched his step, what with dropped weapons and bits o’ people layin’ about. He appreciated the distraction; it kept him from lookin’ o’er at Ivy and seein’ what were happenin’ to her. Or, maybe worse, what she did to them. The big muddy thing stood watchin’ ‘em come. Soldiers o’ both the king and Goddess poked it with swords and spears, but with no effect. Occasionally, it’d flick an arm and send an attacker flyin’ away like a ragdoll tossed by a child pitchin’ a tantrum. He wondered if Rilum’d ever had any tantrums. Or toys. When they’d got within ten steps o’ the monster what’d stolen Thorn, the one-armed swordsman and the woman broke into a run as if they planned it without tellin’ him. Catchin’ him off-guard and unawares, he fell behind by a step or two. Their legs was younger and more energetic than his. Though his own limbs didn’t have no interest in runnin’, he forced ‘em into it all the same. She reached it first, swingin’ her sword with an unusual backhand blow what Horace’d never seen. It made him impressed, ‘cept the blade hardly slowed as it passed through the thing’s muddy side. The one-armed fella followed up with a downward swing o’ his own with no more result than the other. As the ol’ sailor pulled up in front o’ the thing—he half expected to find it nothin’ more’n a huge pile o’ shit and smelled as such, but it didn’t—he watched the wound left by one- arm pucker and heal while he gawked. “Fuck me dead.” He took a couple steps to the side, careful not to get in the path o’ the others tryin’ to kill the beast, slippin’ around behind it. The ol’ sailor gulped air into his lungs, gettin’ his muscles ready, then launched his own attack. He possessed no pretty moves like the woman, or as much strength in both arms as the other fella did in his one. He owned nothin’ but a hatred he’d never experienced in his life. Horace raised the axe Ivy’d given him, the weapon feelin’ awkward and unwieldy in his grip. He didn’t really know what to do with it, so he thrust it forward, usin’ the spike stickin’ out its top, same way he’d done with the spear-thing given him before. The tip sank in, then the rest right up to the axe head, like it’d stuck into a patch o’ soft ground. Hands still hangin’ onto the weapon’s handle, he twisted, then dragged it back and forth. The creature kept standin’ in place, takin’ what he gave along with whatever the other two doled out, too. Frustrated, Horace yanked the steel from outta the clay monster. It exited without a spot o’ dirt on its length, and with a noticeable slurpin’ sound; the noise turned out bein’ just the thing to draw its attention. The mud fucker jerked around, arm raised, and the ol’ sailor

stumbled away, his poor feet movin’ as fast as they’d go. Despite his legs spendin’ so many turns o’ the seasons settin’ his body right while ships’ decks pitched beneath his soles, they refused to help him keep his balance this time. His boots caught up, one with the other, and his ass hit the ground. Turned out the exact right time to fall backward; if he didn’t, the monster’s swing would’ve smacked him upside the head. Instead, it passed above as he fell, a puff o’ clay-stinkin’ wind brushin’ up against his face. Before the creature followed up, one-arm and the woman lit into it again, though their attacks did no more good’n before. At least it distracted him. Horace pistoned his feet, pushin’ back while also pullin’ himself with his free hand what weren’t holdin’ the stupid and useless axe. His fingers sank into somethin’ soft, wet, and vaguely warm; he pulled it out quick without lookin’ to see what stuck to his palm. In front o’ him, the mud beast pushed against one-arm’s chest and sent him flyin’ through the air. The warrior woman attacked again, dodgin’ a punch what the ol’ sailor thought likely to take her head from her shoulders if it’d connected. She went to pull away, and the thing caught her by the arm, tossed her with a flick o’ the wrist. And then Ivy stood between them. “No,” he intended to yell, but his mouth and tongue lacked the proper amount o’ saliva for makin’ sound. As he pushed himself up on his elbows, a shadow fell across him like a cloud crossin’ the sun. Wind stirred what little grass remained upright and blew his own hair onto his forehead and in his eyes. He brushed it away on his forearm, avoidin’ touchin’ his face with whatever he’d sunk his hand into—horse manure or man guts—and raised his gaze skyward. He spied the black wings, and his heart jumped in his chest. Father Raven. He looked away from the sky in time to see a big clay foot come down right on top o’ Ivy. *** Every time Ishla attempted to move away, the sergeant-at-arms’ grip kept her from going anywhere. She flashed him a frown, but saw he wasn’t looking at her. Instead, he watched as Yoli and Trenan attacked fruitlessly over and over. Despite his injuries, she realized he wanted to be fighting beside his compatriot, defending the kingdom, not babysitting the queen. And yet he refused to relinquish his post, this she knew. She set her jaw, tensed her muscles, ready for the instant his vigilance waned. The fight continued nearby, but didn’t spill to them. Ishla raised an eyebrow and glanced about. Without word from anyone, a group of

Goddess’ warriors had formed a rough circle around them to stave off any attacks. She should have been grateful; her combat training had happened a long time ago. Instead of gratitude, frustration bubbled inside her, fueled by the depth of her rage that demanded quenching. When the inexplicable clay man sent Trenan flying with a shove to his chest, she gasped, the irritation dispersing like dried leaves before a brisk wind. Despite everything, she wanted to go to him, make sure he was all right. She pulled lightly against Osis’ hold, found it remained strong, then had her attention once again stolen when the beast grabbed Yoli by the arm and threw her. Her heart thumped against her ribs. The creature rounded on the old sailor who lay on the ground staring up at the thing with wide, scared eyes. A shadow slipped across them—a cloud drifting in front of the sun—then disappeared. And then the small one called Ivy got between Horace and the beastly statue. If anyone can vanquish this beast, it’s a Small God from the Green. But Ivy did nothing, merely glared at it. Another darkness fell, and wind stirred Ishla’s hair. A noise disturbed the sounds of battle, a loud rustling like a tree shaken hard, though no trees grew anywhere on the plain. She let her attention wander for an instant, glimpsed black wings, then turned to see the golem raise its foot. Ivy remained resolute. “Ivy!” she called. The foot came down and the Small God disappeared beneath it. Ishla cried out, this time pulling from the sergeant’s hold as the man stared, too. She wanted to rush to her fallen compatriots, offer whatever help she might, but the surrounding warriors became a swirling crowd. She realized none of them swung weapons anymore. Instead of fighting, they hastened away, some of them bumping into one another to do so. Stiff wind beat against Ishla, but it didn’t come from sunrise or sunset, or anywhere in between. This gust originated from above. She raised her head, caught a flash of ebony, then a hand grabbed her, pulled her to the ground. The queen crumpled, and the enormous bird passed close enough above for her to reach out and stroke its dark feathers if she desired. It landed smoothly, bounced a couple of times. A man in a black robe stepped in front of it, raised his arms, and the huge raven snapped its beak, cutting the priest in two at the waist. Everyone else backed away, giving it room as it hopped in a half-circle to face the golem. Only then did Ishla notice the figure dressed in golden armor sitting on its back. “Father Raven.” The words sounded as though carved rather than spoken; they came from the clay man. “I thought the foolish creature

we sacrificed had let you free and we’d never see you again.” The giant bird clicked its beak together three times, hopped closer to the living statue. If it was in any way intimidated, it gave no indication. The figure perched atop it threw one leg over its back and slid down the side, landing lithely on the ground. The queen rose from where Osis had pulled her aside, took a step nearer and saw the woman. She wore a breast plate of gold, golden epaulets, and a helmet of the same material garnished with red plumage. “And who have you brought me, old bird?” Ishla sidled away from the sergeant-at-arms, keeping her eyes on the newcomer who stood beside the raven, one hand resting on its wing as though calming it. Flaps on her cheeks hid her face until she shifted, turning toward the queen. She inhaled quickly, breath catching in her throat. “Danya!” When she tried to rush to her daughter, Osis caught her by the arm again, having found his way to her while they distracted her. She pulled against his grip and heard him grunt, the jarring of her movement causing him pain, but he didn’t let go. “No, my queen,” he said between clenched teeth, the words compressed. Danya gazed at her mother without recognition in her gaze. Ishla’s heart sped. She raised her arm, reached out toward her daughter; she never expected to see her again, had thought her dead, yet there she stood. But is it her? It closely resembled her, but the lack of awareness, the way she radiated, gave Ishla pause. The raven opened its beak and let out an ear-splitting caw, startling everyone around it except for Danya. And the golem. The creature laughed with a sound nothing like laughter. Danya—or the warrior who resembled her—turned her attention toward the clay man. She crossed the ground gracefully, hand dragging along the raven’s side. The bird stuck its beak out, snapped at the air in front of the living statue; it didn’t so much as flinch. When the woman reached its head, the raven bent forward, as though it bowed, then backed away, leaving her to face the mud thing on her own. Ishla held her breath, aware of the tightness of Osis’ grip on her arm as she watched. She wanted to do something—run to her daughter, shout in warning, attack the clay beast. She did none of those things, left only to observe, and hope. Danya closed the distance between them with an unhurried gait, the battlefield around them quiet as though everyone held their breath the same way Ishla did, then stopped a pace from the golem. The red

plumage bobbed as she looked up into its eyes. She made no move for the sword slung at her side. The creature didn’t threaten to attack, only smiled. The brown indentation serving as its mouth moved. “I’ve missed you, sister.” Without words or warning, she sprang forward, catching the beast off-guard. She did so with no weapon drawn or fist raised. Her body struck the living statue’s chest, and the mud parted like she’d dived into the sea. The armored princess disappeared, swallowed up by the creature of clay. “Danya,” Ishla screamed. For the space of five heartbeats, silence reigned. No one moved, not even the golem. It stood like the statue it resembled, a surprised expression on its face if a face of mud could show surprise. The raven clicked its beak together twice, and the sound snapped all those about it out of the trance. Off to her left, steel clashed against steel. A man cried out. The battle resumed.

XIX Horace – Diggin’ Horace’s gaze slipped from the gigantic ebony bird what once dropped Thorn outta the sky onto him to the big gray foot what’d taken Ivy away. He knew a battle raged around him, one he should’ve been payin’ attention to keep from gettin’ murdered, but right then he weren’t sure he saw the point o’ keepin’ on. Rilum. Thorn. Ivy. Everyone I cared for. Then the simple deckhand’s face flashed through his mind. Dunal. He’d felt small concern for the boy, but no denyin’ he’d ended him. He’d taken no one else’s life—slain little more’n fish, really. A few crabs and other shellfish, but only because they tasted so good. Dunal he’d murdered to protect himself, a fact what weren’t right. Killed the man just to keep from goin’ back out on the sea. Maybe it explained why he’d lost Thorn and Ivy—his punishment for chokin’ the deckhand to death. I gotta set it proper before ev’ryone dies. He shifted, movin’ to climb to his feet despite the pains in his knees and hips, and somethin’ struck him in the backbone. Startled, he rolled aside, tryin’ to do it in a way such as to allow him to bring his weapon to bear without cuttin’ himself. When he finished rollin’, he found Yoli standin’ facin’ away from him, lungin’ at a fella in a black robe. It’d been her leg what’d knocked him. “Don’t just lay there. Fight,” she said over her shoulder. She dodged a strike from the priest and ran the man through, the tip o’ her sword pokin’ right outta the backside o’ him. She pulled the blade first up then down before yankin’ it free to move on to the next. The black-clad fella crumpled, the darkness o’ his robe disguisin’ whatever blood might’ve been leakin’ from his gut. The ol’ sailor scuffled on the ground and made his way up to his feet. He surveyed the area quickly, the awkward and heavy axe gripped in both hands; the skin on the one what’d sunk into a pile o’ who-knew-what felt tight with whatever’d been dryin’ on it. He resisted takin’ a look because it didn’t matter so much if he discovered it shit, blood, or guts—didn’t want to know. Turned out weren’t nobody fightin’ near the clay man. Goddess warriors, king’s men, black priests, and ev’ryone else gave the thing lots o’ room. Even Father Raven didn’t get close, the enormous bird havin’ hopped off into the midst of the fray, snappin’ his beak at robe- clad monks, sometimes takin’ to the air with a soldier caught in his talons. Horace thought if anyone—anythin’—might’ve stood a chance against the golem, the feathered behemoth did, but no. And so it were an ol’ sailor what not so long ago wished never to

set foot on a deck again, and now found himself wishin’ to be on any ship far, far away, were the lone soul close to the thing what wanted to take o’er the kingdom. But it didn’t move. Since the woman who the queen thought looked like Danya—but to Horace were no doubt Ailyssa—had climbed off the raven and disappeared into the clay fella, the monster hadn’t moved by so much as a hair. The ol’ sailor crept closer to it, keepin’ the axe held out in front o’ him. He glanced one way and the other, eyes always returnin’ to the mud beast in case it were only playin’, same as them fish what lay on the sea bottom, not movin’ until it were too late for its prey. Horace circled around the thing, stayin’ outta what he thought’d be its reach. When he got to the front, he peered up at what passed for its face. He’d looked at it before without realizin’ how much it resembled the features o’ the creature Rilum’d become. It possessed dents where eyes should be, a bump for a nose, lips what opened on a shallow, gray-brown mouth. The ol’ sailor’s chest tightened. For some reason, after ev’rythin’ he’d done—and hadn’t—his son not only forgave him, but saved him, too. He’d sacrificed his life for a man he barely knew. Now he were dead like ev’ryone else. Rilum. Dunal. Thorn. His eyes dropped to the clay creature’s foot. “Ivy.” With no more thought, Horace tossed the near-useless axe aside and sank to his knees at the golem’s feet. It might’ve appeared he did so to offer prayer, or beg for mercy, but neither was true. The first o’ those things he’d never made a habit o’ doin’ and the second, though he might’ve considered it not so long ago, he’d gotten well past now. He ignored the pain tweakin’ his back when his knees hit the ground jarrin’ his spine, and stared at the foot he’d watched come down on top o’ Ivy. Weren’t no sign o’ her pokin’ out from under, not so much as a gray finger. Horace inhaled a breath through his tight lips, hatin’ the gritty remnant o' clay the air left on his tongue. He released it, leaned forward, and set to diggin’ into the muddy flesh with his fingers. The space under his fingernails filled up with mud, leavin’ grooves in the foot’s surface. The details with which someone’d sculpted it struck the ol’ sailor; not that he’d seen many sculptures to compare the quality, but if it weren’t for the color, it might’ve been real. Had it been, the scratches he left behind would’ve stayed. They didn’t. By the time he finished diggin’ at it and got ready to go again, the lacerations he’d made’d already healed themselves. He dug faster, harder, deeper, all the while wonderin’ if a heavy clay fist’d club him

in the head, puttin’ an end to his pathetic attempt to rescue his friend. No one touched him. He saw nothin’ but the furrows healin’ themselves, his hands covered in gray mud to the wrists. He heard nothin’ but his heart beatin’ in his ears, his own breath raspin’ in and out o’ his lungs. The muscles in his arms and shoulders ached and tightened. Breathin’ heavy, Horace stopped and settled on his haunches. Without him diggin’ at it, the foot returned to lookin’ as though he’d never touched it. His body sagged as he pictured Ivy, remembered how much she resembled Thorn. Eyes closed, he tilted his head skyward, let out an anguished sigh. A warm breeze made him aware o’ wetness on his face. Sweat? Tears? Both more’n likely. A drop splattered on his forehead and he jerked his eyelids open, worried he’d find someone loomin’ o’er him, drippin’ blood from a ghastly wound. Findin’ it weren’t so should’ve given him relief, but Horace didn’t think anythin’ in the world would offer him respite again. Not even the rain what’d started fallin’. *** Osis pulled his sword from the gut of a man with no business being on a battlefield. No armor, a curved blade meant for cutting wheat as his weapon. This was someone who began his life on a farm, where it should have ended, as well. The fellow stared first at the sergeant-at- arms, as though surprised such a thing happened, then looked at the hand clutching his midsection, blood seeping between his fingers. His knees buckled, and he pitched forward onto his face. Osis winced against the pain in his side as he whirled around, ready for the next attack. None came, a brief reprieve giving him the opportunity to catch his breath. He inhaled, his damaged ribs limiting the volume of air he could offer his lungs. As he let it out, something in the sky caught his eye. At first, he thought it another of the banished falling to the earth, and he whispered a curse. He’d noticed no more of them come crashing down for a while and had hoped they’d seen the last of them. Each of the naked bastards was worth ten or more of the men he’d just slain and wreaked havoc through their ranks. The fewer they needed to contend with, the better. This one appeared different, though. Instead of a smoky, gray-white trail, it left a darker cloud in its wake to spread out behind it, refusing to dissipate. He checked his perimeter, saw nobody close, and squinted toward the anomaly. It wasn’t a fireball at the front of the haze, but a small, dark spot, moving at a slower pace. Someone cried out in anger, as untrained fighters so often do when they attack. Osis spun, took a step to the side, and let the man who’d

rushed him stumble past, his strike cutting nothing but empty air. As much as he didn’t relish killing men with little chance of defending themselves, he’d do whatever he needed to do to keep himself alive and protect the kingdom. This fellow kept his balance and got himself righted, spinning to face the sergeant. He held the sword out in front of him, the length of the too-long blade dotted with blooms of rust. The thing should have been left mounted over the fireplace mantel, where it had likely been before it ended up in this man’s hands. To the fellow’s credit, Osis saw no fear in his eyes. They gleamed with a maniacal hatred—similar to what he’d seen in most of the men he’d faced on this battlefield. Rage deserved no place in a fight. He swung the weapon from left to right, twisting at the waist. Osis jumped back and used his own blade to sweep it aside, the momentum of the sword meant more for show than battle pulling its wielder off balance again. He gritted his teeth against the pain in his side, even as he marveled at this untrained fighter staying alive as long as he had. Osis darted forward, striking the man in the chest with his right shoulder and sending him onto his ass. The ceremonial sword flew from his grip and the sergeant inserted the tip of his own blade through the fellow’s neck, giving it a twist before pulling it free. He gurgled and coughed; Osis moved away, leaving him to die choking on his own blood alone. During the brief skirmish, the unusual dot in the sky advanced closer. Osis dared a look up and realized it was a bird, each flap of its wings belching out more of the dark cloud spreading behind it. Beneath its trail, the air faded to a hazy gray, obscuring the forest beyond the plain. He sidestepped a youth swinging an axe meant for chopping wood, drawing his sword along the fellow’s side as he did. The wounded man howled and dropped to his knees. Another fellow jumped at the sergeant-at-arms; he punched his adversary in the face with his left hand, grimacing with the jolt of pain it sent through his shoulder and down his side. The attacker fell to the ground and Osis kicked him in the head with the toe of his boot. When he looked up again, the bird was overhead. He watched it fly by, the cloud puffing out behind with each sweep of its wings. A few heartbeats later, raindrops touched his cheeks. A drizzle hastily turning to a downpour. Osis sighed. He hated fighting in the rain—too much tended to go wrong with mud underfoot and wet grips. Water pattered against his armor and he wondered if it might have been better had it turned out to be one of the banished rather than a bird bringing precipitation. He rolled his left shoulder, trying to shrug away the discomfort
throbbing out of it, and directed his attention to the next untrained fighter awaiting his blade. The black priest standing before him raised his hands, the tips of his fingers glowing.

XX Danya – Inside She opened her eyes after what felt a very long time. She had memories: Evalal, Teryk and the knife, flowers, the Mother of Death. Stress, fear, exhaustion muddled everything until she lay bleeding on the ground, but all after seemed distant, as though not her remembrances. More like half-remembered dreams, or a story she’d heard and now imagined as her own. She concentrated, trying to remember why she might have impressions of colorful plants, and of the Mother of Death. Could they be images from when she received the Seed of Life, but recalled out of order? It didn’t matter, so she pushed the thoughts aside to take in her surroundings. Despite the oddity she gazed upon, she believed her eyes this time. She peered out at a flat expanse, the ground a deep and shimmering blue, as though a frozen ocean lay beneath her feet. Sparse trees sprouted from it at irregular intervals, with black trunks and leaves of red, yellow, and silver. No grass, no shrubs. She heard no sounds, either—no birds chirped, no animals scuttled, no insects buzzed. Never had she seen such a place, or even imagined anything like it existed. The unusual panorama left her short of breath. “Where am I?” she whispered, not intending to speak aloud and break the silence. “I am not sure.” The other voice startled her. She jumped away, raising an arm in defense, though the person beside her gave no sign she’d attack. Danya spun toward the speaker; finding a familiarity to her surprised the princess. She relaxed her defensive stance, stared at the other woman. She didn’t know her, yet recognized her face. Lines wrinkled the corners of her eyes, a downward slope to her mouth, and gray- speckled short hair giving the impression of a much shorter cut growing out. In Danya’s foggy memory, these features blended with the flowers and the Mother of Death. “Barren Mother?” The woman nodded, gaze darting between her new companion and the peculiar landscape. “Ailyssa.” A pink sky swirled above them, highlighted by streaks of gold. A warm breeze touched her cheek. “I don’t understand,” Danya said. “The Seed of Life and the Barren Mother. You bore one, and I was the other.” The princess turned a tight circle, taking in their surroundings. “But am I alive? What is this place?” Ailyssa shrugged. “I don’t know. We have to trust Goddess has put us where we need to be.”

Danya glanced at her, expecting to see the expression she’d have found on Evalal’s face whenever she talked of faith and the Goddess. But this woman’s features showed something different, a shadow easily interpreted as doubt. Without real knowledge, the princess assumed her a woman who’d seen sadness and heartbreak, experienced things which pushed her belief to the brink. Completing her task and arriving here was likely a miracle on its own. She returned her attention to their surroundings. The blue beneath their feet stretched on and on, unbroken but for the trees, until it touched the pink sky in the distance, creating a horizon tinged with gold. It appeared this way in every direction. “How did we get here?” “What do you remember?” “Very little after…” she hesitated. “After my brother killed me. I have a vague impression of flowers, you, the Mother of Death, not much more.” “The Seed of Life created the garden you recall. The Mother of Death told us where to go, what to do. We faced the golem; we are inside him. She said nothing of what to expect after.” She fell silent for a brief time. “Perhaps she didn’t know.” Danya stifled a shiver, hugged herself. The sensation of being alive, of feeling the solidity of her own body after so long in the darkness before the Barren Mother rescued her, should have been comforting. It wasn’t. Stunning as she found this extraordinary vista, she realized she didn’t want to be in this place. “What do we do?” she asked. “Wait,” the other woman responded, though her tone suggested it might have also been a question rather than an answer. The princess let her arms fall to her sides. The golden armor bestowed by the Mother of Death hadn’t come with them, nor the robe she’d worn during her journey to the Green with Evalal. Evalal. She inhaled a quick breath. Is she all right? She faced Ailyssa, saw her clad in a similar gauzy white dress. The material shifted with the smallest breeze, the wide sleeves filling with air and billowing out. If Goddess or the Mother of Death meant them to go to battle in this attire, they’d made a poor choice. “Do you know what happened to Evalal?” she asked. “The girl who tended you? She was fine, last I saw. Haggard, tired, but alive and safe.” A weight she hadn’t realized she’d carried lifted from Danya’s chest. She inhaled deeply through her nostrils, noticed this world they found themselves in lacked any odors, then let out a sigh through her mouth. “And what of my brother?” Ailyssa shook her head. “Gone before I arrived.”

The princess nodded to herself, but wondered what had happened. Did Trenan escape from the weapons merchants and take Teryk with him? Had they left together, her brother and mentor, under citizen’s arrest? No, it was Ive who gave him the knife he used to end her life; she’d seen it happen. But why? Why did he murder her? Her chin dropped, and she looked at her feet, the tips of her bare toes poking out from beneath the white dress. Her heart sank along with her gaze. All those turns of the season, he’d been more than merely her brother—her friend, confidant, the most important person in her life. She couldn’t imagine intentionally hurting him. Yet a simple revelation—he wasn’t the firstborn of the rightful king, not the chosen one named on an ancient parchment—proved enough to thrust murder into his heart. Look where being firstborn gets you. Her throat tightened, emotion threatening to choke her. Despite everything she’d been through with Evalal, this was the first moment she wished they hadn’t gone to retrieve the scroll after their father— her father—burned it. If they never read the words written on it, none of this would have happened. Or would it? The touch of the Barren Mother’s hand sliding into hers startled her. She raised her chin, surprised by the coolness of the breeze touching her cheeks, drying the tears she hadn’t realized had spilled from her eyes. Ailyssa looked at her with a soft and understanding expression. “Grief and despair. These are understandable. We have much to mourn, many reasons to resign. But I won’t fill your mind and your ears with words of faith and of Goddess’ plan. These we must find for ourselves. And right now, other things require our attention.” Ailyssa turned, gazing toward the horizon. The princess did the same, following her line of sight. At first, she saw nothing other than the solid blue ground, the unusually colored trees. After a moment, she discovered what the Barren Mother had seen. A pair of figures, silhouetted against the sky, approached. *** The evenstar towered over Vesisdenperos, standing at least as tall to his eye as the clay vessel he’d fashioned to contain him. The height difference necessitated the sculptor taking two steps to each of the man’s strides. Though he appreciated having and using legs of his own again after so long without, the pace left him short of breath. They crossed the odd blue ground, its surface soft against his bare soles despite its hard appearance. While they closed the distance between them and the two women in the white dresses, Vesisdenperos occasionally glanced up at his companion’s face, trying to read the

evenstar’s expression. It gave away nothing. More than once, he opened his mouth to ask who they were but thought better of it every time, closing it without speaking. The surreal nature of the place reminded the sculptor of the temple at Teva Stavoklis. It lacked the impressive water walls, and the shrine’s startling architecture, but possessed a similar undeniable atmosphere, as though the ground they trod upon and the unusual trees held ancient secrets told in lost languages. He wondered if even Ine’vesi himself understood them. It also reminded him Teva Stavoklis was the last time he saw his friend alive. Through his entire life, Vesisdenperos had known two things: Kuneprius and the clay. No one else—no friends, no family, only the man who raised him, took care of him, mentored him—and nothing outside his discipline. No chance to play, and no schooling; they’d even excused him from religious practices, so important was his role. Now Kuneprius was dead, and he’d fulfilled his purpose. What remained for him? The thought drained his energy, and he tried to decrease his pace. It didn’t slow. The evenstar carried him along with him, dragging him toward his fate. Toward his destiny. Toward his death? His mind wandered to Kuneprius greeting him every evening when he returned from the cave, a repast always prepared and awaiting him. Each time, his friend asked him about his experience. In the early days, when young and learning his craft, he’d go on and on detailing new techniques and daily successes, Kuneprius listening intently and nodding along. Later, when he came home covered in drying clay after repeating the same thing for the hundredth time, his hours more spent killing time waiting for the day to come than training, he’d still ask, and they’d laugh together. Sometimes until tears streaked the gray dust on his cheeks. Then the man who raised him would encourage him to wash up and enjoy a meal. Despite so few people having been part of his life, Vesisdenperos couldn’t recall an occasion when they lacked for things to talk about. In the end, it had been the clay that killed him. The sculptor’s breath came in ragged gasps, the pace of the evenstar taxing his lungs. They’d drawn close enough now for him to make out some details of the two women. One appeared older, with short hair, the other younger, perhaps near his own age. They both wore filmy white dresses fluttering with the breeze and expressions reflecting both fear and determination. Though he knew not who they were—if he counted the number of females he’d met in his life on his hands, he’d have fingers to spare—he sensed a familiarity in the older one’s features. He didn’t understand how it might be possible.

Maybe when we get closer… Ine’vesi stopped, dragging the sculptor to a halt alongside him. Vesisdenperos bent at the waist, planting his forearms on his knees and gulping air into his chest. The world spun, and he closed his eyes to make it stop. When he did, the older woman’s features swirled out of the darkness and into his mind. What about her vexed him? He thought of the women he’d encountered—captives brought before Kristeus, though Kuneprius had harbored suspicions the term wasn’t exactly correct. Each one he met merely in passing; he didn’t recognize her face among his memories. His breath settled, and he straightened, opened his eyes. Ine’vesi stood with his arms crossed in front of his chest, staring across the space at the women. They had both adopted defensive stances, mirroring each other. “I can’t say I’m surprised to see you, Rak’bana,” he said, voice rumbling through the quiet air. “Surprised you are here, perhaps, but not surprised to see you.” Rak’bana. The priestess. Sister to the evenstar. Vesisdenperos wondered which of the women was his kin. Would Ine’vesi’s sister resemble him? Neither of them did. Not all relatives looked similar, he supposed. They nodded, then shifted their stance, moving in perfect unison as if to a choreographed dance. They stood like they held shields before them, and brandished swords, though nothing filled their empty hands. The evenstar sauntered a few paces closer, drawing the sculptor along with him. He stopped again. “Leave now and I will spare you, sister.” He chuckled, a sound reminiscent of rock rubbing rock despite coming from the mouth of a man, not the throat of a clay golem. “In fact, I’ll give you a place at my side. We can rule together, you and I.” He moved two paces closer, Vesisdenperos along with him. The women shook their heads in tandem and the sculptor frowned. How did they act so perfectly in unison? He peered first at the younger of them, examining her face, but her eyes remained on the evenstar, looking to burn a hole through his head. He shifted his gaze to the older one with the inexplicable sliver of familiarity. She, too, stared at his companion, but for an instant, her attention flickered toward him. Their eyes met. It lasted for less than a heartbeat, and then she’d returned her concern to the evenstar. In the brief span, he realized. Gooseflesh crawled along his arms and a shudder trembled through his shoulders. Not all who are related look similar. But sometimes they do.

XXI Ailyssa – Priestess Many seasons had turned since the Sisters of Ikkundana had trained Ailyssa in the art of combat. In her youth, she’d practiced regularly with the other Sisters close in age, using sticks as weapons, rehearsing forms. With time passing, most of her companions moved to other temples, and she found herself older and without friends, so the habit passed and her technique slipped into disuse. Spending her life in prayer and making chalk lines on a wall, she’d never imagined a need for the skills. So it surprised her when she struck the ready pose alongside the princess. They did it in unison—left foot forward, left arm across their bodies, right raised as if brandishing weapons, the way they’d taught her so long ago. A stance used with shield and sword, though they held neither. “Leave now and I will spare you, sister,” the taller of the two men said. A rumble he possibly meant as a laugh came from his throat. “In fact, I’ll give you a spot at my side. We can rule together, you and I.” She shook her head; out of the corner of her eye, she noticed Danya do the same. Ailyssa understood who stood before them, but refused to think his name. The sound of it brought fear, and this was neither time nor place to allow unease to keep her from the role meant for her. He moved two steps closer, the other, smaller fellow following. The Barren Mother found her gaze drawn to the younger man. Their eyes met, held for a few heartbeats. Her pulse quickened—some things a mother knows instinctively. “Rak’bana,” the priest intoned, shattering the silence. “We—” “No, Ine’vesi,” Ailyssa said at the same time as Danya. Their voices combined, became one. “Goddess banished you for a reason. You cannot come back.” “A matter of opinion, dear sister. The prophecy on my scrap of parchment says something altogether different from yours.” With no words or signal between them, the princess stepped to her left at the same instant Ailyssa moved to her right, the two of them separating. The Barren Mother’s perception swam as they did. She blinked to dispel the odd effect; it didn’t help. Instead, it appeared her field of view had expanded. She took another step and Danya mirrored her movement, the range of her vision increasing along with it. “And so far,” Ine’vesi continued, “everything foretold came to pass. The Small God is dead, Rak’bana. The stars fall. Nothing left for you to do but decide if you will stand by my side or die with the others. Again.” Ailyssa and Danya each took another sideways step, the unreal

sensation of seeing through two sets of eyes expanding further. The tall man—the one his followers called the evenstar—stared straight ahead, in between them, as though unaware of their movement. The shorter man’s gaze darted back and forth between her and the princess, occasionally found its way to the face of his master. Fear and concern contorted his features, pulling his lips into a frown and etching a line on his forehead. His obvious anxiety tugged at Ailyssa’s heart. Ine’vesi waved his hand. “Did your Goddess expect this fancy armor to scare me? Impress me?” His mouth twisted into an evil grin and he raised his arms, extending them out to the side. Ailyssa blinked. In the tiny space of time, armor appeared on his body—black plate shot with silver veins. The younger fellow with him jumped, startled by its sudden appearance. His feet tangled, and he fell; where he hit, the ground turned from blue to purple before fading to its original color. Ine’vesi grabbed the hilt of a weapon materializing at his waist along with the armor. A black blade shrieked as he pulled it from its scabbard. Ailyssa wanted to throw her hands against the sides of her head, protect her ears from the sound, but she couldn’t move from her position. The man they called the evenstar lofted the sword skyward, striking a threatening pose. “Is this what you want, ’Bana? Is this how you’d have it end between us?” Ailyssa felt herself reach for her own waist, fingers wrapping around an unseen leather-bound hilt. Her arm made the motion of drawing a blade; Danya did the same beside her. “No, brother. This is not what I crave,” the two of them said with the same voice. “I wanted to save you, but you didn’t allow me.” The former priest side-stepped to his left; the women mirrored him. His companion on the ground scuffled his feet, pushing himself away to avoid being trod upon as they circled. The Barren Mother’s gaze fell on him, recognized the terror on his face, and she found a piece of the same fear in her own heart. “Save me?” Ine’vesi laughed. “Is that what you call letting me burn to death after being banished?” “You brought it on yourself.” “Your Goddess did it to me,” he snapped. He lowered his sword, pointed the tip at a spot directly between the two women at eye level. “If you’d listened to me before. If you had seen the way.” “No, ’Vesi. If you had listened to me, she would have saved you. If I’d followed you, we’d both have burned.” “Ha,” he snorted. “Despite your faith, you have fared little better than I. Except I have followers willing to do anything to restore me.

Your Goddess leaves you to languish in the death lands.” “Misguided miscreants hardly rank as disciples.” Ine’vesi’s expression hardened, the cords in his neck showed; Ailyssa anticipated he might lunge, but he didn’t. Not yet. “Those men, your followers, as you call them, are but sheep,” she said, Danya along with her. “You and your priests lead them to slaughter for your own gain while offering nothing for them.” “You know naught of it, Rak’bana. I will give them the kingdom stolen from them by jealousy. A fake goddess has fooled you so completely, it leaves you blind.” Ailyssa felt a prickle at the nape of her neck at his last word. Too long she had fumbled through the world without seeing, both before they took her sight and after. Now was the first time in her life she truly saw things clearly. Her mouth opened to say so—at least, she thought it did. When her lips moved, the other voice came out again. “You give them false hope and lies. Your promises are as empty as was your faith.” “I guess I have your answer, then.” “You do. I wish it different, my brother. My love. You will never return to this place from which she banished you.” “We shall see.” His upper lip curled, exposing his teeth. For an instant, absolute silence fell, as though everything around them froze. Ailyssa’s eyes flickered to the man on the ground staring at the proceedings with wide-eyed disbelief. Her mind jumped in time to a babe taken from her practically right out of the womb. Her third-born. She’d never known where he’d gone, what they did with him. Until now. Ine’vesi elevated his sword overhead and leapt forward, forcing every thought from her head. She and Danya raised their arms, protecting themselves with swords that weren’t there as his blade arced toward them. *** The sculptor gasped, noticing the lack of smell or taste of clay to the air he drew. Had he ever experienced a time its scent didn’t cling to the inside of his nostrils, gather in a layer along the lining of his throat? The evenstar swung his weapon at the space between the women wearing flimsy white dresses. Vesisdenperos tensed, awaiting the tip to embed itself in the strange blue ground. It didn’t. At the height where the two of them held their arms, hands empty, the sword struck something solid, and an unseen bolt of lightning flashed. It revealed a figure to him, a woman clad in golden armor with a blade of gold deflecting Ine’vesi’s blow. The priestess.

The world changed. The blue beneath faded to gray and the pink sky turned yellow. New trees burst forth from the ground. Ine’vesi jumped back and his sister’s form flickered away, leaving the two women standing on either side of where she’d been. Vesisdenperos pumped his feet against the surface, pushing himself backward, struggled to hands and knees and stood. For a second, he thought the earth moved beneath him, then realized weak legs and a spinning head caused the sensation. He stumbled to the nearest tree, put his hand against its smooth, orange bark to steady himself. The three figures circled. The evenstar twirled the tip of his sword, offering a threat, a promise of pain and death; the two women held their poses, moving in exact harmony as though marionettes controlled by the same set of strings. He stared at the older woman, his pulse sending blood racing through his veins, pounding at his temples. Sweat dampened his brow. Could it be? Despite the stance, her face didn’t hold the aspect of a warrior. Her features knew the passage of time and experience, but they lacked the etching of the faces of those who’d experienced horrors, taken lives. It held softness, even if it hid beneath the current expression of intent and tension. For so many turns of the seasons while he honed his craft as sculptor, Vesisdenperos had learned as part of his lessons to study physiognomy. The shapes of eyes, the sets of mouths, the curves of noses. These things he noticed more than most; they spoke to him, told him tales of a person’s life and heritage. And the more he looked at her, the less he doubted his assessment. Ine’vesi leapt forward again. The two women disappeared, the priestess taking their place as steel contacted steel with an echoing impact, jarring his eardrums. Their swords came together again and again. Beneath his feet, the sculptor watched the ground shift from gray to brown, then yellow, then green. Three paces to his right, a tree shot up, leafless branches unfolding. He cowered against the trunk he’d been leaning on, its bark having shifted from orange to pink. Above, the sky darkened to black, though it brought no change to the light. “You know how this will end, sister.” Ine’vesi’s voice shook the very air around them. “Don’t make me kill you.” The women replaced the priestess again. A fine line of red ran across the front of the younger woman’s white dress. Vesisdenperos inhaled a sharp breath upon seeing it; his fingernails dug into the tree’s pink bark. “One of us leaves here, Ine’vesi,” they answered with two mouths and a single voice. “It will not be you.” The evenstar snarled. He feinted one way, then struck the other.

Metal clanged, the priestess appeared; colors changed, trees sprang forth. If they battle long enough, they’ll be doing it in a dead forest. The sculptor took a step away from the tree, forgetting the danger of more like it springing up from the earth as he watched the fray, breathless. Ine’vesi forced the fight, his opponent flickering between two women who appeared to have no right nor reason to be on a battlefield, and the priestess, born his equal. As they clashed, Vesisdenperos moved closer, feet scuffing against the ground, its color unnoticed as he stared at the evenstar’s adversary. Every time Rak’bana disappeared, replaced by the others, he found the face of the older one, assessing the height of her cheekbones, the fullness of her lips, the size of her ears. He raised his hand, touched his own features. During his training, he’d spent many evenings with his eyelids closed as he ran his fingertips over the nose and chin of his caretaker, or anyone else willing to volunteer for the cause. His heart twinged again. Kuneprius. In one of the brief instances between swords clashing, his gaze met the older woman’s. Fear and desperation clouded her eyes, unlike the confidence and certainty flashing in Rak’bana’s. Then Ine’vesi struck again, and she disappeared, the plea in her expression gone along with it. But the look convinced him. My mother. Their swords came together, and a tree sprouted immediately behind the priestess, giving her nowhere to retreat. She fought back, spine pressed against the red trunk; branches devoid of leaves curled around her, as though seeking to hold her in place. She struggled against them, trying to pull away; the evenstar laughed. An instant later, they’d wrapped themselves around her arms, keeping her from swinging her sword at her brother, stopping her from defending herself. Held thus, the priestess’ appearance remained, his mother and the other woman nowhere in sight. Vesisdenperos froze for a few beats of his heart. What happens to the women if Ine’vesi kills his sister? The evenstar took a nonchalant step, bounced his sword in his hand. “Last chance, Rak’bana. Renounce your Goddess, join me and rule at my side.” “Never.” Her lip curled, the muscles in her neck strained as she pulled against the branches holding her. “I’d rather die.” “Then I suppose you will get your wish.” He raised his blade again, directing the point toward the unprotected spot at the top of his sister’s breastplate and below her

chin. The sculptor’s heart leaped into his throat. Before he realized what he was doing, he jumped forward, a single word escaping his mouth. “No!” Two steps passed beneath his feet, leaving a good five more before he’d reach the siblings. The evenstar didn’t glance away as he spoke. “Sculptor.” Vesisdenperos froze again, but not out of fear or any other emotion this time. His limbs were no longer under his control, as though branches held him in the same way they confined the priestess, but no tree grew anywhere near him. Ine’vesi’s power constricted him. “What an honor this must be for you, sculptor,” the evenstar said. “Getting to see your life’s work come to the ultimate fruition. All you worked so hard for and dreamed of, completed right before your eyes.” As he spoke, the colors of the landscape changed again. The sky turned red, but everything else became translucent, as though formed by sheets and chunks of ice. Ine’vesi leaned toward his sister, the tip of his sword coming within two finger breadths of her throat. “Behave yourself, sculptor. Watch the world change.” The hold on Vesisdenperos released, his muscles going slack all at once and spilling him to the ground. He hit hard, jarring his spine and clicking his teeth together. His attention remained on the priestess imprisoned by the tree for an instant before he diverted it. He didn’t want to see what happened, didn’t want to consider what it meant to the other women. His gaze fell to the space in front of him and he gasped, surprised by the gray face peering up at him from beneath. Without a thought to his actions, the sculptor inserted his fingers into the unusual dirt and started digging.

XXII Yoli – Fight Yoli spat a curse toward the sky even before the stormbird flew overhead. She knew of the birds—they numbered amongst the animals caught behind the veil when the Small Gods erected it—so of course she’d never encountered one. Nor had she seen any of the small gray beings, either. Now she battled alongside dozens, perhaps hundreds, of them. And they fought with a ferocity she found surprising. As the first drops of rain touched her face, washing away dirt already streaked with sweat, she surveyed the battlefield. Father Raven had taken to the sky, swooping down and plucking men from the fight, taking them to a significant elevation and letting them fall—usually screaming—to the ground. The golem stood unmoving in the same spot as when the bird arrived; the sailor crouched in front of it, digging away at its foot. Scattered around the battlefield, she noticed signs of the fallen, their height making them visible above the fray. Most of them appeared to have been engaged by the Small Gods from the Green, which suited her fine. It meant they allowed her warriors to take care of the black priests. Off to her left, she saw Trenan, his sword-work since his recovery demonstrating how he’d earned his title. Beside him, Ishla held her own against the untrained of the priests’ army. They accounted for almost all of her small party from which she’d gotten separated. One more soldier to find… She spotted Osis halfway between where the master swordsman and the queen defended themselves and where the old seaman dug at the clay foot with little success. He stood with his back to her, head tipped skyward, accepting the fat raindrops splattering on his cheeks. Like her, he’d fought hard and likely found the downpour refreshing, if only for a moment. No soldier relished fighting in the rain. A man approached from her right; he didn’t rush her the way most others had, and she wondered if he had more discipline than most of the fighters. She faced him. Blood soaked his shirt from an unseen wound. Pain flickered in his eyes. He brandished the polearm he held awkwardly in both hands, extending it out in front of himself, poking the air as though it was the enemy he sought to vanquish. Nothing about him suggested he possessed either the training or desire to be there. Yoli sighed. “You don’t have to do this.” He responded with another jab in her direction; too much space remained between them for her to even flinch away. “This isn’t your fight. You want to return to your home, yes?” The muscles in the fellow’s arms relaxed, his shoulders sagging so his weapon’s tip drooped toward the ground. His expression went

slack, his eyes distant. “Do you have a wife? Children? Return to them alive. Don’t waste your life here.” He glared at her, head canted to one side. His hands tightened and loosened on the staff of his weapon. Through it, Yoli remained vigilant, waiting. Her gaze darted from him to the surrounding area, watching for other attackers. She listened to what went on behind her, kept her sword at the ready, all the while hoping for this fellow to put down his arms and leave the field of battle. For an instant, she thought he might. Rain ran down her cheeks, along her neck, between her breasts. Without warning, a cloud fell across his face. The ill-prepared man raised his weapon again, features tightening into hatred, eyes narrowed, teeth bared. He leapt forward, polearm extended. “For the evenstar,” he shouted. It took one swipe of Yoli’s sword to knock the weapon from his hands. It clattered against the ground, and again she wondered how so many of these men without fighting experience had kept their lives this long. The fellow glanced to where it lay, then up at Yoli; she placed her foot on the shaft, pinning it to the wet grass lest he try to reach for it. The pain returned to his eyes, frustration coloring his brow. “Go,” she said, pointing with her sword. The man threw himself toward her, onto the tip of her blade. He reached out and grabbed her arm, pulled himself farther onto it, blood bubbling at the corners of his mouth. Surprised, Yoli jumped back, pulling the length of steel out of him. His hands slid along her forearm, then down the weapon, the sharp edge cutting into his fingers. He gripped so tightly, it severed the index finger on his right hand, the digit plunking to the ground beside his weapon. When the sword came free of him, he dropped to his knees, a smile crossing his lips showing stained teeth. She stared at him until he fell forward, face first into the grass. They’re mad. She stared at him an instant longer before spinning away. She shouldn’t have spent so long ignoring everything else going on around her. Luckily, no other adversaries came within striking distance. She found Trenan and Ishla again, then Osis. When she saw the sergeant- at-arms, she froze for a heartbeat. The king’s soldier stood as though made of stone as the black priest approached him, hands extended, evil glowing at his fingertips. “Osis!” She pushed off with her rear foot, boot slipping on the wet grass, slowing her. She’d never make it in time to stop the priest, so cast her

gaze toward her other companions standing closer to the sergeant. “Ishla,” she yelled. The queen pivoted, and Yoli pointed. “Osis!” Ishla’s attention snapped to the king’s soldier and the black priest, and she acted without hesitation. In a smooth movement, she shrugged out of the top of her robe, transferring her sword from one hand to the other and back to pull her arms free, and darted toward Osis and his attacker. Yoli watched as the robed man reached out. The sergeant swiveled away, turning his injured left side to his adversary. The priest’s fingers touched his arm before Ishla arrived. Lightning crackled. Osis screamed. An instant later, the queen’s sword arced down on the black priest’s forearms, knocking his touch aside. The king’s soldier sank to the ground as the robed man faltered, the blood wetting his sleeves invisible against the dark material. Ishla stepped forward but hesitated. Yoli rushed to her side, rain streaming down her face. “Are you all right?” The queen nodded. Two more men emerged from behind the black priest, these clad in armor and brandishing well-kept weapons. They advanced on the women, putting themselves between them and the robed man. Yoli didn’t know how Ishla might fare against a trained opponent, so she chose not to wait for their attack. She lunged at the one nearest to her. He brushed aside her advance and countered. Their steel came together again and again as they feinted and dodged. He offered little opportunity for distraction but, when she found the chance, Yoli’s gaze flickered to the priest, to Osis, to Ishla. The queen’s attacker had driven her back two steps, his quick strikes forcing her into a defensive posture. If she didn’t help, it appeared unlikely Ishla would be able to continue protecting herself. Yoli pushed forward with a vicious attack, pushing her adversary backward a step, then half turned her head to call over her shoulder. “Trenan!” Then the man before her advanced again. His thrusts and jabs usurped her attention, leaving no time to make certain the master swordsman had heard, no opportunity to establish the queen’s safety. *** It felt good for his body to do what it had trained so long to do— swinging a sword in defence of the kingdom. But Trenan’s mind didn’t relish it the same as it used to. He took no joy in spilling blood, gained no pride from ending the lives of these men. He’d never boasted of his triumphs. Despite his innate ability to deal death when needed, he wished another way existed. He heard Yoli’s voice call his name as he put down the latest man to stand before him and turned toward the sound of it. Rainwater ran into his eyes and he wiped it away on his already wet sleeve. He

picked out the woman’s bare back close to the now-frozen clay golem where the sailor crouched by its feet; Osis writhed on the ground near her. Then he saw Ishla. The man facing her was quickly overwhelming her skills. Each of his blows drove her backward, her defence wilting under each attack. Trenan rushed toward them, batting aside farmers stepping in to oppose him, worried only about getting past them and not whether he left them alive or dead. Ishla’s attacker beat her sword down and leaned in, striking her with his shoulder and sending her sprawling to the ground. She hit hard, the impact jarring her weapon from her grip. The enemy loomed over her; she raised her arms defensively as he lifted his blade to strike the killing blow. Trenan gritted his teeth and willed his legs to push harder. He jumped forward, tackling the man around the waist as his weapon began its downward arc. They tumbled to the ground in a tangle, rolling over and over and sending both of their weapons skittering away on the wet grass. Despite being a master swordsman, he suffered a distinct disadvantage at hand-to-hand combat, requiring he rely on surprise. He shifted mid-roll to make sure he ended up on top of the other man, pinning him to the ground with his weight. The fellow peered up at him with a startled expression before Trenan’s fist crashed into his nose. Blood spurted. It occurred to the master swordsman the soldier looked familiar to him; he thought he might have run across him somewhere, a member of the king’s army now fighting for the side of wrong. He raised an arm and wriggled under Trenan, who rained more blows at his head. Some he caught or deflected with his forearm, others contacted nose, eyes, cheekbone. He struggled in vain to get away, but the master swordsman kept punching his face, the shape becoming softer under his anger. Blood squirted up in the air. Any trepidation and remorse he’d experienced before at killing the enemy ran out of him like water out of a bucket with a hole. This no longer represented defending the kingdom, this was Ishla, Danya, Teryk. The soldier’s struggles lessened beneath him; he continued as his knuckles grew sore from the beating. A presence to his right, near his shoulder, stole his attention and he finally stopped, peering at the man’s pulped face before looking up. He expected to find Ishla, perhaps with disappointment on her brow. Instead, he found a man in a black robe. Blood dripped from the ends of his sleeves, coloring the yellow grass red before being washed away by the rain. Trenan watched the drops plummet, knowing he should do everything in his ability to flee, but his body refused to do what it knew it should. He continued

watching as the priest moved toward him, raised his arm. The light at the end of his fingertips dazzling, mesmerizing. The air shifted above Trenan’s head, pushed aside by the blade cutting through. It nicked the black priest’s shoulder, catching enough to send him stumbling. Another presence, to his left this time, and a woman in a robe darkened by the rain, bare from the waist up, rushed past. Ishla lunged at the priest, her lack of training pronounced in how she held the weapon, and the way her feet moved. Not precise and effective, but adequate to make him dodge, and he did so right onto Yoli’s blade. A shriek of pain escaped from under the cowl, and the light at the end of his fingers extinguished. The female warrior pushed the sword further, twisted it, lifted it, pulling the priest up on his toes, before yanking it free. He crumpled to the ground and Yoli separated his head from his shoulders for good measure, sending it rolling out from under the hood and across the grass. The man beneath looked like any other—brown hair, beard, and of similar age to Trenan. Somebody one might have seen anywhere without indication of his genuine nature. Yoli’s gaze met Trenan’s, her eyebrow raised. She didn’t need to say or do any more; the master swordsman nodded to let her know he was unhurt. An instant later, Ishla dropped to her knees beside him, her hands on his shoulders and the same question on her lips. “Are you all right?” Trenan looked from Yoli to her, then his gaze drifted to the man he’d killed with his own hand, his features barely recognizable. Blood oozed from his nose and mouth as fast as the raindrops washed it away. The master swordsman inhaled a slow breath and returned his attention to the queen. Rain plastered her blond hair to her head, her shoulders and chest gleamed with the wet. Her eyes—so blue, so deep—held his, her concern plain and unhidden. He nodded slowly. “I am.” She leaned in, startling him, and pressed her lips hard against his. For an instant, he forgot where they were, her kiss transporting him through the turns of the seasons to those nights she’d visited him as he recovered. The last time their mouths had met. She put her hands on his cheeks, pulled away and looked into his eyes. The concern was gone, replaced by something else he hoped might be forgiveness. “Oy!” The cry came from the sailor, still crouching at the foot of the golem. “Fuck me dead.” Trenan tore his gaze from the woman he loved—and always had—

and turned his attention to Horace Seaman. The old sailor’s head was canted, fingers buried to the third knuckle in the statue’s feet as he looked up at the hulking figure. The master swordsman stood, took three steps toward him before realizing what had caused the exclamation. Rain was washing the clay man away.

XXIII Danya – Chasm The princess looked along the blade, its tip held to a spot directly between herself and the Barren Mother. At its end, the priest— Ine’vesi, the evenstar—stared at them, lips pulled away from his teeth in a grin easily mistaken for a grimace. The expression, the entire situation, reminded her of Teryk and the treacherous knife. Her mind flashed to when her brother snatched the dagger from the weapons merchant and dove toward her, catching her unsuspecting. Was this how the priestess felt now? “Last chance, sister. Rule with me. It’s what we are meant for.” Over his shoulder, Danya spied the other, smaller man on his knees, digging with an unexpected fervor. She wondered why he should do such a thing before her attention crept to the face at the far end of the sword. Her mouth opened, and she spoke along with the Barren Mother. “No, ’Vesi, it is your last chance. Lay aside your blade, offer your life to Goddess and she might forgive you. Perhaps she will allow you to live.” The priest threw back his head and laughed toward the boiling red sky. The sound parted the clouds and a beam of golden light fell upon him, glinting on his sword, shining on his brow. He closed his lips and his eyes, let it touch his cheeks before returning his attention to his sister. One side of his mouth tipped up in a sad smile. “I’m sorry, Rak’bana. I wish it could be different, wish you realized your misplaced faith. But what must be must be.” The hint of a smile disappeared and its sadness clouded his face for a heartbeat. He forced it away and leaned forward, pushing his weapon toward his sister’s throat. Danya and the Barren Mother stepped aside, leaving the space where he’d seen the priestess empty. The sword tip sank into the tree’s smooth bark and a shriek of pain rang out. Thick, dark liquid squeezed out around the steel. The world shifted colors, the sky going black, the earth now red beneath their feet. The princess took another step away, as did her counterpart. Ine’vesi’s gaze flickered between them, surprise shining in his eyes as he saw both of them for the first time. “What trick is this, ’Bana?” He yanked on his sword as he spoke, attempting to free it, but the injured tree refused to relinquish its hold. It shrieked again, and he gave up the effort, releasing his grip and taking a step away. He glanced between the two women, nodding as he did. His eyes settled first on Danya’s companion. “The Barren Mother, I presume,” he said, then looked to the

princess. “And I suppose this makes you the firstborn? Not who I expected.” Me neither, Danya wanted to say, but her mouth remained beyond her control. As he peered toward Ailyssa again, she regarded the other man. Loose earth streaked with many colors littered the ground around him. She caught the anomaly of the colorful soil only briefly because the gray hands gripping the edge of the hole he’d dug garnered her attention. She opened her mouth, more in surprise than out of a desire to speak, then shut it and looked to the priest before he realized the happenings behind him. The sobbing of the tree hid the scrape of fingers in dirt from his ears. Danya took a step away from him, as did Ailyssa. Ine’vesi glanced between them once more, still nodding. The lopsided smile crept onto his lips, but with no sadness this time; instead, it hinted at knowing. “I don’t see your face anymore, sister, but I know you remain with us. A brilliant trick.” The princess blinked, the odd effect of seeing through both her own eyes and those of the Barren Mother causing mild vertigo. They both took another step away from him, drawing them parallel with the tree on either side. She glanced at the sword, wondered if they might use it on him. A wave of laughter tumbled from the evenstar’s mouth and the women each stepped to the side, farther from the tree and the weapon protruding from it. His mirthless amusement waned, and he fixed them with a hard stare. “This deceit won’t save you. These two are each less than half of you, Rak’bana. And I have no hesitation in ending their lives.” A dim glow sparked at the back of his eyes, as though someone had struck a flint. It brightened as if by wind blowing on a hot coal. Ine’vesi raised an arm toward the swirling sky, the red billows streaked with flashes of yellow lightning. Danya and Ailyssa moved another step to the side. The priest stared straight ahead, as if he still saw his sister held in place by the tree’s boughs. The flickering light grew in intensity, his expression pinching into a frown to match; he curled his lifted hand into a fist. “As my twin, you have glorious power. Not so when you are apart, I think.” Fear jolted Danya like a kick to the gut. She turned her gaze away from the priest toward the Barren Mother as her companion did the same. For an instant, she looked upon Ailyssa while simultaneously seeing herself from the other woman’s perspective. The effect spun her head, and she forced her lids shut. Even then, she continued seeing through Ailyssa’s perception, regarding herself standing with her eyes closed, shoulders sagging as though already defeated.

It’s not over yet. The words didn’t belong to her; they formed inside her mind rather than in her ears. She opened her eyes and nodded toward the Barren Mother, who returned the gesture as Ine’vesi spoke again. “Sculptor, the time has come for your final act,” he said without looking over his shoulder. “Separate, they are no match for us.” On the last word, the evenstar dropped to one knee, bringing his arm down and slamming his fist against the ground. The earth jolted under the force, throwing Danya off balance; she stumbled and fell, the impact jarring her spine and bending her hand back. Her wrist popped, and she bit her lip to keep from crying out. A crack snaked out in front of and behind Ine’vesi. The fissure ran past the tree he’d used to hold Rak’bana captive; it screamed again as it tipped, tumbling backward into the widening chasm and disappearing. The crack expanded, pushing her and Ailyssa farther apart. The priest raised his chin and laughed. *** Though he knew the evenstar spoke to him, Vesisdenperos ignored his words as he continued scooping dirt from around the gray creature he’d found trapped in the ground. Colored soil clogged the space under his nails and the swirls and loops at the ends of his fingers, the same as clay did when he practiced creating the vessel for the priest’s return. The way it packed tight between nail and fingertip flooded his mind with memories, reminded him of Kuneprius’ life lost, made him think of his own gone unlived. The gray creature looked up at him with dark and pleading eyes; it scrabbled at the edge of the modest hole, trying to pull itself free. The earth shook and a clap of thunder assaulted his ears. A crack in the ground shot out from where Ine’vesi crouched on one knee. It hit the spot where he was digging; he jumped aside as it passed, and he reached out to grab the little one’s hand as he did. He gripped it by the fingers, but its weight increased as the dirt fell away, opening a gaping chasm beneath its previously buried feet. The slender gray digits slipped from his grip. His heart sped. He leapt forward to the edge, reaching out with his free hand and grasping the creature by the other wrist, holding on despite the ache in his shoulders from digging. He peered down at the thing, its life literally in his grasp, without knowing what it was. Likely the evenstar wanted him to let it plunge to its death. Too many have already died because of me. Kuneprius’ face flashed into his mind again, his mouth drawn up in the same smile he wore every time Vesisdenperos arrived home from his toil in the cave. Always happy to see him, always proud of him. Now dead.

He pressed himself hard against the ground, snaked away from the fissure, pulling the gray creature along with him. It scrabbled its way up onto the edge, rolled away from the gaping hole. The two of them lay flat on their bellies, looking at each other, when the priest spoke again. “Come, sculptor. It is an honor I offer you to help me vanquish the firstborn and the Barren Mother, and with them my sister and their hope. With your aid, because of you, the Small Gods return from their banishment in the sky and take their rightful places as the rulers of the kingdom.” Small Gods. The gray creature stood and brushed dirt from its—her—front. Now, standing before him, he realized her to be the same creature he and Kuneprius had captured and taken to Teva Stavoklis. Thorn, he recalled his friend calling him. Though it had been what Kristeus sent them to do, the man responsible for raising him had appeared unhappy from the start. She nodded to him, then turned her attention to Ine’vesi. Her small hands curled into tiny fists, her forehead creased. Vesisdenperos rolled over and gazed up at the evenstar, the embodiment of everything he’d wrongly worshiped for so long. He stood with one foot on either side of the crack in the earth—narrow beneath him but widening both directions as it ran away—his back to them as he faced the women. “Sculptor?” The priest pivoted, turning to find out why his subject hadn’t responded, and the Small God of the Green leapt forward. Vesisdenperos’ eyes widened and his jaw dropped as the creature bounded toward the evenstar without showing a sliver of fear. She caught the much larger man by surprise as she hurtled into him, shoulder impacting him in the stomach, driving air from him with a whoosh. He stumbled back, one foot slipping on the edge of the crack in the earth; his arms pinwheeled, and he kept his balance. In the time it took him to do so, his attacker was at him again. She climbed him as though his body was a tree, her slender fingers digging in anywhere they found bare flesh and leaving behind red welts. He grabbed her arm, pulled hard to wrench her off him, but her grip held. The sculptor scrambled away, pushing his heels into the ground to propel him, worried they might tumble into him and send him falling into the chasm in the earth. Beyond the two Small Gods wrestling, the women waited. One crouched, arm cradled against her body, while the other stood—the first time Vesisdenperos had seen them not moving in unison. The instant he thought it, the younger woman rose, and they both moved aside from the crack.

Ine’vesi forced his arm between himself and the small gray creature, used it to lever her off him. She dropped to the ground, nimbly avoided a savage kick he directed toward her head. Vesisdenperos pressed his lips together and held his breath; if the evenstar got her in his grip, she’d meet her end. But what she lacked in size and strength compared to he who’d been banished to the sky, she made up for with speed and craftiness. She darted one direction, prompting him to go after her, then jumped the other way, across the fissure to the side with the older woman, leaving him grasping at empty air. “You’re not supposed to be here, little thing,” he said with a chuckle free of mirth and full of menace. “We already sacrificed a Small God. Perhaps you knew him?” Her gaze held his, her expression remaining unchanged as she ignored his baiting. He stepped over the crack in the ground and she jumped away, leaping to her right, where the split widened. “But you are likely all related, aren’t you? Inbred vermin hiding behind your magical veil. Don’t think I wasn’t watching your kind, too.” The sculptor noted the muscles in her back flex and tighten. “Thorn is Ivy’s brother.” This time, the evenstar’s laughter rolled across the strange landscape like the peal of a tolling bell. The sound of it sent a shiver cascading down the sculptor’s spine. “Brother. Father. Uncle. I’m surprised you can keep your kin straight with one another.” Ine’vesi jumped the divide and Ivy leapt away again, farther along the chasm, past where the tree had toppled into the earth and disappeared. It shocked Vesisdenperos how far her short legs propelled her with a single bound. The evenstar walked toward her with slow, purposeful steps. “Come now, we both know how this will finish. You are no match for me. I could snap my fingers and end you.” The two women worked themselves down the crack, both of them a few paces from the edge with no chance they might fall in. Ivy stood her ground, as though she waited for him to reach her, and shook her head. “Your tricks mean nothing to Ivy,” she said. “No, I suppose they don’t,” he conceded and looked skyward. “Smart of you to send all women, Rak’bana. Except for the treacherous sculptor.” Vesisdenperos froze at the mention of his name, expecting Ine’vesi to turn around and lurch toward him, to punish him for his betrayal by beating him, tossing him into the yawning abyss.
