Maybe it’s what I deserve. But the evenstar didn’t remove his attention from the small gray figure standing before him. He stopped moving, and crouched ever so slightly, coiling in readiness. “Watch out,” Vesisdenperos shouted as he leapt toward Ivy. The Small God of the Green needed no warning. She jumped at the same instant as Ine’vesi, sailing across the wide fissure as if blown by a powerful wind. She landed with her toes on the far edge and spun to face her attacker, standing right on the lip. The older woman on her side moved to stand behind her, four strides farther. The younger of the two did the same on the other side, positioning herself a similar number of paces behind the priest. If he knew of her presence, he did not care. The evenstar pivoted his head on his neck, his gaze finding the sculptor. Dark eyes pierced him and he the urge to crawl away from the formidable man’s attention nearly overtook him. He lacked the strength to do so, for what little good it might have done. “Enough from you, traitor,” Ine’vesi grated. “Perhaps I should have killed you and left your friend to live. Alas, it wasn’t a choice…until now.” He raised his arm, an open, grasping hand directed at Vesisdenperos. The sculptor sensed a pull and dug his heels into the ground, but the strength of it proved too great. He began moving across the colorful earth, clawing and scraping as the evenstar’s power drew him forward. Ivy seized the moment, coiled, and jumped at the priest. He was ready for her; his free hand shot out, catching her by the neck, the distraction mercifully halting the sculptor’s journey toward death. Ine’vesi turned his gaze to the Small God dangling in his grip. “You thought to fool me? I’m disappointed.” She clung to his wrist with both of her small hands, using the leverage to keep him from crushing her throat. A sad and knowing smile crept over the unusual being’s face. Five heartbeats sped by and the evenstar’s expression changed, a question creasing his brow, a tinge of confusion coloring his features. “For the Small Gods to live,” Ivy said, voice choked by his grip but understandable. “A Small God must die.” Ine’vesi’s bewilderment transformed to surprise in the instant before the two women rushed forward. The younger one struck him in the back, sending the evenstar—Ivy in his grasp—tumbling into the fissure. He reached out with his free hand as they fell, releasing his invisible hold on Vesisdenperos, but the Small God grabbed him. His fingertips scraped colorful lines into the dirt, but found no purchase. Ivy’s gaze met the sculptor’s for half a breath, then they disappeared.

The younger woman’s momentum propelled her, and she jumped, trying to reach the far edge, but came up short. At the same time, the other woman fell flat to the ground, reached out for her friend, caught her by the hand. The princess slammed against the side, the force and her sudden weight pulling the Barren Mother forward until her stomach pressed against the lip, but they went no farther. Vesisdenperos found his strength and jumped to his feet, rushed to the lip of the crevice across from the women. He stepped to the brink with care and peered down, half expecting to find the evenstar clinging to the edge or lying on an outcropping, hatred and death shining in his eyes. But he wasn’t. He was gone, and Ivy along with him. The Barren Mother grunted, jarring his attention to them and their precarious position. The world rumbled beneath his feet and the space between him and them widened. “Hold on,” he said, then rushed along the crack to where it wasn’t as wide. The shaking earth threw him off balance and he fell to his knees as he reached the part. The edges on either side broke off and tumbled into the opening, the distance between the sides growing. He scrambled to his feet, took an instant to notice the way the red sky ran toward the ground like paint thrown against a wall, and how the trees wilted, their branches sagging, colored bark turning gray and sloughing off the trunks. More of the edge dropped away, forcing him to take a step. He looked to the women, hoping to find them where he’d left them. They were, a glow starting where they clasped hands. An instant later, the princess disappeared, her white dress fluttering into the darkness below, and the sculptor’s heart leapt into his throat. He glanced at the widening fissure, then to the Barren Mother. He found something far different from what he expected. Instead of the Barren Mother lying flat on the ground, perhaps mourning her failure at saving the other woman, a warrior dressed in gold plate stood at the edge of the precipice. Vesisdenperos tensed. The priestess, Rak’bana. This is what the evenstar saw. An imposing figure, but not threatening. He relaxed, a relieved smile creeping across his lips. She dipped her head toward him, the feather on her helmet bobbing. “Thank you, sculptor. But you are his heart.” He opened his mouth to respond, to tell her what her brother had done to her friend, to ask if the world would be all right now. No words emerged as the earth beneath his feet slipped away. Vesisdenperos inhaled a surprised breath, waved his arms to keep his balance, then tumbled into the opening. He twisted in the air,

watching the melting red sky as he plummeted into darkness. The fissure above him narrowed as he fell. Whether it appeared so due to distance or because it closed up, he didn’t know, but calmness filled him as he awaited the sudden end of the fall, of his life. Perhaps he’d meet Kuneprius again.

XXIV Horace – Meltin’ Water streamed down Horace’s cheeks, coolin’ and washin’ away the sweat what’d been makin’ his forehead damp and stickin’ his hair to his head. He brushed his hand across his face to move stray strands outta his eyes, knowin’ he smeared gray mud on his skin as he did. The rain’d wash it off quick enough, too. He inhaled a shudderin’ breath between his lips, hatin’ the earthy grit on his tongue more’n he ever despised the sea’s briny flavor. He rolled saliva around the inside o’ his mouth, spat on the ground, though he knew he couldn’t escape it. The muddy taste lay all over him, all around him. The ol’ sailor leaned forward, aware o’ the fight goin’ on behind him. He could only hope no one killed him; he needed to rescue a small, gray woman, and he’d do so if it meant his life. He reached out to the clay foot what’d restored itself yet again and dug his fingers in at the ankle, scraping down the front toward the toes like he’d done more times’n he cared to count. His effort left deep furrows, same as before, and dirt forced its way under his fingernails. By the time he got to the foot’s end, they’d already filled themselves in, leavin’ the leg as unscathed as when he began. Horace bit hard on his back teeth, mashed his lips together into a thin, bloodless line. An empty feelin’ o’ uselessness leeched itself through his bones, same as when he’d watched this thing carry Thorn away, and while holdin’ his son when he took his last breath. Not an emotion he enjoyed, nor one he ever wanted to experience again. Frustrated, he swung his open hand at the clay monster’s knee. It hit with a wet slap, stingin’ his skin; his fingers passed right through, knockin’ a chunk out o’ the leg what flew a pace or two through the air and plopped on the ground. He watched, waitin’ for the fresh wound to close up, healin’ itself the way it did ev’ry other time before, only it didn’t. Horace narrowed his eyes and looked closer, examinin’ the hole he’d left. Before, they’d kinda puckered and filled, like sets o’ lips closin’. Not so now. Rivulets o’ rain water ran down the front o’ the leg, reachin’ the space his slap’d made and drippin’ from the top. Bits o’ mud started dripping along with them, the upper edge beginnin’ to collapse instead o’ healin’ up from the sides like the other times. Horace shook his head, droplets flyin’ from his beard, then tilted his chin up to look at the thing towerin’ o’er him. Its shoulder didn’t appear so broad, its chest not as thick. Raindrops struck it and left dimples behind, water and clay alike runnin’ down ev’ry exposed bit o’ the thing’s surface. The ol’ sailor reached up, wiped his hand down one sculpted thigh, and came away with a palm full o’ muck. Again, the divot remained,

except for where the downpour washed more into it from higher on the golem’s body. It’s melting. “Oy,” he called out, unsure if anyone who he’d want to hear stood close enough to do so. Then he exclaimed to himself: “Fuck me dead.” He rose, stoopin’ because his back and knees hurt so bad from kneelin’ in front o’ the thing for so long, and shuffled away a step or two. He kept his eyes on it, expectin’ it to lurch forward and grab him at least as much as he expected to get skewered on a sword or pitchfork. The sounds o’ fightin’ swirled around him, and he knew he should be careful, but he couldn’t make himself shift his gaze from the monstrosity. What’d passed for ears, a nose, and holes for eyes now sagged, smearin’ and dissolvin’ into the rest. Instead o’ drippin’, streams o’ watery clay runnin’ from its chin and hands splashed on the ground at its feet. The one foot the ol’ sailor’d been diggin’ at so diligently finally began shrinkin’; his fingers couldn’t make a difference, but a thing as simple as rain’d prove the creature’s undoin’. Not just the rain, though. Somethin’ else changed. He stumbled three more steps and sensed people beside him, pulled his gaze away from the meltin’ statue. Trenan stood to one side o’ him, the queen and Yoli on the other, supportin’ the sergeant-at-arms between them; the twist to the man’s face made Horace think he experienced more pain than anyone might comprehend. “It’s melting,” the master swordsman said. “We have to end it now, while we can.” He brandished his sword and took a step forward, but the ol’ sailor halted him with a hand on his arm. “No. Ivy’s inside.” “And Danya,” Ishla added in a breathless tone. Tired or not believin’ her own words, Horace didn’t know. And Ailyssa, maybe. So they watched, waited. The fight continued around them, but nobody came close or threatened them, as though no one else wanted to be anywhere near the golem. It explained why Horace’d spent so long diggin’ to find his friend without bein’ poked with a sword nor bashed in the head. Would’ve been easy if they gave it a go, but none did. Luck, fear, someone watchin’ o’er him? Didn’t matter. The sculpture what’d started out muscled ridges and powerful limbs were becomin’ more akin to a pile o’ mud. The shoulders sagged; as Horace watched, a finger fell off and splashed in a shallow puddle o’ clay-colored water. The whole thing sank the width o’ his hand as the ankles folded up on themselves. The ol’ sailor held his breath, suspected those around him did the same.

A moment later, the heap in front o’ them weren’t no longer recognizable as havin’ been man-shaped and towerin’ o’er ev’ryone on the battlefield. The legs’d fused together as its torso sank toward the ground. Its arms melded into its side as the statuesque fella began more resemblin’ a cone than anythin’ else. Mud pooled in a widenin’ puddle at the bottom, runnin’ away into the yellow, beaten-down grass as rain diluted it. After a short time, it became plain the vanishin’ thing left somethin’ behind in the golem’s place. It stood straight up in the middle o’ the meltin’ beast, like a column built in its center to keep it upright and true. Horace rubbed his hands together unconsciously, using the rainwater to wash clay from himself. It came off in wet little balls, which he rolled around between his palms without thinkin’ about doin’ it. The pillar-like thing got down to a bit lower than the same level as the ol’ sailor, then stopped shrinkin’. The mud around it continued sloughin’ off, and it didn’t take long before it became narrow at the top, grew wider a little farther down, then stayed a uniform width the rest o’ the way to the ground. Horace blinked water outta his eyes. A head and shoulders? He took two careful steps toward it, leavin’ the others where they stood. Rivulets ran down what remained o’ the fearsome golem on all sides, makin’ it take shape and convincin’ him he saw what he thought he did. Another step forward and he came close enough to reach out and touch it, though, not knowin’ who or what might hide beneath the last bit o’ mud, he didn’t. A spot in the top, narrower portion shifted, moved. Two eyes fluttered open under the weight o’ the clay remainin’ on them and looked at the ol’ sailor. He inhaled a sharp breath between his lips, suckin’ rainwater and the ends o’ whiskers what’d gotten too long into his mouth along with the air. He thought he recognized them peepers. Horace scrubbed his palms on his trousers, doin’ his best to remove the last few clay balls before he raised his right hand and wiped it carefully across what he expected to be a cheek beneath the dirt. Whoever hid inside watched him with a noticeable mix o’ emotional pain and relief. His first two tries succeeded in smearin’ the mud. He rubbed his palms again and gave it a third go around. This time, a swipe from his thumb exposed pink flesh. The person blinked and the clay farther down on the hidden face moved, the lips beneath curlin’ into a smile, or tryin’ to speak. The golem’s remnants left them gummed up, so he didn’t know which. Another stroke o’ his hands on the front o’ his thighs and more rubbin’ at the cheeks revealed faint wrinkles clogged with gray at the corners o’ the eyes. “Ailyssa?”

She nodded ever so slightly, confirmin’ his thought. He smiled and let out a laugh what most might’ve misconstrued as a sob. The clay on her right side flexed and moved, and a finger poked through. Horace saw it, grabbed it with one hand, forced his fingers underneath it. The golem didn’t want to give it up easily, but together they worked at it until she separated the arm from bein’ stuck to her body. He did his best to clean dirt from her palm before she raised it to her face to rub mud from her cheeks, her forehead, her lips. “Horace,” she whispered when her mouth got mostly free o’ it. He guessed she must’ve tasted the fowl stuff, but gave no sign. The ol’ sailor fought against the urge to throw his arms around her, welcomin’ her back to the world. It weren’t the muck coverin’ her what stopped him, or his feelin’s about embracin’ her; they’d both be better usin’ their energy for gettin’ her outta the muddy cocoon entrappin’ so much o’ her. As he gave her aid, he couldn’t help but wonder why none o’ the others came forward to lend a hand. He paused in his helpin’ and looked o’er his shoulder. They remained where he’d left them, starin’, but it weren’t their inaction what caught his attention. Beyond them, ev’ryone on the battlefield did the same nothin’. Not a single man or woman—king’s soldier, warrior for the Goddess, black priest, nor anyone else—swung a sword or fought. Ev’ry one o’ them stood stone-like, as though the revealin’ o’ the Barren Mother hidin’ inside the golem’d turned them into statues. Maybe it did. He thought on sayin’ somethin’, then changed his mind and returned his attention to Ailyssa. He got her other arm free and, with the rain’s assistance, the clay came off more easily. Horace could see most o’ her face, though muck clogged up her hair and clung to her body in chunks. When he went to help her remove what remained, she raised her hand, stoppin’ him. He respected her wishes, allowin’ his arms to dangle at his sides while their gazes came together and they looked into each other’s eyes for the space o’ ten heartbeats. The battlefield lay strangely quiet around them, no more’n the crackle and hiss o’ the odd fire soundin’. The ol’ sailor finally broke the silence. “Ivy?” The Barren Mother’s expression turned sad. Horace needed no more response, but she shook her head, anyway, and said, “I’m sorry.” The pain o’ loss what’d been showin’ up in Horace’s life more’n more blossomed in his chest, expanded to clog his throat. His chin sagged and Ailyssa took a step, passin’ him and restin’ her hand on his shoulder as she did. He appreciated the gesture, but it did nothin’ to take away the grief spreadin’ through him at losin’ another friend. One more person he’d cared for gone.

One more life lost. She moved past, takin’ her touch from him, and he sighed, the stink o’ clay strong in his nose. A scent he hoped to never have to stomach again. *** As soon as the woman took her hand from Horace’s shoulder, the trance gripping Ishla released its hold, as it appeared to do with everyone else, too. She heard them shift and shuffle, but Yoli was the first to move. She took two steps forward, then sank to one knee, bowing her head. “Mother of Death,” she said. The words sent a shiver coursing up the queen’s spine and goose bumps along her arms and across the top of her chest. It wasn’t so long ago she’d visited the Mother of Death in her temple near Fishtown, a visit which set her upon this path leading to her standing on the battlefield outside Ikkundana. Put me on the road to committing regicide. But this meant the Matron she’d known must have passed over to the dead lands, Goddess’ will fulfilled. The new Mother of Death stopped in front of the genuflected warrior, rested her hand atop her head, then her eyes found the queen’s. Ishla hadn’t met the Barren Mother, but realized this was her, a woman who looked to have seen the seasons turn perhaps fifty times, her close-cropped, graying hair growing out. Though her facial features differed from the Mother of Death the queen had so recently visited, she wore the same expression—understanding, intelligence, compassion. She took her touch from Yoli and strode past, approaching Ishla. “Mother,” she said, lowering her head and preparing to drop to one knee, but the woman caught her by the arm, stopping her. “Ailyssa,” she corrected. “Many seasons lay ahead for people to use my new title. This last time, please let me be Ailyssa.” The queen straightened, nodded. Her sword dangled in her grip, the tip hovering, nearly brushing the ground. Her other hand flexed into a fist and released, flexed and released as she fought against the emotion welling up inside her. She sensed Trenan beside her, watching, but was glad he didn’t speak or offer any attempt at comfort, for none could suffice. Without prompting, he stepped away from the two women, leaving them to as much privacy as might be afforded on a field of battle. “You are wondering about Danya,” Ailyssa said, her tone quiet, filled with understanding. Ishla nodded, unable to do more. The newly proclaimed Mother of Death closed her eyes. She drew a breath in through her lips, then

released it as the queen waited to hear of the princess’ fate, impatience growing in her chest. When Ailyssa’s lids fluttered open again, her brown irises had turned blue and, though the rest of her face remained unchanged, the queen realized the Barren Mother no longer gazed at her. “It’s okay, mother.” The voice wasn’t her daughter’s, but it didn’t matter. “Danya.” The single word came out choked by the threat of tears. “Shh.” The Mother of Death reached out to take the queen’s hands. Ishla released her grip on the sword, letting it fall to the ground, the heavy hilt splashing in an unseen puddle. “I will always be here. Always close.” Ishla stifled a sob, felt wetness on her cheeks and told herself it was just the rain. She opened her mouth to speak, then closed it for fear of nothing emerging except the suppressed lament hidden in her chest. Her hands rested in Ailyssa’s, palms facing down as her daughter in the guise of the Mother of Death stroked them with her thumbs, waiting. Ishla swallowed hard and tried again. “I am so very proud of you,” she said finally, voice squeaking. She sighed a shuddering breath, collecting herself. “You sacrificed yourself for everyone.” The mouth on Ailyssa’s face smiled and, though the lips were someone else’s, the expression belonged to Danya without a doubt. “Not just me. So many did so much, gave so much. Some lost their lives while I am still here.” She paused, considering her words. “Of a fashion.” “But I won’t ever see you again.” The smile faltered but remained. “Not in the manner you were used to, but I am here. I promise.” Ishla attempted to match her daughter’s smile on the Barren Mother’s face, but her lips resisted and she gave up. Ailyssa squeezed her hands, offering comfort. “You must look out for Teryk,” she said. “Assure him he is not to blame. He was a tool for us to reach this end. It’s not his fault. Tell him I love him and I believe he will make a fine king.” Her words pushed Ishla’s control over the edge; pain pinched her features, and a sob escaped her throat. The Mother of Death released the queen’s hands and took the last step toward her; the queen melted into her embrace, face pressed against her shoulder as she wept. A warmth radiated from the woman, an energy flowing from her and into Ishla, its presence calming her, bringing her relief and understanding. Ailyssa shifted, put her palms on either side of her head and touched her lips against her forehead.

“And I love you, too, mother.” She leaned back, still holding on, their gazes coming together once more. Danya’s blue eyes sparkled in the Barren Mother’s face as rain ran from her temples and along her cheeks. The woman closed her lids, inhaled through her mouth, held her breath for four heartbeats before releasing it. She opened them again, revealing brown irises now, as Ishla knew they would be. Her lips curved up in the smile meant to be there, not the one belonging to the princess. “You are a brave and mighty woman, Ishla of the Windward Kingdom. Come to me and visit your daughter whenever you please.” She nodded and the Mother of Death took her hands away, as well as her gaze, and stepped past her. Yoli hurried to follow, touching Ishla’s shoulder on the way by in a gesture of support. The queen offered a wan smile in thanks. And then she stood alone, rain pelting her cheeks and torso, rivulets running along the sides of her face, between her breasts. She stared ahead at the pile of mud, each raindrop diminishing it further as it returned to the earth whence it came. She shivered, crossed her arms in front of her bare chest and hugged herself. An arm encircled her shoulders, and she looked up into Trenan’s eyes. He wore an odd expression, a combination of his obvious effort to comfort her and the unease he must have experienced at how she might accept his gesture. She slipped her arms around his waist, settled her cheek against his chest. In the middle of the battlefield, they indulged an action they hadn’t considered before—admitted their love.

XXV Trenan – Mercy Ailyssa strode across the field of battle, Yoli trailing behind her. The knot of fighters parted before her. Most of the king’s soldiers wore expressions like they didn’t understand why they should do so, but did it anyway. The men who’d fought for the evenstar abandoned their weapons and backed away. Goddess warriors bowed or dropped to one knee, understanding who walked before them. The Mother of Death. Ailyssa paid little attention to any of them, for more work for her yet remained. She scanned above the heads of the fighters, and found the first of what she looked for ten paces to her right. She amended her path to take her to the tall, naked man. “Mother?” Yoli said from behind her. Ailyssa raised her hand, silencing the Goddess warrior’s question, and increased her pace until she halted before the Small God fallen from the sky. This fellow must have been one of the last to fall; his pale flesh bore no wounds, and he remained a few steps from the scarred earth where he’d come to rest. He stared at her as she approached, at first frowning and angry, but his expression soon melted into confusion, concern. She stopped two paces away from him, not close enough for either of them to touch the other, but reach out she did. She raised her arm, palm turned out toward the man whom Goddess had banished to the sky with his brethren a hundred hundred turns of the seasons past. His eyes fell to her hand, curious, until his lids widened and his jaw dropped open. He inhaled a sharp breath, sucking rain into his mouth along with it. His cheeks sank into his face, his shoulders sagged. The entirety of his being shrank until the husk of him folded up on itself and crumpled to the ground. Ailyssa stared at him, sensing his essence inside her, the seed of him already changing, growing in her belly. It filled her with unexplainable energy which she neither loved nor loathed; it simply was. And this was her life now. Hers and Danya’s. She faced Yoli, who watched her with a mixture of surprise and wonder. When the warrior noticed her looking at her, she took a knee. “The black priests,” the Mother of Death said. Her voice sounded odd to Ailyssa, but she supposed she’d get used to the change. “Take your warriors. They are no longer a danger, but we cannot let them leave.” “Yes, Mother,” Yoli said. She rose, bowed her head, and headed off to collect her soldiers. Ailyssa watched her go, admiring the way the woman carried herself

and knowing she’d make a fine general. The Mother of Death swung her gaze over the battlefield, above the heads of warriors and farmers and priests, until she found the next of the fallen. She set out toward him to take his soul as her own. *** He’d have held her forever. So long he’d imagined it after watching her with Erral. He’d always hated the way the king treated her. How many sleepless nights had Trenan laid awake thinking of her, wondering what it would be like for them to be together, then spending his sleep dreaming of it? Here they found themselves, finally embraced, in the middle of a battlefield. It seemed all too appropriate. He held her an instant longer, then leaned away, putting some separation between them, and looked into her eyes. The rain continued falling, sticking strands of hair to her forehead; he released her and brushed them away as he wondered how much fault for the wetness on her cheeks belonged to the stormbird, and how much to tears. “I’m sorry about Danya,” he said, his voice quiet to keep the words between the two of them. She stared into his eyes for the space of four heartbeats and then nodded once. “I understand it needed to be. The firstborn child of the rightful king. She lives on with the Mother of Death.” He opened his mouth to say more, but realized he didn’t know what, so closed it. Would he have offered more condolence? Tried to make sense of it? It seemed she’d done so on her own; his words would have been for himself, not her. Surely Danya didn’t have to die, not by her brother’s hand, at least. But what Trenan thought of the way things had played out meant nothing; Ishla was all that mattered. He looked away from her, surveying the battlefield. Yoli and the Mother of Death had left on their own missions; the sailor crouched where the golem had been, now little more than a mud puddle remaining of the fearful beast; Osis waited between them and him, respectfully distant but in obvious pain. Around them, the battle had ceased. Those who’d taken up arms to fight on the side of the creature were abandoning their weapons and retreating. Some of the king’s men stood by, watching, others pursued them with killing on their minds. Seeing it pulled Trenan from his thoughts. “I have to stop this.” He gestured toward a knight cutting down an unarmed, unarmored man, then faced Ishla. “Can you take care of Osis and the sailor?” “Yes,” she said with a nod. “Go.” He took half a step away, then tuned to her. She looked up at him

expectantly, and he saw her as the most beautiful woman he’d ever set his eyes upon, though he’d harbored no doubt of that. He moved close, brought his lips beside her ear. “The king died in battle, as far as anyone knows.” He leaned away and peered into her eyes. “Only we know different. Do you understand?” She nodded. “And Dansil?” “We’ll worry about him when he shows up.” He glanced over his shoulder toward Osis and Horace. “Take care of our heroes. I’ll return soon.” She rose on her toes and pressed her lips against his. Energy swept through him at the touch of her kiss he thought would be nothing more than a memory until the day he met his end. He let it linger as long as she allowed, then smiled at her when she drew away. He stepped back, pulled her robe up to her shoulders to give her a measure of protection from the chill rain, then jogged off, sword out before him. The master swordsman made his way across the field of battle, searching for any other generals, commanders, soldiers of rank. “Show the farmers mercy,” he said to any king’s man he met. “They were not here of their own accord. Let them return to their lives, their families. Capture the warriors who fought against us. They will pay their due. Kill no one.” More than one soldier looked at him with confusion; to them, Trenan reiterated his order. “Give mercy wherever you can.” He found sergeants, captains, lieutenants, generals. To each he spoke the same, directing them to pass his orders on to every remaining man of the army. Some asked after the king; he relayed how one of the fallen had slain the regent as he protected his queen. The lie depicting Erral as brave and honorable left a sour taste in the master swordsman’s mouth, but he needed to tell it; the king’s noble death would ensure the proper secession to the throne. After a while, Trenan reached the far side of the battlefield. The rain had ceased, and he paused on the verge where plains met forest, water dripping from boughs. He stared into the trees, wondering how many men from both sides might have fled, looking for relief and safety in the woods. Once, he’d have plunged in after them, determined to put an end to any thought of rebellion and the lives of any cowardly enough to desert. Not today. Life was more precious today, and every day from now on. He was about to turn around and return to the battle field to follow up his orders and find his way to the queen when a movement caught

his attention. A branch shivered, disturbed by something more than the wind. Cautious, Trenan stepped into the forest, sword held out before him. He strode by a broad shrub, its wide leaves weighed down by rainwater, and past a thick tree trunk. With the odor of wet cedar sharp in his nose, he found the source of the noise. The man stood looking at the master swordsman, the deep red mark marring his face, his split skull glistening with blood and rain. Trenan easily saw the trees and shrubs behind him through his translucent torso. The other men with him were the same, with their severed limbs, their empty abdomens, their bloody faces. They stared at Trenan, the same way they had every step of his journey from the Green to Ikkundana, but their regard lacked the accusation it held before, as his reaction lacked the guilt. One by one, each of the dead turned and walked away, fading to nothing as they strode into the forest, until one remained. The first man ever to find his end by Trenan’s hand. They peered at each other for a time, the space around them silent but for the drip-drop of water rolling off leaves, splashing on the ground. Trenan lowered his sword, slid it into its scabbard with the quiet shish of steel on hard leather. Another moment passed, then the ghostly man nodded, turned, and faded away into the greenery of the woods. The swordmaster stayed for a while, remembering them all. He’d never assume they found mercy in the dead lands, or that he’d earn forgiveness for what he’d done, but he realized their memories would never leave him. He swore to never let them. With a sigh filled with the scents of loamy earth, damp wood, and the essence of life, Trenan tuned and left the woodland, headed back to find his love.

XXVI Dansil – Ends Sweat streamed down the former queen’s guard’s face as he crouched, spine pressed uncomfortably against the plain gray wall. In front of him, many of the canvas tents continued burning; tongues of flame licked toward the sky until the strange bird flew overhead. Each flap of its wings belched out plumes of vapor, leaving clouds pregnant with rain in its wake. And then the downpour began. Fat drops hissed and sizzled as they spattered on the fire, more smoke and steam rising into the air. Dansil turned his face skyward, imagined the raindrops evaporating as they splashed on his own forehead and cheeks. The burning tents had provided excellent cover for him, hiding him from Trenan and the others, from the fight. Out of sight, out of mind. With the rainfall, his asylum would soon disappear; he needed to find another solution to the problem before him. And with Erral dead, he’d be at the mercy of the queen and—worse—the swordmaster. In his estimation, he possessed two choices: flee, or convince people of what he’d seen. If they knew Ishla had slain the king to save the man she loved, the father of the so-called prince, their lies would go up in flame, same as the tents. Then he’d have his revenge on the one-armed traitor. Trenan would get what he deserved. And imagine my reward. He cocked his head to the right, where a line of women passed buckets of water along, fighting the tent fire. To this point, he’d ignored them as much as they’d paid him no mind. He hadn’t wanted to draw any unnecessary attention, and they’d been too busy with the blaze to care about him as long as he posed no threat. Now they mattered to him, at least. Them water buckets must come from within. Getting into the fortress was the key. Inside he’d find someone to tell of what happened, convince them Trenan and his whore queen were the enemies of the kingdom. He shivered at the thought of returning behind the walls of Ikkundana, but told himself chilly rainwater dribbling down his neck had caused the shudder. He set his jaw, swallowed a mouthful of saliva, and got to creeping along the wall toward the women, keeping low to attract as little attention as possible. It didn’t take long for him to realize he needed to use extra care. Anyone who might have been close before—other than those fighting the fire—had left, off to join the battle, most likely. With the rain blurring his view of the distance, he presumed the fight raged somewhere beyond his vision. He paused, wiped water from his face,

and listened. No noise over the hiss and pop of raindrops falling on flames. He straightened, walked at a quicker pace toward the women. The first gave him but a fleeting glimpse of attention as he went by; the next few didn’t so much as glance at him as they handed full buckets one direction, then passed empty ones the other way. Part of him knew to feel relief at their lack of notice, yet his lip curled at what his mind considered a slight. Who were they to ignore him? He fixed his gaze straight ahead, to the front of their line where it curved closer to the fortress wall. He walked with determination, hoping doing so might convince them he wasn’t out of place. Not one woman said a word or made a move to stop him. As he neared the end of the row, he saw the opening in the wall through which they passed the pails. He set a stern expression on his face, let his hand rest on the hilt of the dagger at his belt. Fighting his way in didn’t appear the best option, but he was ready should the need arise. “Ho,” he called out as he approached the woman closest to the portal. She paused and looked up at him, an empty bucket dangling from her fingers. “I am a man of the king and I must get into the fortress.” He curled his grip around the dagger’s hilt, expecting her to question him at the very least, maybe try to stop him. She did neither, simply nodded and stepped aside, giving him space to pass. Dansil hesitated before entering, searching her face for any sign of treachery. He found none, so crossed the threshold. Inside, the line of women stretched to the left. He peeked that direction and saw a fountain flowing from the wall at the end of the lane—the place they filled buckets to fight the fire. The last few between the doorway and the stream—six of them—watched as he entered. He stopped to look at them, then continued straight. Better to get past them in case they changed their minds than to linger. Tall walls rose on either side of the narrow lane ahead of him, the height of the buildings giving him little cover from the rain. Sporadic windows looked down from overhead, but the walls lacked doorways. The road stretched on for thirty paces before he came to a crossroads. He stopped at the intersection. The small street he walked continued on while the wider avenue crossing it ran straight in both directions. Dansil scanned right, then left, noticed the more frequent occurrence of windows and doorways, and decided one of these two to be better than continuing his current path. But which one? He rubbed his chin. Finding his way to the wide boulevard down which he’d seen Trenan and the female warriors ride seemed the best

choice. He chuckled to himself, amused by the thought of putting the words ‘female’ and ‘warriors’ together, but quickly dismissed the diversion. Which path? The rain pattering against his cheeks increased in the widened intersection as he hesitated, considering his options. Water dripped from the end of his nose and he wiped it away with a finger, looked both directions and shrugged. One is as good as the other when you don’t know. He swirled his tongue around in his mouth, developing a healthy amount of saliva, then spat. A gust of wind took it, splattering it on the wet cobbles to his left. He nodded and headed that direction. The walls of the buildings on either side of the avenue stood as tall as before but, with the path being wider, it offered less shelter from the rain. Fat drops pattered on his armor, ran down his face. The former queen’s guard did his best to ignore the inconvenience, occasionally wiping water from his eyes or off the end of his nose or chin. Where is the damn boulevard? As he walked, he began thinking about his plan—people needed to know what had happened to the king. If he told the truth about Ishla committing regicide to save her lover, it might net him a reward and the appreciation of the king’s council, but what about after? Surely they’d sentence Trenan to death, and he doubted they’d allow her to continue ruling. No, they’d throw her in the dungeon, at the very least, or relieve her of her head, too. After that, he’d prove the boy illegitimate, with no right to the throne. And with his sister dead, who’d rule the kingdom? He didn’t so much as glance at any of the doors he passed, worried for what he might find. It had turned out Ikkundana wasn’t the City of the Sick he’d thought it, but he doubted the stories lacked roots in truth. Soon, he arrived at another intersection, this street of similar size to the current one he traversed. He summoned a second mouthful of spit; this time, it flew straight, so he continued on. With the king dead, the queen disgraced, and the royal children deceased or not royal at all, many people would seek to place the crown on their heads. Council members, generals, merchants, the list was virtually endless. Whoever ended up on the throne may not understand Dansil’s value. In fact, if he’d been the one to tell of what truly happened to Erral, a new monarch might see him as a threat, someone untrustworthy. Then what would happen to him? Jail? Exile? Torture? Death? Dansil stopped in the middle of the avenue, scratched his jaw. He looked over his shoulder at the empty street, then back the way he

headed. It also stood empty. Could everyone either be fighting fires or engaged in battle? Didn’t seem likely. He shrugged and carried on. What if they think Trenan killed the king? Dansil nodded to himself as he reached another intersection, spat, took the right-hand path. Now he was onto something. The master swordsman would do anything to protect the woman he loved, so he’d accept blame. Doing so would provide the revenge the former queen’s guard wanted. Somehow, though, he also had to make sure Ishla stayed quiet. The boy. Of course! He’d promise to keep hushed about her son’s true lineage—at least for the time being. To ensure his safety, she’d have to denounce Trenan and punish him for his crime. The dungeon or banishment weren’t severe enough penalties for the murder of a king. Law decreed the loss of his head. And then she’d marry Dansil, making him prince consort, and name him general of the army, or have her ugly truths revealed. I’d be the most powerful man in the kingdom. He stopped again, let a smile slide across his lips. The key to the plan was to make sure his story got out and believed before Trenan and Ishla had any chance to give their version. He started out, increasing his pace to a trot. Time, it turned out, was of the essence. At the next intersection, he went left without bothering to spit. Nothing looked familiar, but he felt guided, as though having his plan solidified in his head gave him both purpose and direction. His boots splashed on the wet cobbles, each step caring him closer to his destiny. When this began, the night he saw the queen leaving Trenan’s chamber, he never imagined he’d end up ruling the kingdom. Yet here he found himself. Left. Right. Right. Another left. The intersections came more frequently, demanding him to make decision after decision. He stopped in the middle of one and turned a circle, head lifted as he looked up at the sky. Thick cloud hid anything with a chance of giving him a hint about direction. Without the sun and with the high walls around him, he’d lost all sense of the points of the compass. He cursed, spat. The line of spittle dangled from his lip, stretched out and touched his chin, the front of his armor. He wiped it away on his forearm and continued straight ahead. This lane narrowed, snaked right, then left, then right. For the first time, he suspected he might have chosen the wrong direction. At the next intersection, he’d right himself, get on the correct path. The boulevard must be near. But no more intersections presented themselves. Two more turns later—enough he should have ended up where he’d started, he

thought—the lane came to an abrupt halt. An ancient wooden door set with a rusted metal ring dominated the wall ending the street while no openings of any kind lay on the walls to either side. Dansil stopped short, heart beating quicker in his chest. He stared at the portal for a moment, then spun on his boot heel to face toward where he’d come from. The lane ended in a blank wall. “Impossible,” he said aloud, the stone barriers surrounding him, deadening the sound of his voice. He walked the three strides to the end with no right to be there, set his hand upon it, pushed against it. It refused to move. He leaned closer, examining it, ran his fingers along the corner where front wall met sides. “A trap,” he muttered. An unseen mechanical device must have slid the wall into place on his passing. How it did so without his notice, he didn’t know. Could it have been so silent? Or was he so lost in his plan, he forgot to pay attention? At any rate, it was an entrapment laid by the city builders, not set out for him; he’d stumbled into it. With a sigh, he put his shoulder against it, pushed with all his weight. He grunted. His boots slipped on the wet cobbles. It refused to budge. He gave up his attempt, stood straight, cleared his nose and spat the resulting contents of his mouth at the smooth, gray surface. The sputum splattered against the stone and commenced a slow, inexorable slide toward the ground. “The door it is.” He turned his back on the sagging glob of mucus, facing the portal. Its weathered wood was nearly the same color as the walls surrounding it, the iron ring so caked in rust, he worried it may fall to flakes of red dust in his fingers when he grabbed it. He crossed the small space to it, halting less than an arm’s length away. Without reason, the rate of his heart increased, the sound of its pulse beating in his ears. Ran rain into his eyes, blurring his vision and, for an instant, the ancient door smeared and became a gaping maw of a hideous beast. He hastily wiped his arm across his face and the doorway returned to itself. “Soon I’ll spend my days commanding the army, making decisions to better the kingdom, and my nights fucking the queen. Nothing for me to be afraid of.” He shuffled from one foot to the other, scratched his jaw. “Someone in here will direct me, show me the way to the boulevard, the path to my destiny.” He grasped the iron ring and a few flakes of rust came off on his palm, but the handle did not fall to pieces at his touch. The door opened smoothly with the sound of hinges used to opening, despite

their appearance. Dansil hesitated, peering in. A hallway with stone walls and floor, free of any decor or covering, dimly lit, though he saw no torches, nor sconces to hold them. He put one foot across the threshold, holding his breath. “Hello?” His voice trailed away down the corridor, bouncing from wall to wall, but no answer came. With no other choice, he stepped through the doorway. “Hello?” The door swung shut behind him, moved by another hidden mechanism working as quietly as the one which had blocked him into the alley. He spun around, intending to grasp the ring and open the door to relieve the sudden onset of claustrophobia, but he found no such handle to grab. His fist thumped against the old wood, rainwater spattering from his sleeve. One thing he had to concede: whoever had designed this trap did a fine job. “No choice, I guess,” he said, and turned to the hall. The dim glow hadn’t changed with the closing of the door; somewhere ahead, he heard water dripping, as though rain squeezed through cracks and found its way through the stone. He sighed and started along the corridor, footsteps echoing, announcing his presence whether he liked it or not. “I’ll be like a king,” he muttered. The hallway ran straight and curiously free of doors or alcoves. Whoever had designed the fortress of Ikkundana had done a magnificent job with their traps and mechanisms, but lacked in their efficient use of space. How could so many roads and corridors run so far with so few methods of ingress and egress? “When the power is mine, this place will come down.” The farther he went, the faster he walked. With no doors to either side, the need for care became minimal. The only way someone might sneak up on him was from front or rear, so he glanced over his shoulder periodically, saw nothing more than stone walls stretching out behind him. He laid his hand on the hilt of his sword, anyway, its rough grip giving him a sense of ease. Ahead, the light changed. He slowed, gripped the weapon tighter. It took him a moment to realize it wasn’t a change in the light. Instead, the hallway opened into a room. He sneaked up to the doorless access, peaked around the edge into the room. A dozen beds lined the chamber, six on each side wall with their heads pushed tight against the stone. Rusted frames, mattresses sagging in the middles, but no coverings or pillows of any kind. Otherwise, the room lay empty; light shone in through another doorway on the opposite wall.

Dansil entered, stepping with care. At the first bed, he bent at the waist and peered underneath. Nothing but cobwebs and dust. He straightened again, glanced behind him to make sure no one followed him along the hallway, only to find no hallway to glance down. Where once had been a doorway, now stood a plain gray wall. “Fucking traps.” He resisted the urge to approach the place where the portal had been, to test the wall. If he found a way through, where would it take him? Down a hall to a door without a handle. No, with no point backtracking, he had to continue. He gave the underside of each of the beds a cursory glance before passing through the doorway into an eerily familiar featureless corridor, this one not as long as the last. Not far along, he saw it opened on yet another chamber, though he couldn’t see into it from where he stood. The source of the increased light, with torches flickering within. And sound. The snap and crackle of a fire burning in a hearth, the drip of water he’d heard before, the muted rustle of cloth. Finally. Someone to tell me the way. Excited to get out of this place and on with his plan, the former queen’s guard gripped the hilt of his sword as a good soldier always did when entering the unknown, and hurried through the doorway into the chamber. The light brightened within as torches lined the walls and a brazier burned in one corner. The collected fires made the space not only brighter, but much warmer, too, and sweat broke out on his brow almost immediately upon crossing the threshold. Torch soot colored the ceiling black, the tendrils of smoke getting trapped against its stone surface before snaking to a hole in the center which presumably vented to the outside of the building. This he noticed in the three strides he took into the room before he stopped, his gait halted by the other contents of the chamber. The area was larger than the previous, providing space for more beds—twenty of them, at least, he thought without taking the time to count. He didn’t want to count, because each of them was full except for the last one on the left. Women old and young, large and small, sprawled on the thin mattresses. He saw some bundled up in blankets as though keeping away a winter chill. Others lay naked, covers thrown off and their withered skin and weeping sores exposed for all to see. He sucked a startled breath and regretted doing so immediately as the odor of the room found its way to him: piss and shit and puke and sweat. The stink of the ill. Panic welled in his chest, flowing in like rainwater filling a hole dug in the ground. A woman in the line of beds to his right groaned, a

sad and pathetic sound confirming what he suspected. Another raised her hand, arm shaking with the effort, her slack skin shivering with the movement. “Help me,” she croaked, her voice reduced to a creak more appropriate from an ancient rocking chair than a person. Dansil faded half a step, the soles of his boots sliding along the smooth floor. His mouth fell open in disbelief and he snapped it shut, worried whatever had brought these women to this place, to this state, might get into his body if he left it gaping. He readied himself to flee, unsure what he’d do when he got to the room with no way out or, if he made it past, to the door with no handle. The muscles in his legs bunched, but he found it difficult to take his gaze from the patients, their boils and fevers, their pus and their sweat. A quiet noise behind him—the gentle scrape of a soft leather sole on stone floor—caused him to spring deeper into the room. He spun around, trying to pull his sword from its scabbard, but it refused to move after the first three fingers of steel came free. The trio of women clad in red robes regarded him with kind, concerned expressions. “Hello,” the one standing ahead of the other two said. “We are never happy to have newcomers, but we will make you welcome and comfortable.” “And so unusual to see a man,” another added. Their calm voices rang with melodious tones. “Comfortable?” Dansil repeated, shaking his head. “No. This is a mistake. I’m trying to find my way to the boulevard.” He thought about telling them of Trenan killing the king, setting his plan in motion, but the color of their robes suggested these women cared nothing for the machinations of the world outside the walls. “Mistake? Oh no, child,” the third woman said, her tone as pleasant and comforting as the first two. “Goddess makes no mistakes. She sent you here because you are ill. This is Ikkundana, the City of the Sick.” Sweat rolled off his forehead, along his temple and the bridge of his nose. He let go of the sword’s hilt—it declined to come free anyway— and wiped perspiration away on the sleeve of his jerkin. His heart beat hard against his ribs and he tried to breathe deep to control it, but his lungs refused to fill to their capacity. His attempts at breathing turned to shallow pants. “See, child? Your body burns with fever; the color of your cheeks and the sweat upon them tells us. You are in the place you need to be.” “You are a danger to others,” the first woman who’d spoken agreed. “We will take care of you, along with our sisters. Strange Goddess has sent a man, but you must be someone important to her cause.” “No. I have to get out of here.”

“You can’t. There is nowhere to go.” The three women parted. Behind them, where he should have seen a doorway opening on a hall leading to a chamber with no way out, lay nothing but blank, featureless stone. “No,” Dansil whispered. He did his best to suppress a shiver and failed miserably, his teeth chattering with it. Sweat ran down his neck, soaking his undergarments. He coughed into his hand, stared at the slimy green mucus left behind on his palm. He looked at the three women again. “No.” “Sorry, child,” the nearest one said. She stepped forward, reached out and rested her touch on his shoulder. “Luckily, we have recently had a bed come open.” She applied pressure against him, prompting him to turn, and he let her guide him. As they marched slowly down the aisle between the lines of beds, a fatigue he hadn’t noticed before settled into his limbs. It weighed on him, made the mattress for which he was destined seem so far away. The women sensed his struggle; they stopped him, removed his sword belt and armor, stripped him to his underclothes. The shirt stuck to his chest and spine, plastered in place with sweat. He looked down at himself, his stomach roiling now, threatening to return his last meal to the world. “What’s wrong with me?” “We’ve got you,” a woman said. He didn’t know which one, nor did he care. Someone groaned; a long, low sound reserved for those in excruciating pain without the ability to properly express it. He thought to seek the source as the women guided him again, but his eyelids became heavy. His chin drooped to his chest and his knees threatened to buckle. “Almost there,” one said, her tone soothing. They made their way past the beds to the last bunk on the left, the lone empty mattress he was lucky had recently come free. The gray blanket on top of it looked rough, the type to scratch at any spot of bare skin. It was pulled down to reveal the sheet beneath. It had been white once, he supposed, but those days lay in the distant past. The yellow of old sweat discolored the cloth, a brown stain as likely blood as shit or vomit drew a broad island across the woven map. Had he been in better health, he’d have refused to set himself upon it, but he didn’t. His legs no longer wanted to hold him. Dansil collapsed on the mattress, the frame creaking and groaning under his weight. Without the three of them directing him, he’d likely have ended up on the floor, peeking at the cobwebs under the bed, or with his head resting in the honey pot. They helped him maneuver his way onto his back, staring up at the soot-stained ceiling. Two of the

women left, leaving the third crouching at his side. She took a wet cloth from somewhere unseen and rubbed it across his forehead. The cool water felt blissful as it ran along the curves of his face. With an effort, he opened his eyes and levered his gaze toward her. She blocked his view of the torch mounted on the wall behind her, but its glow gave her the aspect of an angel. She smiled at him, comforting, knowing. “I’m meant to be king,” he said, his own voice little more than the croak of the woman who’d begged him for help. “Of course you are, child. You are a great man, I’m sure. But illness makes us all equal, I’m afraid.” She wiped his head again. “Don’t worry, though. We’ll take care of you until Goddess comes for you.” Dansil closed his eyes. He thought about his plans to blame Trenan and blackmail the queen, to seize power for himself, and silently offered all of it up to whoever could take away the pain.

XXVII Teryk – Awake Teryk awoke in the dark, confused and in pain. He didn’t move at first, staring at what he presumed to be a ceiling above him, though the darkness hid any feature to prove it. The hard and narrow mattress pressed uncomfortably against his spine, unlike the one in his bedchamber. Where am I? What happened? He began sorting through recollections, but stopped when the memory of sinking a dagger into his sister’s neck replayed itself over and over. His mind got stuck on the single thought and moved no further. He abandoned the attempt and returned his attention to the unfamiliar room. His eyes became accustomed to the darkness, found a sliver of moonlight shining through a slit in the wall. A shift in his position sent dull pain across the top of his chest, and he clenched his jaw to keep from crying out. Without knowing where he was, or who might be near, making noise would be a poor idea. Instead of moving his body, he settled for turning his head, though this also caused considerable discomfort. The change in perspective gave him little more in the way of clues, so he remained still, held his breath. He detected a small sound—the gentle inhalation and exhalation of a person deep in slumber. Darkness made it difficult to determine from what direction the breathing emanated; he concentrated, squinted. After a short time, he realized a shape in the corner, slumped in a chair. Not large, so likely not a soldier guarding him. Perhaps someone left to care for him. Evalal. The name tumbled into his mind, no face or understanding attached to it, but with it came the surety it belonged to the person slumbering nearby. He saw her better now—young and wearing a robe of the Goddess’ order. Seeing her garb brought more memories. This is Ikkundana. An answer to at least a portion of the where, if not the specific of the chamber; the more important question of what had happened to put him here remained a mystery. He laid his head on the thin pillow, let out a quiet breath. The pain persisted, a dull throb through his shoulder and across his chest, up his neck and along his side. The quality of it made him suspect someone had given him something to numb the hurt; if it pained him this much with the aid of some poultice or potion—or both—he shuddered to imagine how severe it might be without the ministrations. He recalled arriving at the fortress. Trenan had been in a bad way, cursed with visions of the dead and unable to fight or protect himself.

Teryk vaguely recollected having to defend him. But then what? He closed his eyes, listening to the gentle rhythm of the girl’s breathing, hoping for it to soothe his mind enough for memory to return. Balls of fire crashing to the ground; Yoli and Osis; a clutch of tents in flames. More and more came to him, yet nothing to explain his current predicament. He clamped his jaw tight, let out a frustrated breath through his nose, louder than he intended. A shuffle of cloth answered and his eyelids popped open. He lay unmoving, holding his air, and waited to see if it repeated. Evalal shifting in her chair? Or something else making the sound? Another moment of waiting and a second noise found him—the distinct scuff of a leather sole on stone floor. He turned his head, looking toward the spot where his keeper sat. From what he made out, she hadn’t moved. He stared at her, watching. When the shuffle happened again, it clearly didn’t come from her. Teryk shifted his gaze to the other side of the room, to the robed and cowled figure standing in the corner. The healer! His heart leapt to a rapid pace and his body jerked, attempting to bring him to an upright position. But he lacked an essential piece to accomplish his goal: an arm. He crashed to the mattress, agony erupting through him as recollection exploded through his mind: the king, his axe, the threat to Trenan’s life, his own sacrifice to save his father. Teryk cried out, as much from the memory as from the physical pain. His feet pushed against the bed, bunching the blanket atop him in his desperate attempt to get away from the unholy robed creature as it approached his bedside. The torment caused by his wound flashed light in front of his eyes, blinding him to the monster’s advance until long, pale fingers touched his shoulder where his arm used to be. The discomfort died with it, clearing his vision and enabling him to see as the thing reached up with its free hand and lowered its hood. Teryk closed his eyelids and turned his face away, the muscles in his neck tight with the effort. He waited for searing pain to emanate from its touch as it stole another part of him to get whatever it wanted. The healer didn’t take my arm. He gritted his teeth, body quivering with morbid anticipation. His mind flashed to a time when the thing stood before him, robe open to reveal its hairless, genderless self. He considered Stirk, the man who gave his limbs and so much more for the healer to achieve its goals. His mouth filled with fearful saliva, and he swallowed it around a lump in his throat as he awaited his end at the monster’s hand. “Teryk.” The voice was not what he’d expected, but one he knew better than

any other, save his own. One he couldn’t possibly be hearing. A trick. Maybe so, but he opened his lids anyway, faced the robed thing standing beside him. The sliver of moonlight finding its way into the room fell across her, and he realized he shouldn’t recognize her. Short hair he suspected should be speckled with gray based on the lines at the corners of her mouth. She wore a peaceful expression tinted with concern, caring, but he didn’t know her. Except for the eyes. He’d peered into them more times than he could count, more than he’d looked in any others, but they didn’t belong in this face. “Danya?” he ventured, skeptical. The head with closely cropped, graying hair that wasn’t Danya’s nodded. A smile crossed the woman’s lips and, though the mouth didn’t belong to his sister, he saw the tilt of it did. “You’re alive.” A statement; a hesitant question. “No,” she said, the smile remaining. “Not in the way you mean. I am here.” The woman raised her free hand and put her palm flat against her chest, over her heart. “But who…?” “Ailyssa. The Barren Mother. Now the Mother of Death.” Teryk shuddered at her words. Was this someone come to take him from the world of the living? She must have sensed the quake through her touch on his shoulder, because she responded as though he’d asked a question. “You are safe, my dear brother. Your injury will heal, your life will go on. Oh, and what a life!” He stared up at his sister’s eyes regarding him from a stranger’s face, and tears threatened at the corners of his own. His mind flashed the memory of the knife entering her throat again, her blood pouring from the wound, her skin turning pale. He inhaled a halting breath to compose himself. It took another after to enable him to speak. “But it will be a life without you.” He looked away, a tear spilling along his face, finding its way to wet his pillow. “I killed you.” “That’s why I am here.” Teryk turned toward her, expecting her expression to have changed. He expected to find anger, hatred, revenge. Instead, he found love. “I don’t understand.” He moved to wipe wetness from his cheek with his left arm, realized it didn’t exist. The gesture would have given him extreme pain if not for her touch laid upon him. He adjusted and wiped them away with the other hand. “You did what Goddess required of you, what the kingdom needed.

You had little choice in the matter.” His lips pressed together, turning them into a thin line, and he shook his head. “No. I—” “Shh.” She leaned closer, put her palm on his cheek. “I understand this knowledge will not free you from what happened, Teryk. Your love for me is greater than that. That is not why I came.” He felt the beat of his heart in the veins of his neck and temple, the force of it threatening to shake his vision, but her touch on his face settled him. She leaned in closer, put her dry lips against his forehead damp with perspiration, and kissed him. “I forgive you.” He couldn’t deny the tears any longer. They burst forth from him along with a sob from his tortured throat. He threw his one arm around her, an action which should have sent him tumbling, but she caught him, pulled him toward her. They embraced, his body shuddering, her touch on his shoulder quelling his physical pain, her hand on his back seeking to do the same for his emotional distress. He buried his face against her, crying and snuffling for what felt a long time until his torment waned. As it did, she leaned away, rested him gently on the mattress. Hesitant, he let her go. “Will I see you again?” She smiled. “Of course. Whenever you wish.” She removed her hand from his shoulder and the pain crept in like thick honey flowing from an overturned jar. He did his best to ignore it as she made her way across the room to the corner where she had begun. “Danya?” The unfamiliar woman with the familiar eyes faced him, one eyebrow raised. “I love you.” “And I you, brother. You are forever in my heart.” He smiled at her, a sad smile, then closed his eyes to squeeze the last of the tears from them. When he opened them again, she’d disappeared, the corner of the room as empty as it should have been. He lay on the mattress, staring at the ceiling. Now when he thought of her, it wasn’t the knife and the blood appearing in his mind, but adventures and fun, all the good times they’d shared. And pride. Together, we saved the kingdom. He sighed heavily. “Teryk? Are you awake?” The voice came from the chair where Evalal stirred, sitting up. He considered asking if she’d seen the Mother of Death, but he knew she hadn’t—she’d been asleep. He doubted she’d have known the woman’s presence if she’d stood beside him while it happened.

“I am,” he replied. She got up and crossed the room to the side of the bed. “I’m—” “Evalal,” he finished for her. “You’re here to take care of me.” She nodded. If it surprised her he knew these facts, she gave no sign. This was so often the way of the followers of the Goddess— acceptance, faith. Perhaps he might find these attributes for himself now. “Are you all right?” Her gaze dropped to the bandage on his shoulder. It hurt—he suspected it likely to do so for a very long time, sometimes badly, other times less. At the moment, the pain was bearable, partially because his heart and soul had settled in a way they hadn’t in longer than he could recall. “I think I am,” he said, turning to her and offering a weak smile. “I think I am.”

XXVIII Horace – The Sea The sea weren’t no flat mirror what reflected the sky and the sun’s heat on this day. A cool wind blew in from somewhere on the vast ocean, stirring the water’s lappin’ waves, shiftin’ the gray clouds o’erhead, and bringin’ hard bumps to Horace’s skin. He pulled his coat closed o’er his chest and continued starin’ out at his salty mistress, lookin’ past His Majesty’s ships bobbin’ by the dock. A deep breath filled his nose with tangy brine and the sharp odor o’ the sticky oil they used to treat the wood. Gulls circled and wheeled, occasionally adding their white paint to decks and wharf; one dropped its cargo a couple paces away with a wet plop as it hit the timbers. “Shitbirds,” the ol’ sailor muttered. Familiar sights and sounds. Ones what, not so long ago—not long if measured by season, but an eternity in his mind—he’d hoped to never find himself partakin’ in again. After survivin’ gettin’ dunked in the ocean with the God o’ the Deep, he swore to give up his life before settin’ boots on a deck’s creakin’ boards. It didn’t take too much time with his feet on dry ground to reconsider. How things change. He dug his fingers into his front pocket and pulled out the pipe he’d tucked away in it when he left this mornin’. It’d been a long while since he held it with the intent o’ smokin’, its worn-smooth surface both familiar and foreign against his palm. He contemplated it, scratched at his beard along his jawline with the other hand while tryin’ to remember the last time he’d packed a bowl full o’ tobacco and inhaled the smoke into his lungs. Sometime before Dunal’d shoved him in the drink. The memory o’ the deckhand took any joy he might’ve got from puffin’ right outta him like the wind dyin’ upon a sail. He bounced the pipe in his hand, then flicked his wrist and sent it o’er the wharf’s edge, ploppin’ in the sea and disappearin’ beneath the modest waves. “It’s a proud day, Horace Seaman.” “Fuck me dead,” he whispered, startled by the unexpected words from a person what he didn’t expect to be standin’ behind him. The ol’ sailor turned to see the group o’ folk gathered to send him off. He should’ve heard them approachin’, but his thoughts might as well’ve been fingers stuck in his ears. Each stood wearin’ smiles and, though he didn’t feel up to havin’ one o’ his own, he forced his mouth to curve up at both ends ’cause he liked these people. “I guess so, yer Majesty.” “Of course it is,” Teryk said. He took a few steps forward and put his hand on the ol’ sailor’s shoulder, his other sleeve hangin’ loose and empty at his side. What little light squeezed through the clouds

glinted on the gold ringlet he wore on his head, and on the polished pommel of the crownsword hangin’ at his hip. “If ever a man deserved to command the flagship of my fleet, it’s you.” Despite his trepidation, Horace’s cheeks got warm. “Well, I thank you for your confidence. And for not temptin’ fate when you named her.” “No Devil of the Deep this time,” Trenan said. His opposite sleeve from Teryk’s hung by his side, makin’ them look like a set o’ livin’ bookends. “You will be the first captain of the Princess Danya.” Teryk rejoined the others and the ol’ sailor looked at them standin’ together. Ishla held onto Trenan’s arm, her expression contented, but with a hint o’ sadness hidden away underneath, and he understood why; havin’ lost a child himself, he knew the pain she kept stashed from the world. And congregatin’ in front o’ the boat what bore her daughter’s name likely did nothin’ to help matters. Ailyssa stood beside the queen, arms folded o’er top o’ a pregnant belly the thick, gray cloak couldn’t hide, and Evalal to the other side o’ King Teryk. A mess o’ soldiers assembled behind them, Osis and Yoli amongst them; Horace recognized they’d come to watch out for the royalty, not to see him off, but it pleased him to gaze upon their faces, anyway. The former sergeant—general now, and next in charge after Commander Trenan—appeared nearly all healed up. He didn’t expect the soldier’d ever have full use o’ the one leg, but what did he know? He were a sailor, not a doctor. Seems ocean water runs in my veins. Yoli looked as uncomfortable as always bein’ around so many what each possessed a cock. He figured she’d never get used to the company o’ men, but a proper warrior like her’d make it work. With her watchin’ out for the queen, neither Ishla nor any what came after’d need no shitty guard again. Seein’ them gathered in this way put a pain in Horace’s chest, a tightenin’ what he struggled to keep control of. The urge to turn away, ponder the sea’s vastness, get right aboard his ship and get going’ threatened to overtake him, but he resisted. Maybe it hinted at why he’d spent so many turns o’ the seasons on the deck o’ one ship or another. Might be he shared more in common with the waves than with other people. Ailyssa must’ve spotted the look in his eye, for she separated from the others and stepped forward, crossin’ the space between them with a waddlin’ gait what made him want to chuckle. Her hair’d grown in more, streaks o’ gray by her temples he’d’ve guessed she didn’t have the last time her hair were longer. She sported wrinkles around her eyes when she smiled what’d escaped his notice before. Mind, he hadn’t gotten to see her smile too often before, neither. She stopped in

front of him, far enough away not to prod him with her belly, and laid her hand on his whiskered cheek. “We are here because of you,” she said, keepin’ her voice loud enough for him to hear, but quieted so her words stayed mostly between them. “Without you, the kingdom wouldn’t have survived.” “Weren’t nothin’ I did, Ail…Mother o’ Death.” She smiled and shook her head. “I am always Ailyssa to you, no matter where or who we are. And your humility be damned; Danya and I couldn’t have done our part if you’d failed in yours.” Right before him, her eye color changed from brown to blue. Appeared some o’ them wrinkles might’ve eased up, too, and a younger woman peeked out at him from the same face. “No one will ever forget what you did,” a slightly different voice said from the same mouth. Then she became Ailyssa again. Not quite the same person he’d helped keep from gettin’ ate in a forest behind the veil—there were a lot more to her now, and not just the belly full o’ child. He felt he should say somethin’ to her—both to the Mother o’ Death, and the princess hidden inside her—but she didn’t want him to. Plus, he suspected if he tried speakin’ right then, he’d find himself chokin’ on the words. He gave her a brief thankful nod instead. The two-women-in-one rejoined the group, and they stood lookin’ at each other for a bit, nobody sayin’ anythin’. It lasted long enough to start bein’ uncomfortable, so Horace put an end to it. “Guess I should make sure the boys’ve got ev’rythin’ ready to go.” He bent at the waist, snagged his duffel’s strap, and pulled it up onto his shoulder. Its weight gave him a little discomfort, despite the time what’d passed for him to recover. He imagined a bunch o’ those unfamiliar aches and pains weren’t never going to leave. “When will you return?” Evalal asked. “Hmm. We’ll be gone for a while. End o’ next season, maybe, dependin’ what we find.” He swallowed hard, felt the lump in his throat rise and fall with it. If he spoke the whole truth, he’d’ve been tellin’ them how his nerves played havoc with him about gettin’ out on the sea. He might explain how many other things he’d rather be doin’, but he couldn’t stay put on land after ev’rythin’ what’d happened. Not after losin’ Rilum. And Thorn. And Ivy. Not after what he’d done to Dunal and anyone else he hurt on the field o’ battle. Hurtin’ people didn’t sit so well with him, turned out. “The best chamber in the castle awaits your return, Horace Seaman,” Teryk said. “We are ever indebted to you. The kingdom is grateful.” The ol’ sailor thought the prince’d taken to the idea o’ bein’ king

like a baby bird to the sky. Course, he had Ishla and Trenan to guide him—and he’d need it since his father hadn’t left Windward in the best shape. Either way, he hoped for the lad to prosper at it. He nodded again, then raised his free hand and gave a hesitant wave. Instead o’ waitin’ for them to return the gesture, he pivoted on the heel o’ his new boot and started along the wharf toward the gangway. His footwear—made by the finest shoemaker in the Horseshoe— clomped on the wood, leather pinchin’ the little toes on both feet. Once they got worked in, they’d be more comfortable, but it were always a challenge gettin’ to that point. With his own choice, he might’ve still worn his old boots, but their condition had usurped the decision from him. He mounted the gangway, the tromp of hard soles turnin’ lighter on the thinner wood with space between it and the water. His eyes stayed down, watchin’ his steps, though he’d trod more gangways’n most knew existed. Truth told, he didn’t want to glance o’er and see the group o’ them regardin’ him because he feared he might lose his nerve. Too late to turn back now, but he suspected if he did, the new king’d make it work. Easier not to look. He stepped onto the deck, the all-too-familiar smell o’ tarred wood so strong it hid the tang o’ the briny sea itself. Ev’ry ship bore the same odor, but this marked the first occasion he’d been on a boat for its maiden voyage. Its pungency made sense—not enough boots trod upon, water washed against it, nor wind whistlin’ o’er it to make it fade. Such’d happen with time. Maybe by our return. If we make it home. A man stepped up and took Horace’s duffel from his shoulder. As unused to being in charge as he were—bein’ first man’d carried lots o’ responsibilities, but nothin’ like those o’ a captain—he refused to let it go at first. He held onto the strap with one hand as the fellow tugged gently. “I’ll stow this in your quarters if you want, Cap’n.” The man waited, a chill wind stirring the shrubbery of whiskers on his cheeks. After a short time starin’ at the feller, Horace relinquished his hold with a nod. The deckhand scurried off, leavin’ the ol’ sailor on his own again. Cap’n. He turned the word o’er in his head as he directed his feet to his right, ignorin’ the bustle o’ activity around him. Checkin’ on his boys were his excuse for gettin’ away before he got choked up with goodbyes, but it weren’t somethin’ what needed doin’; a good crew practically took care o’ itself. All what they required from a captain were tellin’ them when to do things and makin’ decisions when

decisions became necessary. Course, might be some chart readin’ and actions o’ similar ilk, too, but even a first man knew how to navigate. Thing were, with this voyage, he’d likely have more choices to make than normal. And hard ones, at that. Horace mounted the stairs leadin’ up to the foredeck, his cheeks simultaneously warmed by the sun and chilled by the wind. He crossed the deck, stoppin’ when he got to the steps leading to the privy gallery, and peeked o’er his shoulder, though he told himself he shouldn’t. They stood where he’d left them, ev’ry one o’ them, and the group o’ soldiers led by Osis and Yoli behind them. He considered raisin’ his hand, givin’ them a last wave, but decided against it. It were better for them that way, he figured. Ev’ryone he’d ever cared for’d ended up dead, so if he kept hidden from the world how much they meant to him, they might live to see more’n more days. They each deserved it; they’d been through so much. He faced the bow o’ the ship—his ship—again, hand restin’ on the latch holdin’ closed the gate at the top o’ the stairs leadin’ to the privy gallery. A deep sigh found its way in through his nose, the briny scent more noticeable now. He flipped the catch, opened the gate, and descended to the first step. He placed his fingers on the bowsprit’s smooth wood where it rose from the deck beside the stairway, touch trailin’ o’er it as his boot heels thumped on the wooden steps. The ol’ sailor got to the bottom and didn’t stop movin’. He headed to the front, restin’ both palms on the railin’ and leanin’ forward into the breeze blowin’ at his face. Under a clear sky, the bowsprit’s shadow might’ve fallen across where he stood, dependin’ on the time o’ day, but not today. The wind danced upon the sea like a playful child, its pulse and heartbeat marked by ev’ry wave and ripple. At the distant horizon, the sky and ocean connected, a single entity o’ matchin’ colors, the water’s undulations the lone thing separatin’ one from th’other. More gulls’n Horace’d ever seen at once wheeled o’erhead, as if someone’d tipped off the bastards about a fresh deck awaitin’ their contributions. “Shitbirds,” he muttered. Horace Seaman, captain o’ His Majesty’s Ship Princess Danya, stared out across the dull and dimpled sea, watchin’ it stretch to the horizon and prob’ly well beyond, lookin’ similar to a metal sheet what a smith’s hammer’d struck too many times. A gust o’ chill wind tugged at his coat, so he took one hand from the railin’ and pulled it tighter against the cold. Last time he’d stood a deck, he’d near sweat his balls off and wished to see a wave. And then he’d spied the feller in the water, and afterward it all started. He shivered. On that day, the God o’ the Deep’d been nothin’ but a sailor’s tale— one half-believed by him, same as any other sailor. Until he met the

beast face to face. Doin’ so made him the only man what’d seen the creature and lived to talk about it, though he never did. Even thinkin’ on it now caused his pecker to shrink and set his porthole clenchin’. But if the tales o’ the God was true, then it might be Prince Teryk— King Teryk, he corrected himself—were right about others bein’ accurate, too. Maybe he knew and had an inklin’ about what lay beyond the ragged line o’ horizon. Problem were makin’ it all the way to the place, never mind returnin’, too. He sighed again, reflected on Rilum. If ever a time’d been he’d wanted to have his son by his side, now were it. Cap’n Seaman and First Man Seaman possessed a ring what put a grin on his face and squeezed his heart in a fist all at once. Never been, never goin’ to be. As usual, thinkin’ about his boy recalled to his mind Thorn and Ivy, too, and the smile slipped away. He realized their sacrifices was necessary, and they’d done it willingly—and both’d do it again—but knowin’ did nothin’ to ease the pain o’ losin’ them. He sometimes suspected all three remained inside him. Not like the princess lived in Ailyssa, but their memories, at least. None o’ them pointed fingers at him o’er their deaths, but he couldn’t help but point one at himself. It’s for the best. Without him, everyone he cared for’d be safer, live longer lives, find more happiness. He didn’t begrudge them that. Maybe he’d see them again some day; if so, weren’t no guessin’ when it might be. Longer’n a short while, less than forever. Not much of an estimation, but who could expect better when you’re headed to a place what, not so long ago, you didn’t even believe real.
